News.title: Brantham missing boy - latest: Desperate search for Noah, 3, who 'won't respond to his name'
News.content:
Suffolk Police say Noah Woods, who is undergoing treatment for autism, became separated from a relative at a playground

Brantham missing boy - latest: Desperate search for Noah, 3, who 'won't respond to his name'

A massive search operation to find a missing three-year-old Suffolk boy who is non-verbal has entered its second day.

Noah Woods was last seen at approximately 3pm yesterday afternoon (Tuesday) when he became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in Merriam Close, Brantham.

More than 100 people joined the search yesterday evening with Suffolk Police asking residents in the area to check gardens, sheds and outbuildings.

Noah is described as white, with curly ginger hair. He was last seen wearing a white Bluey T-shirt, shorts and black Vans trainers with a white stripe. He is also described as non-verbal, has partial hearing loss and is currently undergoing an assessment for autism. Because of these vulnerabilities, he will not respond to his name.

News.title: Cholesterol, weight, blood sugar and blood pressure drop with one food change
News.content:
Cholesterol, weight, blood sugar and blood pressure drop with one food change

A major new study has found making one change in your diet has multiple benefits

View 3 Images A woman eating wholegrain brown rice

Eating four to six servings of wholegrain every day slashes the risk of a heart attack or stroke, suggests new research. A diet high in wholegrain food lowers body weight, cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure, according to the findings.

‌



Four to six portions corresponds to a bowl of oatmeal, a sandwich made with wholegrain bread, and a serving of brown rice, say scientists. The study, published in the European Heart Journal, brought together the results of 87 clinical trials that tested the effects of eating wholegrain food on risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

‌



The findings show that eating a diet rich in wholegrain food is likely to prevent heart disease by reducing body weight, blood pressure and the levels of cholesterol and glucose in the blood. Common wholegrain foods include brown rice, oats, whole wheat, barley, rye, quinoa, millet, and corn, as well as products made from wholegrain flour such as wholemeal bread, pasta, and cereals.

‌



View 3 Images Swap your toast for wholegrain bread

Study leader Dr Helda Tutunchi said: “Although higher wholegrain intake has long been linked to better heart health in population studies, clinical trials have produced mixed findings. This left an important practical question unanswered: how much whole grain should people eat to meaningfully improve cardiovascular health?

"To address this, we systematically combined and analysed all available randomised controlled trials to identify the amount of whole grain associated with the greatest benefits.”

‌



The analysis included more than 6,500 people from trials conducted across Europe, the United States, Canada, Asia, Australia and Brazil. It showed that eating more wholegrain reduced people’s body weight, waist circumference and blood pressure, as well as reducing the levels of total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) - known as "bad" cholesterol, in the blood.

It also lowered blood levels of triglycerides, glucose and interleukin-6 (IL-6) - a sign of inflammation. The benefits could be seen in people eating 30 to 40 grams of wholegrain per day, but the greatest benefits were found in people eating 60 to 100 grams per day - corresponding to four to six daily servings.

Dr Tutunchi, from Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Iran, said: “This is the largest and most comprehensive meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials on wholegrain intake and cardiovascular risk factors. Unlike previous reviews, we looked specifically at how much wholegrain people need to eat to get the greatest benefits.

‌



View 3 Images You need to add a wholegrain bread sandwich to your diet

"We also evaluated the certainty of the evidence and found high-certainty evidence for improvements in several outcomes, including body weight, waist circumference and total cholesterol. However, most of the trials we included were relatively short, with an average duration of about eight weeks.

"As a result, we cannot determine whether these benefits are maintained over the long term. In addition, relatively few studies evaluated very high wholegrain intakes, above 140 grams per day, so the effects at those intake levels remain uncertain.

‌



“Our findings provide a practical indication of the amount of wholegrain that may be needed to achieve meaningful improvements in cardiovascular risk factors. Increasing wholegrain intake is a relatively simple, accessible and affordable dietary strategy that can complement other lifestyle and medical interventions.

“We found that most benefits occur at intakes of approximately 60 to 100 grams per day, toward the upper end of current dietary recommendations. These findings do not necessarily call for major changes to existing guidelines, but they support public health strategies that help people increase their whole-grain intake and move toward the higher end of current targets."

Dr Tutunchi added: “One important finding is that whole grains may benefit cardiovascular health through several modest improvements acting together, rather than through one large effect on a single risk factor. We observed improvements across multiple pathways, including blood lipids, blood pressure, glucose regulation, body fat and some markers of inflammation.

‌



"Although the change in each individual risk factor was generally modest, improving several risk factors simultaneously could contribute to a greater reduction in long-term cardiovascular risk. However, the included trials did not assess cardiovascular events directly, so longer-term studies are needed to confirm this.”

Modest but meaningful

Writing in the European Heart Journal, Dr Cecilie Kyrø, from the Danish Cancer Institute, welcomed the findings. She said: “For clinicians, the message is reassuringly simple: encouraging patients to replace refined grain foods with minimally processed whole grains is likely to yield modest but meaningful improvements in body weight, waist circumference, and blood lipids, perhaps particularly in individuals with type 2 diabetes.

"At the population level, even small shifts in these markers can translate into substantial reductions in cardiometabolic events. Adding evidence from research into other disease endpoints indicates that the beneficial effects of whole- grains foods even go substantially beyond cardiometabolic disease.

Article continues below

“Current US dietary guidelines recommend two to four servings of whole grains per day within an overall pattern that emphasises ‘real food’ and reduced intake of ultra-processed products. While this is an important step in the right direction, the trial evidence indicates that higher whole-grain intakes than presently recommended in some guidelines may be optimal for cardiometabolic health."

Dr Kyrø added: “From a policy perspective, the challenge is to make minimally processed whole-grain staples accessible, affordable, and culturally acceptable, while avoiding a drift towards ultra-processed products that merely add whole grains to otherwise highly processed formulations.”

News.title: Aldi’s new £15 trainers similar to high-end £109 and £140 pairs in stores now
News.content:
Aldi’s new £15 trainers similar to high-end £109 and £140 pairs in stores now

Aldi claims the shoes 'keep you comfortable whatever the weather' on a budget

View 4 Images A crowd of shoppers visiting a branch of Aldi supermarket (Image: Getty Images)

Aldi shoppers can buy a pair of trainers on a budget as a new Special Buy has arrived across all stores. Some customers may even argue they look similar to more high-end alternatives selling for £109 and £140.

‌



The All Weather Shoes are selling for £14.99 in both navy and black, and they are marketed as unisex - for both men and women. The supermarket brand, which has roughly 1,100 stores across the UK, says each pair is made from "waterproof" material.

‌



Aldi adds that each shoe is "designed for changing seasons and everyday adventures", and that they "help keep you comfortable whatever the weather". The style shares similarities with popular brands sold at Zalando and W J French & Son at more than five-times the price.

‌



The product description continues: "Designed for changing seasons and everyday adventures, these practical shoes help keep you comfortable whatever the weather. Ideal for countryside walks, weekend outings or daily errands, they offer dependable comfort and a versatile style that pairs effortlessly with your autumn wardrobe."

It could be considered a budget alternative to the COASTVILLE Trainers selling for £84, down from £104, at Zalando. Available for men in sizes 6.5 to 12, these shoes boast an all-too-similar navy look with hints of white and brown.

View 4 Images The All Weather Shoes at Aldi (Image: Aldi)

‌



Product features - full list

Shoe tip: Round

Heel type: Flat

Fastening: Laces

Pattern: Plain

Details: Cut-outs

Extras: Reinforced heel

Outsole: Profiled

View 4 Images The COASTVILLE Trainers at Zalando (Image: Zalando)

Meanwhile, there's also the Ecco Stride Ladies Shoe at W J French & Son which is even more expensive, coming in at £140. Similarly to both the Zalando and Aldi offerings, it has a navy blue aesthetic and leather-like tone, as well as being made of waterproof material.

‌



The product description reads: "Ecco Stride is a sporty, lightweight walking shoe with soft leather uppers and a four eyelet lace for good support. Stride has breathable textile linings with GORE-TEX construction for water-proofing. The shoe has a flexible mid-sole for shock absorption and a rubber outer-sole for durability and grip."

View 4 Images The Ecco Stride Ladies Shoe at W J French & Son (Image: W J French & Son)

Yes, the Aldi shoe is very similar to both these options, but there's one huge difference and it's nothing to do with the price tag. Both shoes can be delivered straight to your front door thanks to home delivery, an amenity Aldi does not offer.

Article continues below

To avoid a wasted trip, you can check stock levels at your local Aldi using the online store finder. All you have to do is enter your postcode, and a list of local branches will appear alongside stock levels. For more information, visit the Aldi website.

News.title: UK weather maps show exact date 3C chill hits just days after 29C heatwave
News.content:
UK weather maps show exact date 3C chill hits just days after 29C heatwave

Brits can expect temperatures to plummet rapidly as cool conditions are expected just days after a scorching 29C heatwave - with lows of 3C

View 5 Images Cold temperatures are forecast across the UK at the end of the month

The UK is set to plummet into a cold snap as temperatures as low as 3C are forecast after a 29C heatwave is expected.

‌



The Met Office has forecast 'widely unsettled conditions' at the end of the month, with weather maps turning green showing cooler conditions.

‌



The chill is expected to arrive on the last day of the month, Wednesday, September 30, with areas in the North East and North West of England forecast to be the coldest.

‌



View 5 Images Weather map shows chilling 3C temperatures (Image: Netweather)

According to Netweather maps, using GFS models, at around 3am in the morning parts of Cumbria, Durham and North Yorkshire will all sit at a chilling 3C.

In Scotland, the maps show even harsher conditions as 2C is forecast for several areas.

‌



The temperature is vastly different in the south, with lows of 9C forecast in the South East and London expected to be around 11C at this time.

View 5 Images The cool temperatures come just days after a heatwave (Image: Netweather )

As the morning continues, some areas will feel a fall in temperature with much of the South East and Anglia expected to be around 7C at 6am.

‌



Cheshire is surprisingly one of the warmer areas in the UK at 10C according to the weather maps.

Again, parts of Yorkshire and Cumbria remain at a snappy 3C, with surrounding areas climbing slightly higher to 5C.

By 9am, temperatures will remain mostly unchanged across the UK.

‌



View 5 Images Temperatures will pick up slightly in the afternoon (Image: Netweather )

In Cambridgeshire, Suffolk, Norfolk and Kent lows of 7C are forecast - a stark contrast from the 29C forecast in Cambridgeshire the weekend prior.

Cornwall will be the hottest location at this time, reaching 12C.

‌



As the day continues, temperatures will increase; however, it will still remain exceptionally cooler than the sweltering conditions forecast for the last weekend of the month.

Later in the afternoon, much of England will climb to around 8C, whereas Scotland is expected to stay colder with temperatures of 4C and 5C forecast.

View 5 Images The hottest temperature of the day is forecast to be 14C according to the maps (Image: Netweather)

‌



By 9pm, it will feel much warmer than it did earlier in the day, with London the hottest city at 14C.

However, elsewhere there will still be lows of 8C.

According to the Met Office: "Many areas may remain mostly settled towards the end of September, but there is the possibility of areas of low pressure moving in from the Atlantic bringing more widely unsettled conditions."

Article continues below

The long-range forecast for September 30 to the beginning of October states: "More changeable weather may become established more widely as we move into October, though parts of the west and northwest are perhaps most likely to see wet and windy conditions at times."

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan told to ‘buy alarm clock’ instead of taxpayer-funded security
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan told to ‘buy alarm clock’ instead of taxpayer-funded security

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have changed their children's school following security concerns, but one Royal biographer has slammed the pair for citing security concerns over school run traffic

View 4 Images Meghan and Harry have pulled their two children out of school following security fears (Image: Getty Images)

The Sussexes have been told to “buy an alarm clock” instead of continuing their desperate attempts to gain taxpayer-funded security.

‌



It comes just weeks after they relocated to Britain after spending six years in California. Harry has been fronting the bill for his own personal security team after his taxpayer-funded protection was removed once he ceased to be a working member of the Royal Family in 2020.

‌



Now, with the Sussexes once again living in the UK, Harry’s fight for security is still raging on, as he continues to make appeals to the Home Office. Harry has appealed to the British government claiming he is still a target for terrorists and fixated persons when in the UK.

‌



Suffolk Police share new picture of missing boy Noah and have urgent warning for public READ MORE :

Anxious children as young as 12 to be treated at rehab clinic to get them back in school READ MORE :

View 4 Images According to Hello!, the Sussexes’ bodyguards were not able to carry out a recce of the journey in term time, and only practised it during the quieter summer holidays (Image: AP)

But now their security concerns have branched to Archie and Lilibet’s school, as the children were removed from their new school just two days into the academic year due to security fears.

It is understood that unexpected heavy traffic on the route from where they were living to the school meant a 30-minute journey turned into an hour’s journey at rush hour. And sources close to the couple claimed that sitting in traffic heightened their security fears as it left them as “sitting ducks”.

‌



One incident is said to have raised concerns when the couple and their security’s vehicles found it difficult to remain in convoy.

View 4 Images Archie and Lilibet have been pulled out of their new school (Image: Instagram/Meghan Duchess of Sussex)

Royal biographer Robert Jobson has slammed the pair for citing security concerns over school run traffic for taking their kids out of school. He told The Sun: "“I suggest they buy themselves an alarm clock, set it three quarters of an hour early and join the real world...Nobody asked him to come with his family to a country he deemed was unsafe.

‌



“Round-the-clock security for the non-working royals will cost a small fortune.”

Do you think Prince Harry & Meghan Markle get taxpayer-funded security? Take our poll below and have your say

View 4 Images Prince Harry celebrated his 42nd Birthday yesterday

‌



A family spokesperson told Hello! Magazine: “The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements.

“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family. This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”

As the Mirror revealed last month, the government department will now carry out a new Risk Management Board hearing at Harry's request, after months of appeals. It is understood the new review will look at the risks and threats to both the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Article continues below

The Mirror is not identifying the schools or the family’s location, but they are believed to be staying temporarily on a private estate owned by a friend while they search for a permanent home.

The Mirror has contacted representatives of both Harry and Meghan for comment.

News.title: Kremlin issues chilling threat to NATO capital city as top aide says it will 'cease to exist'
News.content:
Kremlin issues chilling threat to NATO capital city as top aide says it will 'cease to exist'

"If Poland enters into military action against Russia, our country will use the entire arsenal of forces and means at its disposal, and Warsaw will cease to exist within two or three days," an aide to Putin said

View 3 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Getty)

The Kremlin has said it will destroy a city in a NATO country if it enters a conflict with Russia as tensions skyrocket between the countries.

‌



Nikolai Patrushev, a top aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened to eradicate Warsaw in Poland if war with NATO broke out.

‌



Speaking to Russian news outlet Argumenty i Fakty, Patrushev said: "If Poland enters into military action against Russia, our country will use the entire arsenal of forces and means at its disposal, and Warsaw will cease to exist within two or three days."

‌



View 3 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin and top aide Nikolai Patrushev (Image: Getty Images)

His comment follow those of Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that NATO could "quite quickly" defeat Russia if Moscow attacked the alliance.

Poland joined NATO in 1999.

‌



NATO, a 32-member alliance, was formed in 1949 to counter the risk of Soviet attack.

It now focuses protecting ally counties by promising that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

Sikorski told the annual Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv: "If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly."

‌



He said that the alliance's airpower superiority over Putin's army was overwhelming, citing their 2,500 military aircraft at the alliance's disposal.

View 3 Images Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski (Image: Getty Images)

Sikorski's comments left the Kremlin fuming, with Patrushev saying they were an "amateurish assessment of our country's military might."

Article continues below

He also said that Russia was not using "their full potential" in their war against Ukraine.

However, Patrushev reiterated reassurances out of Moscow that his boss has no intention of going to war with Europe, Metro reports.

News.title: Suffolk Police share new picture of missing boy Noah and have urgent warning for public
News.content:
Suffolk Police share new picture of missing boy Noah and have urgent warning for public

Suffolk Police have confirmed missing three-year-old boy Noah is non-verbal, has partial hearing loss and is currently undergoing an assessment for autism. As a result of these vulnerabilities, he will not respond to his name

View 2 Images Noah was last seen wearing a white Bluey T-shirt, shorts and black Vans trainers with a white stripe. (Image: Suffolk Constabulary)

Suffolk Police have urged members of the public not to put themselves at risk by carrying out independent searches for missing Noah overnight.

‌



In the latest update issued shortly after 1am police confirmed Noah is described as white, with curly ginger hair. He is wearing a white Bluey T-shirt, shorts and black Vans trainers with a white stripe. He is also described as non-verbal, has partial hearing loss and is currently undergoing an assessment for autism. As a result of these vulnerabilities, he will not respond to his name.

‌



Noah was last seen at approximately 3pm yesterday afternoon, Tuesday 15 September, when he became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close. Noah is reported to have run off down the alleyway beside the playground towards the new-build housing estate.

‌



View 2 Images Noah is still missing (Image: Suffolk Police)

Police have been searching for Noah since yesterday afternoon, including specially trained officers and dog units. These searches have been assisted by helicopters from the National Police Air Service and HM Coastguard, with further support on the ground provided by HM Coastguard, Suffolk Fire & Rescue Service, Suffolk Lowland Search & Rescue and a vast number of members of the public.

Police are asking local residents to thoroughly check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings, or any potential areas where a child might hide away. Anyone with private CCTV or doorbell cameras in the village are asked to review the footage from 3pm yesterday afternoon onwards for any possible sightings of Noah.

‌



The same is also asked of anyone driving through Brantham with a dashcam fitted in their vehicle.

Superintendent Pete Partridge said: “We are very concerned for Noah’s welfare and need to find him as a matter of urgency.

“A vast number of resources have been deployed by ourselves, our emergency services colleagues and volunteers from SULSAR. These resources have been bolstered by members of the public who have turned out in large numbers to assist and we are incredibly grateful for their help and support.

‌



“Given that fast-moving nature of the investigation, it is important that any public searches are coordinated with police to ensure we are working together, and that our resources are directed where they can be most effective.

“We therefore ask that people do not put themselves at risk or undertake independent searches overnight.

“We will continue to keep Noah’s family and the public updated on the progress of our searches and investigation.

Article continues below

“We know that people want to help and so we are urging local residents to carefully read our requests to check their gardens and outbuildings and review any CCTV or dashcam footage as a priority.

“Anyone who believes they have seen Noah is asked to contact us immediately.

Anyone who believes they have seen Noah is asked to contact Suffolk police on 999, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.

News.title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
News.content:
OpenAI boss Sam Altman thinks people should have more faith in his company and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about all the risks.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.

However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.

Speaking in Washington meanwhile, left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have both called for greater governance of AI.

Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.

"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

The fervour over the claims has led to more scrutiny of AI development in recent days, and in response, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow, external and urged governments to regulate the industry.

The post was applauded by Altman, as well as co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok.

By Tuesday, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.

Altman said that he felt AI companies like his own were capable of essentially regulating themselves.

"We will get it right, I'm very confident in our company's and industry's ability to do this safely," Altman said, adding that he was sure that they would "keep alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" and if they couldn't, they would "slow down or stop".

Despite the assurances, political figures have cautioned against self-regulation.

Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who votes with the Democrats, said decisions over AI's development have been made by "a handful of the richest people in the world", naming Elon Musk, Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others.

Speaking at a conference hosted in Washington, he said: "The people of this country must make the decisions about AI, and not just a handful of oligarchs."

Bannon, who served as a White House strategist during Trump's first term, also cast doubt on the tech industry's ability to self regulate.

"We can never trust what an oligarch says because... they're disingenuous and they lie," Bannon said at the same conference.

News.title: UK in talks about joining global defence bank led by Canada
News.content:
The UK government is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

Chancellor John Healey is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Treasury officials stressed that no decision has been made. A government spokesperson said it was "fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity."

Before he cancelled commitments due to the death of his father, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had been due to meet Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the UK on Wednesday.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte is also travelling to the UK for his first meeting with the prime minister.

He is giving a speech in Oxfordshire, where he is expected to say the UK is "serious about security" and praise the country's efforts supporting Ukraine.

He will also say that Nato will "not be intimidated by Russia's campaign of hostile actions.

"Russia wants to stop us helping Ukraine â but their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine."

It comes after Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And on Tuesday Denmark also accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The DSRB is a multilateral bank aimed at providing cheaper loans to fund defence projects and has backing from Albania, Bulgaria, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine.

Membership of the bank for the UK and other G7 countries would come with an upfront investment cost of around Â£870m spread over three years.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

The government has so far avoided committing to raising defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, only repeating the longer term goal of 3.5% by 2035.

News.title: Three dead after LA news helicopter crashes while covering deadly bus collision
News.content:
Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in the city have said.

NBC Los Angeles confirmed the helicopter was its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, and was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash.

The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson told the BBC.

The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) said it was not yet known how many people were onboard, and no victim names had been released.

Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD said.

During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed.

"We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said.

Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS: "We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed.

"That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said.

Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash.

Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported.

News.title: 'Luck and timing': Matthew Rhys on his historic Emmy Awards double win
News.content:
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys described the "surreal and incredible feeling" after making history on Monday by becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.

Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me.

Speaking to the BBC, Rhys said he wasn't expecting to win the first award for The Beast In Me.

"I hadn't really prepared anything, as may be apparent from the vomit of a speech I came up with," he explained.

Welsh actor Matthew Rhys makes Emmy Awards history with double win.

News.title: Search continues for boy, 3, missing from playground
News.content:
Searches are continuing for a missing three-year-old boy who was last seen at a playground in a Suffolk village.

Noah Woods was with a relative at the small park at Merriam Close in Brantham, but "became separated" from them as they left at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday, Suffolk Police said.

The toddler, who is partially deaf and non-verbal, was reported to have run down a nearby alleyway towards a newbuild housing estate.

Hundreds of people joined searches for Noah, while emergency services carried out door-to-door inquiries into the evening.

News.title: Prolific shoplifters behind more than 28,000 offences, BBC finds
News.content:
At the height of his offending, Jeff Ashman estimates he walked out of shops with goods worth Â£400 to Â£500 on a daily basis.

"It's mind-boggling," he said, describing how much he had stolen from stores in Hastings to fuel his addiction to heroin and crack cocaine.

"I know the misery and grief and despair that I have caused these people for a long period of time."

Shoplifting is now firmly in the past for Ashman, but prolific shoplifters like him continue to plague communities across England.

We asked police about the 10 suspects their forces had most often linked to shoplifting offences between 2020-21 and 2025-26.

It revealed 28,415 recorded offences had been linked to just 270 suspects by the 27 forces who shared data with us.

It is an average of 105 offences per person - and those are just the occasions where a theft was formally reported to police and officers identified a suspect.

The suspects identified include one in Sussex who had been linked to 247 shoplifting offences, the equivalent of a reported crime every 10 days.

Policing minister Sarah Jones said shoplifting was a "pernicious crime that for too long has gone unpunished".

She said: "They need to know that they are going to be punished for what they have done."

News.title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies
News.content:
Mayors and other local political leaders could be given powers to oversee water companies under plans being considered by the government.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plan is to create nine new regional bodies responsible for planning, setting objectives, and holding water companies to account.

The idea was a key recommendation of Sir John Cunliffe's Independent Water Commission published in June last year.

Improving the water industry has been a focus for Burnham since he took to power, as water customers in England and Wales continue to face steep bill hikes.

But there has been little detail of what that could look like, short of full nationalisation - until now.

Some ideas in the Cunliffe report were adopted by Sir Keir Starmer's government, however the recommendation for regional bodies was not.

While no final decision has been made, and the timings for any announcement have not been finalised, officials in the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs are understood to be keen on the idea.

The regional bodies would be given powers to oversee elements of water companies' spending and hold bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges.

The Cunliffe review said: "This would represent a significant change, and ensure that local voices, customers and experts have stronger authority over companies' boards' decisions on investment priorities."

As well as a mayor, or local government figure, the regional bodies could consist of an independent chair, experts, and representatives to cover affected sectors like transport and agriculture.

A Whitehall source said it was just one among a number of ideas being explored to bring greater public control of water companies.

A government spokesperson said: "Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. We're bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."

It comes as the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the industry watchdog rose by a record 84% in a year, driven by customer concern and confusion over rising bills.

The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history and showed "just how dissatisfied" many people were.

In recent years there has been growing public concern about sewage spills and rising bills, as well as decades of under-investment in the sector, with climate change and population growth straining it further.

News.title: Third Heathrow runway should only go ahead if airlines pay for cleaner flying, say advisers
News.content:
Heathrow's third runway cannot be approved without changes to current climate policies, the government's advisers have said.

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) , externalsaid expansion can still go ahead but only if the aviation industry funds cleaner fuels and pays for machines that suck carbon dioxide out of the air.

Making the industry pay could push up the cost of flying with a return trip to Alicante costing around Â£150 more by 2050, and a return to New York up Â£400 in today's prices, it said.

Once built, the expanded airport would produce more carbon dioxide than any other single sector of the economy by 2050. Heathrow said expansion and climate goals were "not a choice" and it would deliver both.

"Our advice today is clear - Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK's Net Zero target," said Nigel Topping, the CCC chair.

"Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today."

The CCC report cannot block a new runway but it wants the government to pass legislation pushing responsibility for the long-term clean-up of aviation onto the industry.

The government would "carefully consider" the advice alongside other responses to its consultation according to the Department for Transport (DfT).

The government has an ongoing consultation which aims to judge any expansion against four tests - economy, climate, air quality and noise.

It does not approve a runway - that will come in a Commons vote expected later this year.

The Â£33bn project would raise Heathrow's capacity to 150 million passengers a year - up from 85 million.

A DfT spokesperson said any expansion would need to align with the country's climate targets, but added it "could deliver around Â£40bn to the economy and support up to 60,000 local jobs".

News.title: Letby doctor says inquiry 'grim reading' and he wishes 'we had been brave enough to follow suspicions'
News.content:
One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Lucy Letby with hospital managers has told the BBC the final inquiry report makes for "grim reading".

Consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby murdered seven babies, and attempted to murder seven more, on the neonatal unit.

He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report.

"I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he told the BBC.

"When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have."

The Thirlwall Inquiry was launched after former nurse Letby was convicted in 2023, and the final report was published on Tuesday.

In the 822-page document, Lady Justice Thirlwall described "a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital".

The report found that the police "should have been notified earlier than they were" and that hospital managers had repeatedly dismissed consultants' concerns.

Reflecting on the findings for the first time, Gibbs said: "I wasn't expecting it to be an easy read and it certainly isn't. I'd imagine it's an extremely difficult read for the parents of the babies concerned.

"As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that."

News.title: Complaints to watchdog about water firms jump 84%
News.content:
The number of complaints made by households about water companies to the industry watchdog has risen by a record 84% in a year, driven by customer concern and confusion over rising bills.

The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history and showed "just how dissatisfied" many people were.

Water customers in England and Wales have been hit with steep price hikes in recent years. The regulator Ofwat has also allowed firms to put up bills by 36% between 2025 and 2030.

Water UK, which represents firms, said it understood that higher bills was never welcome, but the money was needed "to fund vital upgrades".

The total number of complaints to the watchdog rose to 15,115 in 2025-26, from 8,235 in the previous year.

Meanwhile, complaints made by households directly to water companies, which is required before complaining to the CCW, rose by 56% to 321,347.

The top three subjects of complaints to the CCW were measured billing, affordability and billing admin.

Mike Keil, the chief executive of the CCW, said the figures "reflect just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector".

He said customers are "impatient to see the benefits" of higher bills.

"Companies need to be clear and open with their customers about how they are investing people's money to deliver real improvements."

The CCW assessed each water company's performance on the number of complaints it received for every 10,000 households it serves, and the amount of effort customers have to put in to get their complaint resolved.

Thames Water and South West Water rated "poor" for both performance measures.

David Bird, retail director at Thames, apologised to customers who "have not received the service they should expect".

"We know bill clarity has been a particular source of frustration, which is why we have launched a programme to redesign them, so they are easier to understand," he said.

Bills for the average Thames customer rose by 31% in 2024, but were a lot smaller this year at 3.4%.

South West Water said: "We know there is more to do to improve our customers' experience. We are taking action by reducing repeat contacts, resolving issues when people contact us for the first time, and ensuring they receive clear, timely communication."

Portsmouth Water and Bristol Water were the only companies to score "good" in both metrics, retaining their position at the top of the rankings as the sector's best performers.

Last month, Ofwat approved bill increases for 13 companies to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Five of those companies â Thames, Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Wessex Water and South East Water â were already permitted to hike bills in 2024.

A spokesperson for industry body Water UK said: "We understand increasing bills is never welcome, but the money is needed to fund vital upgrades to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas.

The spokesperson said that 94% of complaints are "being dealt with at the earliest possible stage without the need for further involvement from the consumer body".

"The industry remains committed to improving communication with customers and showing clearly how their money is being used to deliver the improvements they expect," the spokesperson added.

News.title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog
News.content:
A series of social media adverts for AI apps have been banned by a UK watchdog for promoting "the creation of sexually explicit content and objectification of women".

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said five ads uploaded to Meta platforms for AI companion and video generating apps had objectified and sexualised women, including through harmful gender stereotypes.

One of the ads used sexualised images of a girl under 18 to promote an AI companion app - while others invited users to upload images of their "crush" and turn images into "sizzling" videos.

Meta had already removed the offending ads. But Nicky Baker of the ASA said such content had the potential "to cause real-world harm".

"We take a firm line on ads that are likely to cause serious or widespread offence and these ads are a clear example of why that matters," she said.

"Encouraging and condoning the objectification of women and the creation of explicit content from people's images has the potential to cause real-world harm."

The ASA also said many of the ads it banned had promoted the creation of sexually explicit content using real women's images without their consent.

It comes only months after the UK outlawed apps to create non-consensual deepfake nude imagery - sparked by outrage over X's chatbot Grok complying with requests to nudify images of women on the platform.

The ASA said the law had changed during its investigations and that ads identified in future would be considered in light of both the law and its own rules.

Where ads are identified as illegal, it said it may notify platforms and law enforcement.

News.title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by data breach
News.content:
An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said.

The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected.

An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told.

The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter.

An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms.

Those affected are being notified directly, the department said.

News.title: 'One in, one out' scheme costs £56,000 per person returned to France, home secretary says
News.content:
The government's "one in, one out" scheme to send migrants who cross the Channel back to France costs on average Â£56,000 per person, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said.

That is higher than the Home Office's estimated average cost for enforced migrant returns of Â£48,800.

The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

Mahmood told MPs the policy had been "difficult" to scale up and the numbers involved were still "relatively small".

She said the total number deported under the scheme since it began in August 2025 was around 1,400.

Asked by the Conservative MP Robbie Moore whether she thought the scheme had been a success, Mahmood said: "On its own terms, can you prove the concept that such a deal is viable, that you can get returns off and up and running - yes.

"It's not been without its challenges, obviously. The numbers are still relatively small.

"What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system."

She said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme.

News.title: British woman abducted in Malawi, police say
News.content:
Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre.

Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement.

The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (Â£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators.

Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm.

A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance.

"I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying.

Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities.

The UK Foreign Office told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.

News.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
News.content:
The state pension is expected to top Â£13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by Â£488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

News.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

The UK inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in the year to August, pushed up by “soaring” petrol and diesel prices.

The latest figures were released on Wednesday morning by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Inflation hit 2.9 per cent in July, which was its highest level in four months, after the price of energy was pushed up by the conflict in the Middle East.

Inflation measures the increase in the price of goods over time. The Bank of England has set a target of keeping the rate at 2 per cent.

The ONS said that the cost of transport, “particularly motor fuels”, made the largest upward contribution to the higher inflation rate.

open image in gallery Inflation measures the increase in the price of goods over time (file photo) ( PA )

“Sharp price rises for petrol and diesel pushed inflation up again in August,” ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.

“Higher airfares, particularly for long-haul journeys, also contributed to the increase.”

Prices in the transport division rose by 4.6 per cent in the 12 months to August, the ONS said.

“The average price of petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre between July and August 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3 pence per litre between July and August 2025.”

On Tuesday, the RAC said that the cost of filling a family car with fuel had risen by almost £5 since the start of September.

open image in gallery The ‘soaring’ cost of petrol and diesel has contributed to the rise in inflation ( Getty )

Average UK forecourt prices reached 170.54p a litre for petrol on Tuesday, while diesel climbed to 192.86p, the motoring services company said.

Diesel is now at its highest price since 29 July 2022, with petrol reaching levels not seen since 23 August 2022.

The Bank of England will meet on Thursday to decide whether to change its interest rate, which it uses to control inflation. The rate currently sits at 3.75 per cent.

Scott Gardner, an investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said that the increase in inflation was “unlikely to convince the Bank of England to hike interest rates just yet”.

However, “it could raise fresh concerns about the outlook for inflation among policymakers”, he said.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey says the war in the Middle East is ‘impacting on inflation worldwide’ ( Getty )

Chancellor John Healey said: “The war in the Middle East is impacting on inflation worldwide, not just here at home.

“In our bills, our weekly shop and at the petrol pumps.

“We have taken early action to help families and businesses breathing space, by cutting tax on electricity bills, capping bus fares at £2 and lowering rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues.

“Despite this serious global uncertainty, our UK economy is proving resilient, and our determination to deliver and growth in every postcode continues.”

An Oxfordshire village has “voted” to become independent from the UK in protest at the government’s plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

The proposal, which would mean 1,256 people would move into the base near Piddington, has sparked anger among many village residents.

Residents cast their ballots in the symbolic and unofficial referendum on Tuesday.

Their ballots on Tuesday were returned into a small box outside the village hall, the community hub of the village of 350 people which does not have any pubs, cafes or shops.

The result was announced by a returning officer to an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall on Wednesday morning.

The village voted overwhelmingly in favour of independence from the UK.

Some 285 villagers backed “independence”, with a turnout of nearly 92 per cent.

Only 26 residents voted against the motion, with one spoiled ballot recorded.

On 4 July, marking the 250th anniversary of American independence, 96 per cent of Piddington voters backed holding an unofficial independence referendum, which will take place on Tuesday.

The government wants to use the Urgent Crown Development Process, which would allow home secretary Shabana Mahmood to bypass local planning authorities.

Senior minister Jonathan Reynolds acknowledged “none of this is pleasant” but the disused military site was more suitable than housing asylum seekers in hotels.

There was “no imaginary place these people can go”, he said on Tuesday, the day of the vote.

He told ITV’s Good Morning Britain: “Where in the UK would want more of this? We’ve got to share this throughout the entire nation.”

Mr Reynolds said “I think a former military site is a far more suitable location” than a hotel in a town or city centre.

While the asylum seekers are not detained, “you can more easily see who’s coming and going from a site like that”.

Andy Burnham last month said that wealthy areas of Britain “must play their part”, and that the country “cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country” housing asylum seekers.

Speaking the while villagers voted on Tuesday, Piddington parish chairman Tim McNally said the vote was about “hope” for residents.

He said: “Yesterday was the anniversary of the Battle of Britain, and for us, it was the battle for Britain.

“We’ve been identified as ground zero for a whole number of issues.

“I just want to say something to Andy Burnham, the prime minister of this great, great country that we’re in, the Speaker of the House of Lords, Speaker of the Commons, Kemi Badenoch, who is the leader of the opposition and all shadow oppositions: this is an example of democracy in operation.”

He added: “On the 3rd of July, when we started this process, we went into this village hall as what we call the underdogs, not knowing how we were going to go forward and actually fight against this plan, we had a plucky idea.

“We had an idea that we would grow as people, and what I consider as definition of done, is this.

“This is definition of done. We have given an absolute message, not just to the region, not just to the country, but to the world.”

A sign reading the village’s unofficial new name was then displayed outside the hall, while a campaign song created by the village played in the background, with the lyrics: “It’s the battle for Britain, and Britain roars.”

He said: “It doesn’t matter whether they’re priests or vicars, the proportionality isn’t acceptable.

“Your house value has dropped. We’ve had a number of house deals cancelled. We’ve had banks pull mortgages.

“We’ve had people who’ve got pensions in their properties have to be revaluated, because the value of their property is no longer what it was.

“That’s not about saying this is a wealthy area, this is no more wealthy than any other village around the country, but people work very hard, and they worked hard to earn what they’ve made, and they should be entitled to have what they’ve made.

“But overnight, to have that destroyed, ultimately, is disgraceful, and we’ve had no involvement in that process to determine what it means for us.”

A spokesperson for the Home Office previously said: “The Government is closing every asylum hotel, saving taxpayers over £1 billion on asylum support since the election.

“We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites which are designed to be self-contained to reduce impact on the local community.

“As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area.”

Bristol has become the first city in the country to ban adverts that encourage excessive consumption of fast fashion on council-owned billboards.

Councillors voted in favour of proposals that will also prevent the advertising of non-electric cars, flights, cruise holidays and travel agents.

The ban will apply to all bus stops in the city, and some free-standing digital screens and billboards where the council owns the display.

Members of the Strategy and Resources Committee voted eight to one in favour of updating the council’s advertising and sponsorship policy.

The changes follow a review of the policy, which explored the potential for introducing restrictions on the promotion of high-carbon products and services.

The city council already places restrictions on advertising for products such as gambling, payday loans, and food and drink high in fat, salt and sugar.

Bristol joins more than 20 UK councils that already have restrictions on ads for polluting products and services. But none has previously banned advertising for fast fashion products.

Councillor Heather Mack, deputy leader of Bristol City Council, said: “This vote is a win-win for the people of Bristol.

“By banning the  of fossil fuels and products which produce high-carbon emissions on council-owned billboards, bus shelters and digital screens, we can encourage the promotion of more sustainable products which are better for individuals and better for the environment.

“Advertising forces itself upon all of us. Whilst scrolling, whilst walking, whilst waiting for the bus, it has negative impacts on our health and wellbeing as well as the climate, environment and local economy.

“And it is unsurprisingly the most extractive and damaging industries that are able to spend the most.

“In Bristol we are committed to pushing back on this, so I am delighted that as a council we have today banned the advertising of high-carbon products.

“As the first council to introduce restrictions on the advertising of fast fashion, we will continue to look at how we can keep improving our advertising policy so that our outdoor spaces reflect the positive values of Bristol and the local economy.”

At least three people have died and another is injured after a local NBC News helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighborhood on Tuesday while reporting on a bus collision earlier in the day, according to officials.

The helicopter went down between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighborhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson said.

Five patients were assessed, with one person transported to a local hospital in an unknown condition while three others were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the fire department.

NBC4 Los Angeles said it was their news helicopter, NewsChopper 4, that crashed in the city during a live broadcast. Several television news helicopters covering the bus collision were operating in the area, according to media reports.

"We've been telling you that we've been piecing it together here. ⁠We knew it was a ​news ⁠chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received the confirmation that, in ⁠fact, NewsChopper 4 went down just before 7 o'clock tonight ​in ⁠Chatsworth," NBC anchor Colleen ‌Williams said.

open image in gallery First responders work the scene after a helicopter crashed in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles ( AP )

NBC ‌said the helicopter was operated by Angel City Air, which is affiliated with the ​station.

The helicopter crash happened after a vehicle collision in the area in which a Los Angeles Metro bus ‌and a passenger vehicle met with an accident, killing at least two people.

Footage from the scene showed two shipping containers and several vehicles burning and firefighters working to douse the blaze, which has been extinguished.

open image in gallery A Los Angeles Police officer speaks with reporters near the scene after a news helicopter crashed in Chatsworth, a suburban neighborhood of Los Angeles, California ( AFP/Getty )

The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) said the helicopter crashed at around 6:58 pm and its officers responded to the area of Lurline Avenue and Nordhoff Street in Chatsworth.

It said it was not confirmed how many people were on board.

At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the parking lot next to the commercial building, Capt Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the LAFD, said during a news conference. It was unclear if the other two who were killed were on the ground or inside the aircraft.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said she was "devastated" by the loss of life in ‌the helicopter crash and the bus ​collision in Chatsworth.

“I’m absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash,” she said, thanking emergency responders for ‌their swift response.

open image in gallery A Los Angeles Police officer stands guard near the scene after a news helicopter crashed in Chatsworth, a suburban neighborhood of Los Angeles ( AFP/Getty )

California governor ⁠Gavin Newsom also shared his condolences and said "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter ‌crashes in Chatsworth, and with ​the entire NBC4 family".

At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground caught fire from the burning helicopter wreckage, which was quickly put out, according to officials. More than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash, according to the Fire Department.

The ⁠National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation ​Administration will investigate the ‌crash, the Fire Department said.

About two hours before the crash, an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half of the SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus.

The helicopter crashed about a mile and a half from the bus crash.

Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren have defended MobLand co-star Tom Hardy after reports of behind-the-scenes tensions cast doubt on his future in the Paramount+ crime drama.

Reports emerged in May that Hardy would not be returning for a potential third season after alleged clashes with producers during production on season two.

Hardy was rumoured to have delayed his fellow actors during filming, and unnamed sources said the actor “refused to come out of his trailer for hours at a time”.

Days later, a Variety report stated that Hardy had not been fired and that discussions over his return were still under way. The question of Hardy’s future was finally settled earlier this month, when Paramount+ renewed MobLand for a third season and confirmed that Hardy would return.

Brosnan said the reports “blindsided” the cast, as he had not been aware of any such rupture.

“It was my son who sent me the text one morning. I was away on vacation, and I couldn’t believe it. I reached out to Tom, saying, ‘I love you, mate. I love you,’” Pierce Brosnan told The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the show’s second-season return.

open image in gallery Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren have defended MobLand co-star Tom Hardy after reports of behind-the-scenes tensions cast doubt on his future in the Paramount+ crime drama ( AFP via Getty Images )

“And he and I, you know, we communicate. He’s a painter. I’m a painter. Both actors. But anyway, just to say, ‘I’m there. We’re there. We love you.’ So for me, it was kind of a storm in a teacup,” he said.

Directed by Guy Ritchie, MobLand is a London-set crime drama about two rival organised crime families, the Harrigans and the Stevensons, whose battle for power threatens to destroy both dynasties. Tom Hardy stars as Harry Da Souza, a street-smart fixer caught between the warring families, while Pierce Brosnan plays Harrigan patriarch Conrad and Helen Mirren plays his wife, Maeve.

Mirren has already backed Hardy before, sharing a photo of the actor on Instagram in May with the caption: “Love you now and always, Helen.”

On why she chose to intervene publicly, Mirren said: “We live in the world of being talked about and interviewed in newspapers and so on and so forth. Pierce and I have both had many years of this and experience of it.”

She continued: “False rumours just should be knocked on the head, asap, which is why I did my post about Tom, not for Tom, but my absolutely genuine love of Tom.”

The Thursday Murder Club star added that her support was “par for the course” for a show where the cast is “all so mutually supportive of each other”.

“Very often the actors get blamed for this sort of thing, and if there is a rumour, the immediate sort of blame can fall on actors. That’s usually completely unfair,” she said.

open image in gallery Tom Hardy (right) allegedly kept 'Mobland' co-stars Pierce Brosnan (left) and Helen Mirren (middle) waiting on set 'for hours' ( Paramount+ )

Mirren described Hardy and his character as “the anchor of this mad whirlwind”, adding that no one on the cast is “even contemplating” the series without the Mad Max: Fury Road actor.

“Tom is MobLand. Without Tom, we don’t have MobLand,” said Brosnan. “He is the centre. He allows us to play these crazy characters.”

At the second-season premiere in London last week, Hardy, Brosnan, and Mirren appeared together on the red carpet, putting on a united front. Brosnan downplayed the rumours, saying he was a “massive fan” of Hardy’s work.

“We are rock solid as a company, as a family. Everyone shows up for work, and everybody’s just there on the spot. It moves very fast so it’s not like we go out and socialise and go to the pub or anything like that,” he said.

Hardy said it was a “privilege” to work with legendary actors like Mirren and Brosnan and watch them “pushing the envelope”.

“They’re awesome,” he said. “In many aspects of course I look up to them. Coming up, these are actors that came before me.”

A survivor from the ferry that capsized off Indonesia's Java island described the vessel going down in under five minutes, as rescuers continued searching for dozens of people still missing three days after the disaster.

The Virgo Transport 8 was sailing from Surabaya, Indonesia's second-largest city, to Banjarmasin on Borneo when it lost contact with its operator shortly after departure on Saturday.

It capsized early on Sunday during what should have been a 20-hour crossing of some 510km. Rescuers found the vessel inverted nearly 150km from the Banjarmasin port.

Rizky Apriansyah, a waiter working onboard, said he was sleeping on the ferry's top deck when his friends woke him at around 1am and told him to grab a life jacket. By this time, he said, the ship was already listing at around 30 degrees. He and four of his friends rushed from their room as waves he estimated at 3-4m high repeatedly struck the vessel, tipping it further.

There was no alarm and he feared that many passengers might not have known what was happening.

"When I went out that door, I immediately fell onto the ship's railing. I held on and hugged my friends, then we were swept away by the waves," he told Reuters. "It only took minutes for the ship to capsize, even less than 10 minutes."

Mr Apriansyah and his friends clung to a floating 12kg cooking gas cylinder around 15m from the ship as they watched it overturn, before drifting at sea for about 10 hours until another vessel spotted and rescued them.

Separately, five crew members survived by holding onto an empty LPG cylinder, according to the local news agency Antara.

Mr Apriansyah, who worked on the ferry for three months, said he did not intend to work at sea again.

"I felt overwhelmed, exhausted, suffocated, and just accepted whatever will happen," he said.

A woman reacts as police officers display a list of the victims of the Virgo Transport 8 ferry ( AFP/Getty )

The ferry's operator, Virgo Karya Shipping, said that it could not comment on why the alarm was not sounded, saying it needed to check with the crew.

Six people died and 129 remained missing as of Tuesday, according to the Indonesian search and rescue agency Basarnas, figures that hadn’t changed since Sunday. Some 234 people were aboard, according to Reuters. Antara put the figure at 243 and said 114 had been rescued by Tuesday night.

Bad weather delayed the evacuation of 22 survivors by a day before they were brought ashore in Banjarmasin on Tuesday.

“The plan was to evacuate them to the Trisakti port yesterday but adverse weather conditions prevented us from doing so," I Putu Sudayana, head of the local search and rescue agency, told reporters. "We cannot fight nature; the swells and waves in the area were extremely high."

Four more bodies were airlifted to Banjarmasin on Tuesday, Basarnas said.

Nearly 1,100 rescuers, including navy and police personnel, are involved in the search, supported by more than a dozen vessels and five aircraft, according to Basarnas.

Mohammad Syafii, the head of Basarnas, said search teams were alternating their methods daily to adjust to shifting currents in the Java Sea and improve the chances of finding victims who might have been swept away, while continuing to treat the area in and around the wreck itself as the priority.

He said the agency followed international protocols throughout its operations and was subject to annual audits by the International Maritime Organisation.

“What we do strictly refers to legal grounds that can be accounted for," he said, urging the families of the victims and the public to rely on Basarnas for credible updates on the search.

Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia, an archipelago of over 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat travel for daily transport and tourism. Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are the main causes.

News.title: Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town
News.content:
At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.
