World.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Shut clinic deepens healthcare crisis in Benue IDP camp
World.content:
In April 2026, Anaor Saawuan laid her eight-month-old granddaughter on a thin mattress inside their makeshift shelter at the Anyiin Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camp in Logo Local Government Area of Benue State, Central Nigeria.

The infant had been vomiting and stooling for two days. She also had a fever. Grandma thought it was a teething problem, so she gave her a cough syrup and tablets she bought at a patent medicine shop across the road.

But when the vomiting and diarrhoea returned, she took the child to a hospital outside the camp, where health workers said she needed a blood transfusion.

“I had no money,” she said. “And there was nobody to help me.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She resorted to a traditional remedy. However, at about 9 p.m. on 2 May, the child died. She believes the child might have survived if the nearby clinic within the camp had still been operational.

“There used to be a clinic here,” Mrs Saawuan said, pointing towards a building inside the camp. “Medicines were available, and treatment was free, until everything stopped.”

Her case illustrates the healthcare crisis at settlements for people displaced by conflicts in Benue State, where clinics are closed or poorly equipped, medicines are in short supply, referral systems are weak, and many families cannot afford healthcare costs.

Another health burden

Mrs Saawuan also has a young grandson, who was diagnosed with an inguinal hernia and referred for surgery at a general hospital. “We barely feed,” she said. “How can I pay for an operation?”

Mrs Saawuan has again resorted to herbs to manage his condition.

A risky pregnancy

A few shelters away in the same camp lives a pregnant 32-year-old woman, Naomi Teryen.

Her previous pregnancies were difficult, she said, involving prolonged labour and Caesarean sections.

But five months into her current pregnancy, she has little money for regular antenatal care at a health centre outside the camp and has not had an ultrasound scan.

“I don’t have a job, and there is no proper healthcare service in this camp,” she told PREMIUM TIMES.

Mrs Teryen said she previously relied on the health facility in the camp.

“When the hospital was available, we used to get medicine free of charge there,” she said. “But now that the hospital has been closed, when we go to the health centre, we pay for medicine.”

Cost of a closed clinic

Mrs Teryen showed PREMIUM TIMES the medicines she received during an antenatal visit. They consisted of paracetamol and Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS), which contain vitamins and minerals intended to prevent micronutrient deficiencies and improve maternal and birth outcomes.

The MMS supplements are distributed through Nigeria’s public health system with support from the government and development partners, including UNICEF.

They are intended to be dispensed free of charge. But Mrs Teryen alleged pregnant women from the camp are charged for medicines, including MMS, during antenatal visits to the health centre outside the camp.

She said that an antenatal visit to the European Economic Community Health Clinic (CHC) in Anyiin, a government-owned primary healthcare facility in the community, typically costs her about ₦3,000. She recalled an occasion when she arrived at the centre with only ₦1,000. “They told me to go back,” she said.

Mrs Teryen’s husband makes wooden crafts inside the camp. But he often sells nothing.

“Every time she gives birth, it is difficult. Sometimes we spend more than a week in the hospital,” he said.

Terrence Akighir, a medical doctor and UNICEF consultant, told PREMIUM TIMES the supplements should not be sold to patients.

“MMS is supposed to be free,” he said. “If somebody is taking advantage of that to sell the medicine, it should be looked into and stopped. These women do not have money. If they are paying for medicines that should be free, how will they meet their other healthcare needs?”

A UNICEF humanitarian report corroborates Mr Akighir’s claims amid the humanitarian crisis.

In its Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3, published on 18 March 2026 and covering January to December 2025, the agency said that 8.8 million people, including 4.9 million children, required humanitarian assistance, while 2.9 million people were internally displaced.

UNICEF reported that, under its First 1,000 Days Initiative, 489 pregnant women in Benue IDPs received free MMS between June and December 2025.

Clinic declines comment

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the European Economic Community Health Clinic in Anyiin for a response to the allegation. An official on duty said she was not authorised to comment on whether MMS were being sold to patients and declined to provide further information before walking away.

When the clinic closed

The healthcare crisis at the Anyiin IDP camp did not begin this year. It followed the closure of a health facility inside the camp that had once provided basic medical care to displaced residents.

Helen Tsavwua, a former worker at the facility, said the clinic was established by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), which provided medical services to displaced communities in Anyiin IDP at the height of the displacement crisis in 2018.

“When MSF was leaving, Victim Support Fund (VSF) took over until January 2021,” she said. “When they left, the hospital was closed down.”

According to Ms Tsavwua, VSF continued to provide some medicines to support patients, but the absence of medical personnel meant that residents could not reliably access treatment.

“They were giving medicines, but there was no doctor to attend to patients,” she said. “When children or women were sick, they would go there, but there was nobody to give them medicine.”

She said the limited treatment available at the time was also inadequate for some patients.

“Sometimes only malaria medicine or paracetamol would be given without even testing,” she said.

A community health worker at the Community Health Clinic, Anyiin, who previously worked at the camp facility, also attributed its closure to a lack of funding. The worker asked not to be named because of concerns about possible victimisation.

According to the health worker, MSF had provided substantial support to the facility, including medical personnel. Some of the doctors and other health workers who had worked under the organisation were retained when its support ended, but sustaining the facility became increasingly difficult.

“When MSF left, it became difficult to sustain the hospital,” the worker said. “Medicine stopped coming in, and we were asked to return to our former posts.”

The worker said the camp’s health services had depended heavily on support from humanitarian organisations and other non-governmental groups.

“Most of the activities in the camp, especially health and food, were supported by NGOs,” the worker said, adding that the government’s role through the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA) was largely supervisory.

An abandoned clinic

PREMIUM TIMES visited the former clinic located within the NKST Primary School, Anyiin, where internally displaced people still live. The facility appeared deserted, with its rooms locked and no health workers or patients present. Its beige-and-black walls were chipped and peeling, while faded chalk inscriptions remained on the dark metal doors. The concrete walkway was cracked and stained, bordered by bare reddish soil, while children moved through the surrounding school grounds.

Camp residents said medicines supplied by non-profit organisations were still kept inside the locked facility. They said the drugs remained inaccessible because the building was closed and no health workers were available to attend to patients.

MSF exits Benue

PREMIUM TIMES contacted Abdulkareem Yakubu, field communication officer and spokesperson for MSF in Nigeria, for clarification on the organisation’s withdrawal and its implications for communities previously served by its teams.

Mr Yakubu said he could not comment on the current situation in communities where MSF had ended its activities because the organisation had closed its project in Benue. He referred PREMIUM TIMES to MSF’s formal statement on the closure, which he shared with the newspaper, saying the statement contained the organisation’s position on its decision to leave the state.

In the statement, MSF said it had decided to phase out its medical humanitarian activities in Benue after six years of providing healthcare to internally displaced people and host communities. The organisation said basic healthcare and decentralised activities would conclude by the end of June 2024, while family planning and sexual and reproductive healthcare activities would cease by the end of Jul,y and comprehensive sexual and gender-based violence care would end in August the same year.

“MSF operations’ core mission is to provide urgent medical humanitarian assistance in emergency contexts, and we have a responsibility to ensure this capacity to provide assistance at a moment’s notice is maintained,” the statement said.

The organisation said the decision was made after considering medical needs across Nigeria and the need to reinforce MSF’s response in other parts of the country.

“We remain concerned for the safety of women and girls in Benue,” the statement read. “We will continue to advocate for more action by the Nigerian government and the newly arrived international organisations present in the area, to recognise the threat that SGBV poses to displaced people and to provide survivors with the necessary care.”

MSF said that between May 2018 and March 2024, its medical teams conducted 412,832 consultations and treated 223,871 patients in Mbawa, Ortese, Naka and Agagbe camps and host communities. The organisation also said it admitted 1,731 people following instances of sexual and gender-based violence in 2023.

“The arrival of international organisations is a hopeful signal that MSF’s drive to recognise the plight of displaced people in Benue state is being heard,” the statement added.

According to MSF, a new clinic supported by UNICEF and WHO began operating in three camps in late 2023. The organisation said the development offered some prospect of continued healthcare support for displaced communities after its withdrawal.

After MSF’s exit

At the Anyiin IDP camp, the effects of MSF’s departure have continued to be felt by displaced residents. Julius Tema, chairman of the Anyiin IDP camp, said the withdrawal of the organisation and the subsequent closure of the camp’s health facility had left residents struggling to access basic healthcare.

“Our biggest challenges now are food and health,” he said. “There are many sick people in this camp.”

He said malaria remained widespread, alongside cases of hepatitis and other illnesses.

“There was a hospital here before,” Mr Tema said. “Today, that hospital is no longer functioning. We don’t have medicines anymore.”

With no functioning clinic, residents must seek treatment outside the camp, a burden many cannot afford.

“When there is no medicine and no hospital inside the camp, people suffer,” he said. “Some simply resort to herbs because they don’t have money to seek treatment elsewhere.”

Mr Tema said pregnant women, children and older residents were particularly affected and appealed to the government and humanitarian organisations to restore healthcare services.

“We need medicines. We need medical personnel. We need intervention before more lives are lost,” he said.

Officials stay silent

The agencies responsible for managing the IDP camps and providing healthcare to Benue residents did not respond to PREMIUM TIMES’ requests for comments on the findings of this investigation.

During a telephone conversation on 7 July, James Iorpuu, executive secretary of the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), which oversees IDP camps, scheduled a meeting at the agency’s headquarters in Makurdi for 9 a.m. the following day.

The reporter arrived before the scheduled time and waited for more than three hours. But when, at about noon, Mr Iorpuu emerged from his office, he ignored the reporter’s presence, entered his vehicle, and drove away without granting the interview or proposing another time.

PREMIUM TIMES subsequently sent questions to SEMA about the closure of the health facility within the IDP camp, the shortage of medicines and medical supplies, healthcare costs borne by displaced residents, emergency referral arrangements, and support for health workers serving the camps.

As of the time of this publication, the agency has not responded.

The Benue State Commissioner for Health, Paul Ogwuche, also did not respond to repeated requests for comment. During a visit to the ministry at the Benue State Secretariat, Mr Ogwuche’s secretary requested a formal written interview request, which was done.

As of the time of publication, the commissioner had not responded to the questions.

A wider health crisis

The experiences documented in Anyiin are unfolding amid a prolonged conflict that has forced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes across Benue State.

The International Organisation for Migration’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Round 18 recorded 464,543 internally displaced persons in Benue, the highest number across the North-central and North-west states covered by the assessment.

About 376,000, or 81 per cent, were living in host communities, while roughly 88,000 were in camps and camp-like settings.

Women and children account for most of the displaced population, increasing the need for maternal, reproductive and child healthcare in the camps.

For many families, displacement has also meant the loss of farms, businesses, and other sources of income.

An August 2025 assessment by the SEMA and the Internal Displacement Solutions Fund found that 96 per cent of displaced households surveyed wanted to return to their communities.

The healthcare challenges are particularly significant for pregnant women.

A study published in the National Library of Medicine’s PubMed Central (PMC), based on research among pregnant women visiting PHCs in Benue State, reported a maternal mortality ratio of 1,189 deaths per 100,000 live births.

The study drew on data from two cohorts covering 2015–2017 and 2020–2021. The reported ratio is more than double Nigeria’s national estimate and far above the Sustainable Development Goal target of fewer than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030.

Infographic: Benue’s maternal mortality burden compared with Nigeria’s national estimate and the Sustainable Development Goal target

The 2021 Nigeria Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) found that 59.1 per cent of births in Benue State were attended by skilled health personnel.

Traditional birth attendants assisted with 17.7 per cent of births, while relatives or friends assisted with another 17.2 per cent.

Health insurance coverage among women is also low. The same survey also found that only 2.5 per cent are covered by health insurance, leaving most families reliant on out-of-pocket payments for antenatal care, medicines, and emergency treatment.

For displaced women who have lost their livelihoods, those costs are compounded by transport expenses and limited access to functioning health facilities.

Newborns face significant risks as well. According to the 2021 MICS, one in every 56 children born in Benue dies within the first 28 days of life.

Preventable illnesses, delayed care

Mr Akighir, the medical doctor and UNICEF consultant, said many illnesses affecting displaced families can be prevented or treated if care is available early.

He identified malnutrition, malaria, and acute diarrheal diseases as the major health concerns, particularly among children.

“Malnutrition is one of the biggest problems we see,” he said. “When children are malnourished, their immunity drops, and they become vulnerable to infections.”

He said poor access to safe water and sanitation can compound those risks.

“Once they start drinking untreated water, acute diarrhoeal diseases become common,” he said. “Many children also walk barefoot, exposing them to hookworm infestation, skin infections and other preventable diseases.”

Pregnant women face additional risks when poverty and displacement delay their access to care.

“Health-seeking behaviour is generally poor,” Mr Akighir said. “Sometimes labour begins, and the woman delivers inside the camp because there is nobody to accompany her to a health facility. Others present very late, when complications have already developed.”

He said weaknesses in the referral system can create further barriers, particularly for displaced people who were not registered when they arrived at the camps.

“Some of them came into the camps after registration had been completed,” he said.

“When complications arise, and they are referred, they may face challenges accessing support because they are not captured in the system.”

Support, but gaps remain

Mr Akighir said humanitarian organisations continue to support maternal and child healthcare in some of Benue’s IDP camps, including antenatal care, nutrition services, treatment of childhood illnesses and referrals for emergency care.

He said one intervention had supported more than 250 successful deliveries.

However, such interventions have not eliminated gaps in access to healthcare across the camps.

UNICEF’s 2025 humanitarian reporting shows that its health response extended beyond nutrition support. By the end of the year, the agency said essential health services had reached displaced people in 10 IDP camps and two host communities in Benue, with more than 44,000 medical consultations and 16,000 childhood immunisations recorded.

The agency nevertheless identified gaps that continued to constrain the response, including limited government funding, shortages of essential supplies and weak coordination among government agencies.

For Mrs Teryen, whose baby is due in September, those gaps have immediate consequences.

This reporting was completed with the support of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

World.title: 2027: PDP backs Wike’s Rainbow Coalition for Tinubu’s re-election, says APC governors underperformed
World.content:
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has said there is nothing wrong with its member and Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, remaining in the party while mobilising support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid on the platform of the Rainbow Coalition.

The party led by Abdulrahman Mohammed said Mr Wike has a constitutional right to support any candidate of his choice, regardless of the political party on whose platform the candidate is contesting.

The National Publicity Secretary of the PDP, Jungudo Mohammed, said this in a statement on Tuesday while reacting to the controversy surrounding the Rainbow Coalition being promoted by Mr Wike to mobilise support for Mr Tinubu’s second-term bid.

“Wike has every constitutional and democratic right to decide whom he supports politically. His support for President Tinubu is legitimate, and as a serving appointee of the president, there is nothing contradictory about supporting the president while maintaining his political identity and relationships within the PDP,” Mr Mohammed said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Sandy Onor is the PDP’s presidential candidate for the 2027 election.

The formation of the coalition has generated disagreements between Mr Wike and governors of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) over allegations that the minister is using the platform to support politicians who lost the APC primaries and are now contesting elections on the PDP platform.

The APC Governors Forum, chaired by Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, had opposed any political coalition or alliance that could threaten the chances of the party and its candidates in the 2027 elections.

Mr Uzodimma, who is also the secretary of the Tinubu Campaign Council, said aligning with such a political arrangement could undermine Mr Tinubu’s re-election bid and weaken the APC ahead of the elections.

Mr Wike, however, said he had never promised that the PDP would not field candidates in the 2027 elections. He also urged the governors to pay greater attention to Mr Tinubu’s re-election campaign than they did during the 2023 election.

PDP accuses APC governors of fear

The PDP criticised the APC governors for opposing Mr Wike’s support for the Rainbow Coalition.

Mr Mohammed attributed the governors’ opposition to fear of defeat at the polls, alleging that some of them had underperformed in office.

“The APC Governors’ Forum should understand that Wike is not their problem; their problem is their poor governance and failure to meet the expectations of their people. Their opposition to Wike’s support is driven by fear. The fear that their poor records of performance will be exposed at the polls,” he said.

The PDP spokesperson said the governors’ demand that Mr Wike should not support or field candidates capable of challenging APC candidates was a political miscalculation, and that the minister’s support for Mr Tinubu did not mean he had abandoned the PDP.

“The APC governors had initially misconceived Wike’s support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu as an endorsement of the APC. They are now beginning to realise that supporting the President does not mean abandoning the PDP or surrendering the political space to the APC,” he said.

“Their demand that Wike should not support or field candidates capable of challenging the APC governors and their anointed candidates is a fundamental political miscalculation. Elections are contests, and every political party has the democratic right to present candidates before the electorate.

“The APC Governors’ demand is not only politically curious but a complete political miscalculation. It exposes the growing anxiety within the APC over the prospect of facing strong PDP candidates at the 2027 elections,” he added.

Mr Mohammed also claimed that the PDP had become more united and had the capacity to compete effectively in the 2027 elections.

“The reality that appears to have unsettled them is that the PDP has not only stabilised but has also successfully fielded candidates across elective positions who are capable of challenging these APC governors and their anointed candidates in 2027,” he said.

“It is particularly revealing that governors who earlier claimed to be confident of their performance are now asking their opponents not to field candidates against them. If they have truly performed and retained the confidence of their people, they should welcome a contest and allow the electorate to decide.”

PDP defends Wike’s political influence

The PDP spokesperson also defended Mr Wike’s political influence, stating that his support could not simply be disregarded by politicians seeking electoral victories.

“The APC governors should be reminded that no one can jettison Wike’s support and expect to win elections effortlessly. Those who have attempted to do so in the past have learnt the lesson the hard way,” he said.

“The APC governors should also know that Wike is not their problem; their poor governance and fear of electoral defeat are the real problems. Their anxiety is understandable because Wike has demonstrated, both as Governor of Rivers State and as Minister of the FCT, a capacity for project delivery, political organisation and electoral mobilisation that cannot simply be wished away.”

PDP challenges APC governors

The PDP challenged the APC governors to focus on governance and accountability rather than attempting to influence who Mr Wike supports politically.

“The APC Governors’ Forum should therefore concentrate on governance, accountability and performance rather than attempting to determine whom Mr Wike should support. They should account for the enormous resources accruing to their states through FAAC and ensure that local governments receive the funds due to them without undue interference,” Mr Mohammed said.

He described Mr Wike as an asset to Mr Tinubu’s political project and said the minister could contribute to the president’s re-election campaign.

“The Hon. Minister of the FCT is not a liability to President Tinubu’s political project. He is undoubtedly an asset, a mobiliser and a force capable of contributing significantly to electoral victory.

“The APC governors should therefore stop looking for scapegoats. Wike is not their problem. Their governance record, their performance and the confidence or lack of confidence of their people are what will determine their political fate in 2027,” the statement said.

World.title: Gridlock strands motorists on Lateef Jakande Road, Isheri, Berger
World.content:
Motorists were still stuck in traffic on Tuesday night along the Lateef Jakande Road, Omole Phase 1, Isheri and Ojodu Berger axis, more than three hours after the gridlock began.

The traffic started around 6:30 p.m. and was still heavy as of 10:19 p.m., with vehicles moving slowly along several parts of the route.

This PREMIUM TIMES reporter who walked from Omole Phase 1 towards Berger saw long queues of vehicles on the road.

At Isheri, the traffic was particularly heavy, with many workers and business owners returning home caught in the gridlock.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The immediate cause of the traffic was not known at the time of filing this report.

The Lagos State Traffic Management Authority (LASTMA) had also not given an explanation for the congestion on its X account as of 10:19 p.m.

No LASTMA official was seen along some of the affected sections during the reporter’s walk from Omole Phase 1 to Berger.

Traffic was also heavy around the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, where a 40-foot container-laden truck crashed at the exit of Kara Bridge on Tuesday.

LASTMA said the truck suffered brake failure and rammed into the road demarcation blocks and other vehicles.

The agency stated that its officials and police personnel were deployed to the scene to control traffic and evacuate the affected vehicles.

The crash happened while repair work was ongoing on Kara Bridge.

The federal government began a two-week repair of damaged expansion joints on the bridge on 8 September. The work is expected to end on 22 September.

The Acting Controller of the Federal Ministry of Works in Ogun State, Richard Adeleye, stated that the repairs were necessary because the expansion joints had exceeded their service life and posed risks to motorists.

Mr Adeleye noted that the work was being done in phases to reduce its effect on traffic.

“There will be traffic control here from the 8th of this month, which will last for two weeks, precisely because of the curing that is expected before it is opened to traffic,” he said during an inspection of the affected section.

The repairs have led to traffic restrictions around Kara Bridge and adjoining sections of the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

LASTMA also reported another crash on Tuesday involving a loaded trailer and a Sport Utility Vehicle on the bridge inward to Mowe.

The agency advised motorists using the route to drive carefully and obey the instructions of traffic officials.

World.title: 2027: Power-sharing, candidate-substitution disputes threaten ADC’s chances in Jigawa
World.content:
As campaigns for the 2027 general elections get underway, the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Jigawa State is struggling to put its house in order.

Allegations that the ADC leadership replaced primary election winners are at the heart of the crisis.

Also, the governorship candidate, Sabo Nakudu, and party chieftain Bashir Jumbo have had public spats over a power-sharing arrangement, further complicating an uphill battle against the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in the Northwestern state.

In August, Mr Nakudu issued a public disclaimer regarding a purported 60:40 power-sharing agreement. His action is more than a routine legal disavowal; it exposed a deep fracture in the opposition party ahead of the general election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Nakudu’s statement revealed an opposition platform bitterly split along factional fault lines.

Crisis and failed internal reconciliation

The governorship primary had pitted Mr Jumboa four-term House of Representatives veteran and pillar of the ADC in Jigawa—against Mr Nakudu, a late defector from the ruling APC.

Mr Jumbo petitioned the party’s election appeal committee, alleging widespread irregularities, intimidation, and interference by party leadership in the primary. His camp views Mr Nakudu’s emergence as a hijack by wealthy latecomers, while Mr Nakudu’s camp accused Mr Jumbo’s of being bitter losers.

A leaked document indicating a 60:40 power-sharing agreement between the camps, the concession of the deputy governorship slot, and cabinet appointments appeared to be an attempt to broker a truce between the two factions.

But Mr Nakudu’s aggressive repudiation of the document indicated that negotiations not only collapsed, but have degenerated into open warfare.

“I, Senator Sabo Mohammed Nakudu, CON, Governorship Candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Jigawa State, for the 2027 General Elections, hereby categorically disclaim and repudiate the purported agreement currently in circulation and allegedly entered into between me and Hon. Bashir Adamu Jumbo, OFR.

“I did not negotiate, execute, approve, authorise, consent to, adopt or ratify the said agreement, nor am I aware of or bound by its purported terms.

“I specifically dissociate myself from the provisions relating to the alleged 60:40 power-sharing formula, Deputy Governorship arrangement, allocation of elective positions and Federal or State appointments. NI authorised no person or group to make such commitments on my behalf.

“I therefore urge all persons, institutions, political actors and media organisations to refrain from treating, publishing or circulating the document as an agreement duly executed or authorised by me, and to correct any contrary representation.

“In view of the seriousness of the matter, I shall pursue all appropriate legal and lawful remedies against any person found responsible for fabricating, altering, falsely attributing, unlawfully using or circulating the document or my purported signature”, Mr Nakudu stated in August.

Observers stated that Mr Nakudu has crossed the point of no return because when intra-party disputes escalate from political horse-trading to accusations of forgery and criminal fabrication, formal party reconciliation mechanisms become ineffective.

Strategic fallout ahead of the election

The ongoing crisis leaves the ADC structurally compromised on two major fronts: Mr Jumbo is strong in his Jigawa North-west (Kazaure zone) home district. If his loyalists feel excluded and manipulated by forged agreements, the party risks a mass exodus or silent sabotage at the polls.

Instead of mounting a common campaign against the ruling APC, the ADC is burning critical momentum, resources, and public credibility on internal litigation and media warfare.

Analysts say that while Mr Nakudu’s disclaimer may protect his legal position and executive leverage, it confirmed that the Jigawa ADC is divided.

Unless the party hierarchy manages an extraordinary intervention, this bitter battle may render the ADC ineffective well before the first ballot is cast in 2027.

The rift is also threatening to undermine the chances of the ADC presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, in the state.

Mr Jumbo’s faction accused Mr Nakudu of refusing to campaign for Atiku, noting that his campaign posters do not feature an image of the presidential candidate.

Speaking on Freedom Radio, Nasiru Laraba, a loyalist of Mr Jumbo, accused Mr Nakudu of working to weaken Atiku’s support base for the benefit of President Bola Tinubu.

Mr Laraba challenged Mr Nakudu to openly campaign for Atiku, who is widely believed to have backed Mr Jumbo in the party’s primary.

“Why is the governorship candidate not campaigning for Atiku in this state, as is being done elsewhere?” Mr Laraba asked.

He added that individuals who joined the party only a few months ago were attempting to destabilise it.

Substitution of candidates

Mr Nakudu is reportedly furious over the party headquarters’ decision to substitute his running mate, Aminu Ibrahim, with Balarabe Kaugama.

Several other candidates have also been replaced, including Zakari Alhaji-Sidi, a popular House of Representatives candidate for the Hadejia, Kafin-Hausa, and Auyo federal constituency who had won convincingly in the primary.

The state’s ADC chairperson, Sani Muhammad, told PREMIUM TIMES that about eight members who won the party’s primaries for legislative seats were replaced.

Mr Muhammad said the state leadership had raised concerns over the situation.

“Among the affected flagship positions is Zakari Alhaji-Sidi, as well as the deputy governorship candidate initially nominated by Sabo Nakudu, who was unexpectedly replaced with Balarabe Kaugama.

“We believe that a governorship candidate has the prerogative to select their running mate, which Sabo Nakudu exercised. The exact reasons for this subsequent replacement remain unclear.

“The substitutions have been reported across several House of Assembly constituencies, including Birnin Kudu, Taura, Yankwashi, Birniwa, Kaugama, Hadejia, and Bulangu. In each of these instances, duly elected primary winners were replaced by individuals who did not win the party’s primary elections.

“At the state level, we have fulfilled our responsibilities; we do not have the authority to alter or replace candidates locally.

“We have formally forwarded these complaints to the party’s national headquarters and are currently awaiting their response. We hope the issue will be resolved before it is too late”, Mr Muhammad told our reporter on the phone.

World.title: Lagos assembly approves N4.445trn 2026 budget reordering
World.content:
The Lagos State House of Assembly on Tuesday approved the 2026 Budget Reordering Bill, adjusting the allocation of the state’s N4.445 trillion budget.

The bill was passed after lawmakers considered and adopted the report of the House Committee on Economic Planning and Budget, TVC reported.

Presenting the report, the committee chairman, Olumoh Sa’ad, said the review followed differences in the implementation of capital projects by ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs).

He stated that some MDAs had recorded higher implementation of their capital allocations, while others had spent less than what was provided for their projects.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The committee explained that the state’s overall budget performance stood at 69 per cent as of 30 June.

It put recurrent revenue performance at 79 per cent, while recurrent and capital expenditure stood at 73 per cent and 66 per cent respectively.

Under the reordered budget, N2.077 trillion will be spent on recurrent expenditure, while N2.368 trillion is allocated to capital projects.

The areas covered include transportation infrastructure, hospital projects, housing, environmental sanitation and waste management, security and emergency equipment.

After the debate, the lawmakers adopted the committee’s recommendations and passed the bill following a vote by Speaker Mudashiru Obasa.

Mr Obasa directed the Clerk to communicate the resolutions of the House to the relevant authorities.

The assembly later adjourned plenary to 2 November.

Background

The assembly approved Lagos’ 2026 budget in January at N4.444 trillion, after Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu presented a N4.237 trillion proposal to the lawmakers in November 2025.

The governor described the proposal as the “Budget of Shared Prosperity” and said it was intended to improve infrastructure, support economic growth and improve residents’ welfare.

The budget approved in January provided N2.107 trillion for recurrent expenditure and N2.338 trillion for capital projects.

Governor Sanwo-Olu later signed the appropriation bill into law.

The latest review came after the Assembly examined the implementation of the budget by the state’s MDAs during the year.

World.title: Bandits kill two police officers in Benue ambush
World.content:
Two newly deployed Mobile Police officers attached to Ayilamo community in Logo Local Government Area of Benue State have been killed in an ambush by armed attackers.

The incident occurred at about 6 p.m. on Monday, 14 September, while the officers were escorting the Divisional Police Officer (DPO) of Ayilamo, who was returning to the community from Makurdi.

This makes it six police officers killed in Ayilamo within four days, following the death of four Mobile Police officers during an attack on the community on Thursday, 10 September.

The spokesperson for the Benue State Police Command, Peter Aondongu, confirmed the latest incident to journalists in Makurdi on Tuesday.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The DPO’s entourage was ambushed on its way back from Makurdi to Ayilamo,” Mr Aondongu said.

He confirmed that two policemen were killed in the attack.

The identities of the two officers were not immediately disclosed at the time of filing this report.

Residents told PREMIUM TIMES that the attackers were suspected to be armed herders operating from forests and deserted villages within the Tombo Council Ward of Logo Local Government Area.

The residents expressed concern over the movement of armed men through forests and abandoned settlements in the area and called for sustained security operations to prevent further attacks.

Four police officers killed days earlier

The latest attack occurred four days after suspected armed herders attacked Ayilamo, killing four police officers and seven civilians.

The police said the attackers invaded the community at about 6:12 p.m. and engaged the police in a gun battle that lasted several hours.

According to the command, Police Mobile Force personnel, tactical teams and conventional police officers responded to the attack. Eventually, it repelled the attackers into the surrounding forest in the early hours of Friday, 11 September.

The four officers killed in that attack were identified as Paul Ina, Mohammed Yusuf, Oge Ikechukwu and Edeh Andrew.

Their bodies were recovered from surrounding bushes during search and rescue operations, while the bodies of seven civilians were also recovered and deposited at a mortuary.

A resident, Tyolumun Ugande, had told journalists that about 200 suspected armed herders invaded the community, shooting residents and burning houses.

The Secretary of the Ayilamo Security Committee, Umishi Terungwa, also confirmed the attack and said the victims included community elders, residents and security personnel.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on Friday, 11 September, that the police later confirmed 11 deaths in the attack, comprising four officers and seven civilians.

Police pay families of fallen officers

The latest killing came on the same day the Benue Police Command presented insurance cheques to families of deceased police officers at its headquarters in Makurdi.

Presenting the cheques on Tuesday, 15 September, the Commissioner of Police, Cletus Nwadiogbu, conveyed the condolences of the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, to the families of officers who died in the line of duty.

Mr Nwadiogbu said no financial assistance could adequately compensate for the loss of a loved one. Still, he noted that the insurance benefits were intended to provide relief and support to affected families.

He urged the beneficiaries to use the funds judiciously, particularly to address immediate needs and support the welfare of their families and children.

The command said the initiative was part of efforts by the Inspector-General of Police to support families of officers who died while serving the country.

The presentation came as the command continued to deal with fresh losses among its personnel in Ayilamo.

Ayilamo police division

Ayilamo Police Station was upgraded to a divisional headquarters in August 2025 as part of a restructuring of policing in Benue State.

On 20 August 2025, the police announced that the then Inspector-General of Police, Kayode Egbetokun, had approved the creation of two new area commands and the upgrade of five police stations to divisional status.

Ayilamo was among the five stations upgraded, alongside Yelewata, Jato-Aka, Okpokolo and Agan.

The police said the restructuring followed an assessment that identified geographical gaps between police formations and vulnerable communities in troubled areas.

The then police spokesperson, Udeme Edet, said the changes were intended to improve police response in difficult terrain, resolve farmer-herder conflicts and respond more quickly to distress calls.

Despite the restructuring, Ayilamo has continued to face attacks, with six police officers now killed in separate incidents within four days.

The latest attack is expected to renew calls for increased security presence and sustained operations in forests and abandoned settlements around Ayilamo and other vulnerable communities in Logo Local Government Area.

World.title: 2027 Campaign Promises: Can Nigerian politicians be taken seriously?
World.content:
By Gabriel Ewepu, ABUJA

As politicians return to the campaign trail ahead of 2027 general polls, Nigerians are asking whether another season of grand pledges will produce a different reality after the votes are counted.

Read Also: 2027: APC govs at daggers-drawn with Wike

It is an old political ritual in Nigeria. Whenever fresh election approaches, politicians dust off their manifestos, polish their slogans, print colourful posters, mount giant billboards and take their campaigns to the streets, villages, markets, town halls and social media.

The promises come thick and fast – Free education, affordable healthcare, stable electricity, good roads, potable pipe-borne water, jobs, food security, youth empowerment, agricultural interventions, better workers’ welfare, affordable housing, improved security, cheap petrol, functional refineries, and bigger business opportunities among others.

Many Nigerians are not really showing interest in these campaign promises due to past failures by the same politicians, who have frustrated them by not keeping to their promises most times.

Since the military government of General Abdulsalami Abubakar announced Nigeria’s return to democratic rule in 1998, and the country transitioned to civil rule in 1999, campaign promises have remained one of the most powerful tools politicians deploy to win the hearts, and votes of the electorate.

From presidential candidates to governors, National Assembly members, State Assembly candidates, local government chairmen and councillors, the script has often been remarkably similar: promise the people a better life and ask them for their votes.

Yet, decades after the return to democracy, millions of Nigerians still struggle with the same basic necessities that politicians have repeatedly promised to provide.

Electricity remains unreliable, roads are deteriorating, healthcare is unaffordable or inaccessible to many, unemployment and underemployment remain major concerns, access to potable water is still a challenge in many communities, security remains a major issue, while quality education, affordable housing and sustainable social protection continue to elude large numbers of citizens.

And now, with the 2027 general elections approaching, the political machinery is warming up again. The campaign season is expected to be colourful, noisy and heavily choreographed complete with posters, rallies, motorcades, support groups, endorsements, social media campaigns, and inevitably, promises.

There may also be the familiar distribution of food items and other handouts to women, youths and vulnerable voters: bags of rice, beans, garri, semovita, salt, seasoning, pepper, vegetable oil and, in some cases, cash.

For many Nigerians, however, the question is no longer whether politicianscan make attractive promises. The question is whether those promises can be trusted.

Promises at the polls, betrayal in power?

Nigeria’s electoral politics has increasingly come to resemble a theatre of magnificent promises and disappointing realities.

During campaigns, politicians often promise voters almost everything they desire: corruption will be defeated, electricity will become stable, roads will improve, jobs will multiply, hospitals and schools will function better, poverty will decline and living standards will rise. Hope is packaged, branded and sold to the electorate.

But once the election is won and political offices are secured, some of those promises appear to lose their urgency. The campaign language fades, billboards come down, rallies end, and handshakes stop.

And for the voter, reality begins.

The gap between what was promised and what is delivered has become one of the most troubling questions confronting Nigeria’s democracy.

The corruption paradox

The fight against corruption provides perhaps one of the clearest examples. Successive governments have described corruption as a major enemy of national development. Political campaigns frequently feature pledges to eliminate corruption, strengthen institutions, recover stolen public funds and promote transparency.

Yet allegations of mismanagement, patronage, abuse of public resources and questionable public spending continue to dominate national conversations.

This creates a troubling paradox. If corruption is repeatedly identified as a major obstacle to development, why does it remain so deeply embedded in the political system? And if politicians campaign on promises to fight it, who holds them accountable when the promised battle produces little visible change?

The same contradiction appears across other sectors

Promises of better healthcare confront overcrowded and poorly equipped facilities, quality education confront inadequate infrastructure and struggling institutions, reliable electricity confront businesses and households forced to find alternative sources of power, improved transportation, clean water, affordable housing and food security often collide with the economic realities facing ordinary citizens.

For millions of Nigerians, therefore, the promised “better life” has become something repeatedly announced during election campaigns but insufficiently experienced afterwards.

‘Don’t allow sugar-coated politicians to deceive you’ — Thompson

For Daniel Thompson, a civil servant in Bayelsa State, Nigerians should approach the 2027 election with caution.

Thompson believes voters have heard enough promises and should stop allowing political rhetoric to determine their choices.

“Citizens should stop trusting politicians but trust themselves by voting the right persons of their choice”, he said.

His position reflects a growing sentiment among voters who believe campaign promises have become little more than political bait, carefully packaged words designed to attract votes but often abandoned once politicians settle into office.

‘Campaign promises are a hoax’ — Ejegwa

Gabriel Ejegwa, an Abuja-based businessman, is even blunt as he described Nigeria’s political campaigns over the years as deeply disappointing, arguing that the distance between what politicians say during campaigns and what ordinary Nigerians experience after elections remains too wide.

“Nigeria’s elections have never been purpose-driven. Party manifestos or campaign slogans say a lot, but the reality to the common Nigerian says otherwise”, Ejegwa said.

For him, the problem is not a shortage of manifestos, it is the absence of accountability.

“So, do we believe in the loud words of political parties? In my opinion, it is a hoax. Until words are matched with actions, only then will the electorate begin to give attention to the endless promises of campaign slogans”, he stated.

His argument raises a fundamental question about Nigeria’s democracy: What happens when voters repeatedly hear promises but rarely see measurable results?

Voter education must take centre stage — Faro

However, not everyone believes Nigerians should completely abandon trust in politicians. Human rights lawyer and Principal Counsel of Idris Faro & Co., Idris Faro, believes the solution lies in making voters more informed and more demanding.

According to him, civil society organisations and other stakeholders must intensify voter education ahead of the 2027 elections.

This, he said, should go beyond telling people where and when to vote. Nigerians must be taught how to scrutinise campaign promises, interrogate manifestos and assess the records of candidates.

“Some elective office holders have performed well and can be trusted by the citizens”, Faro said.

He noted that some politicians had positively affected the lives of their constituents through important projects, policies and effective representation, “For this group of politicians, they have the continued support of the people.” he added.

”But for politicians who have failed in office, Faro believes voters must be willing to reject them.

“This is the time for voters to employ logic and critically assess candidates and their party’s manifesto before deciding on who to support”, he said.

The 2027 election season, he argued, gives Nigerians an opportunity to “score” political parties and candidates based on their records, promises and capacity to deliver.

For politicians who have previously occupied public office, he said their records should be thoroughly examined before voters decide whether to return them to power.

Performance, not propaganda, should determine political reward. Faro also urged Nigerians to give serious consideration to new politicians who have demonstrated competence and professional accomplishment.

“We can’t make progress if we keep on recycling failed public men in Nigeria,” he warned.

He further urged voters to reject what is often described as “stomach infrastructure” – the distribution of food, cash and other temporary inducements – as a substitute for meaningful development.

“The people, especially those who vote, should shun stomach infrastructures and use physical infrastructure to assess candidates.

“Voter education is crucial in fostering good governance and upholding the rule of law. Without this, meaningful development will not happen”, he added.

Nigerians don’t need promises; they need demands met’ — Usamot

In his reaction, Kayode Usamot, a Chartered Accountant and Principal Partner of Kayode A. Usamot & Co., said the electorate should not be dazzled by campaign rhetoric.

Politicians, he said, must be subjected to a more rigorous test before they are entrusted with public office.

“Politicianswill not give citizens what they deserve, but what they demand”, Usamot stated.

He urged Nigerians to be deliberate about their choices in the 2027 elections, “Test must come before trust”, and also stressed the importance of examining a candidate’s history, previous performance, understanding of Nigeria’s problems and capacity to develop practical solutions.

For him, voters should look beyond speeches and ask difficult questions; What has the candidate done before? What problems has the candidate solved? What is the candidate’s understanding of Nigeria’s economic and social challenges? Are the proposed solutions realistic? And, perhaps most importantly, why should Nigerians believe this particular politician will do what previous politicians failed to do? Those questions, Usamot believes, should form the basis of electoral decisions.

‘99.99 per cent of politicians are dishonest’ — Dabor

Henry Dabor, a Lagos-based businessman, has little faith in the promises politicians are likely to make ahead of 2027.

“Certainly citizens can’t trust politicians and their campaign promises when 99.99 per cent of the so-called politicians are dishonest”, Dabor asserted.

To illustrate his point, he pointed to the legacy of former Lagos State governor, Alhaji Lateef Jakande.

He contrasted Jakande’s reputation for modest living and social programmes with what he sees as the extravagant lifestyle associated with some contemporary political office holders.

“Compare what Alhaji Lateef Jakande did for Lagosians and non-Lagosians and the life he lived, breathing his last breath in his humble Ilupeju residence, and our private-jet-flying governors of today. It’s like night and day,” he said.

He recalled his own experience of benefiting from some of Jakande’s educational policies, “I read Jakande textbooks, free maths-set and didn’t pay a penny.”

He also pointed to the former governor’s low-cost housing programme, arguing that access to such housing appeared less dependent on political connections.

“I know so many people who bought those low-cost housing flats who knew nobody. Can anyone realistically buy a flat today in Lagos if you find any?”, he asked.

Politicians need to face consequences for failed campaign promises – Dr Jerry

A final word from the public affairs analyst and economist, Dr Oboh Sankay Jerry, captures the dilemma succinctly: Nigeria’s democracy will mature when elections become less about attractive promises and more about measurable performance.

In Dr Jerry’s assessment, politicians must be held accountable for their commitments, while voters must approach elections with questions, evidence and sound judgement rather than emotion.

The implication is clear

He said: “Campaign promises should not be treated as disposable political slogans. They should be treated as commitments made to the Nigerian people.

“And when those commitments are broken, there must be political consequences. For 2027, perhaps the question should no longer be: “What will you promise us?”

“The question should be: “What have you done, how will you do it, when will you do it — and how can we hold you accountable if you fail?”

As Usamot puts it: “Test must come before trust.” That may be one of the most important principles Nigerians should carry into the 2027 elections. Trust should not be demanded. It should be earned, and it should be earned through character, competence, history, transparency and results.

Nigeria cannot continue to build its political future on promises that disappear after elections. The country needs a political culture in which voters remember what politicians promised, and politicians know that voters will remember.

That is where accountability begins, democracy becomes meaningful, and that is where the cycle of promises at the polls and disappointment in power can finally begin to break. ‘We can’t make progress by recycling failure’

The warning from human rights lawyer Idris Faro deserves particular attention: Nigeria cannot make meaningful progress by repeatedly recycling failed public officials simply because they have political structures, money, party machinery or familiar names. The electorate has a powerful weapon: the ballot but a weapon unused is a weapon surrendered.

The 2027 election should therefore not be merely another contest over who can make the loudest promise. It should be a referendum on performance, competence and credibility. Candidates should be asked to defend their records. Parties should be asked to defend their manifestos. Governments should be asked to defend their achievements, and voters should be prepared to defend their choices because ultimately, democracy is not just about choosing leaders.

It is about choosing wisely — and making those leaders answer for the choices they make with the power entrusted to them.

That is the conversation Nigeria needs before the next ballot is cast.

World.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, September 16, 2026
World.content:
The Nigerian naira is trading at different levels against the United States dollar across the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and the parallel market on Wednesday, September 16, 2026.

The latest available official data from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) put the NFEM rate at ₦1,329.15 per dollar for the September 15 trading session. The CBN describes the NFEM rate as the volume-weighted average and the official exchange rate for the day.

In the parallel market, the dollar is currently quoted at about ₦1,380 for buying and ₦1,385 for selling, according to Aboki Forex’s latest market update. The platform says its parallel-market rates are updated hourly based on rates collected from dealers across major Nigerian cities.

This means buyers looking to purchase $1 in the parallel market may need about ₦1,385, while those selling a dollar could receive around ₦1,380, depending on the dealer, location and transaction size.

The difference between the NFEM rate and the parallel-market selling rate is about ₦55.85 per dollar, while the gap between the official rate and the parallel-market buying rate stands at about ₦50.85.

The spread between the two markets remains an important indicator for businesses and individuals who rely on foreign exchange for imports, international payments, tuition, travel and other dollar-denominated transactions.

Market rates can change during the day as dollar supply and demand fluctuate. Aboki Forex also cautions that parallel-market rates may vary by location, dealer and transaction size.

For official transactions, the applicable exchange rate will depend on the authorised financial institution and the prevailing NFEM rate, while parallel-market transactions may attract different buying and selling rates.

As of Wednesday, September 16, 2026, the latest figures show the dollar at ₦1,329.15 at the NFEM, while the parallel market is around ₦1,380 buying and ₦1,385 selling.

World.title: ‘Let’s not seek change for sake of change,’ Oba of Benin backs continuity
World.content:
Oba of Benin, His Royal Majesty Omo N’Oba N’Edo Uku Akpolokpolo Oba Ewuare II (middle) and members of the Presidential Campaign Council led by its Director-General, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, during the courtesy visit to the Palace of the Oba of Benin on Tuesday.

By Ozioruva Aliu

BENIN CITY — The Oba of Benin, His Majesty, Omo N’Oba N’Edo Uku Akpolokpolo, Ewuare II, on Tuesday urged opposition parties in Nigeria not to be extremely critical of the ruling party, but to play their role as opposition for the betterment of the country.

Read Also: 2027: APC govs at daggers-drawn with Wike

The Benin monarch also urged Nigerians to support continuity in governance and not seek change just for the sake of change.

The monarch spoke on Tuesday when the Director-General of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council (PCC), Abdulaziz Yari, led members of the council to the Benin Palace to seek royal blessings, prayers and support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election in 2027.

Oba Ewuare II said the Benin throne was not partisan, adding that his position should not be interpreted as support for any political party.

“The Benin throne is not partisan. There is no point for change for the sake of change. That is not to say that I belong to one party or the other.

“Is there anybody who is as perfect as I am talking now? Nobody. I love and like peace and tranquillity. I am American and British trained as a diplomat, and I say it the way it is,” he said.

Oba Ewuare II also appealed to former governors, senators and other political leaders to work together in the interest of the country, stressing the importance of cooperation between the ruling party and the opposition.

“In democracy there must be opposition when a party comes to power. I don’t see why an opposition party can’t support the ruling party,” he said.

Earlier, Yari said the mission of the council to the palace was to seek royal blessings, prayers and support for the re-election of President Bola Tinubu, whom he described as the monarch’s son.

The former Zamfara State governor said the Tinubu administration had made progress in the economy, citing changes in GDP growth, inflation and foreign exchange stability.

Yari said Nigeria’s annual GDP growth had risen from 2.7 per cent in 2023 to 3.9 per cent, while inflation had declined from 22.9 per cent to 15.9 per cent.

He added that the administration had stabilised the foreign exchange market and described Tinubu as the right person to lead the country.

Also, the Deputy Governor of Edo State, who stood in for Governor Monday Okpebholo, Rt. Hon. Dennis Idahosa, thanked the Oba of Benin for his royal blessings, noting that the President deserved a second term and that Southern Nigeria also deserved a second term.

“For us in Edo State, Governor Monday Okpebholo is the leader and he is leading well as we have a lot of projects to campaign with and the people of Edo State will vote massively for President Tinubu to enable him win the 2027 Presidential election”.

In Yari’s entourage were the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Sen. George Akume; former Kano State Governor, Abdullahi Umar Ganduje; former Katsina State Governor, Aminu Bello Masari; and former Borno State Governor, Ali Modu Sheriff.

Also in the delegation were former President of the Senate, Pius Ayim; Hon. James Faleke; Sunday Sunday Dare; Abdul’malik Zubairu; Prof. Joseph Terlumun; Professor Ussiju Medaner Al-Mustapha; Lawal Funtua; Lawal M. Liman; Muhammad Gololo; and Nasiruddeen Abdul’aziz Yari.

World.title: Poco Lee: UK court fixes new date after setback
World.content:
A UK court has adjourned the plea and trial preparation hearing involving Nigerian dancer and entertainer Iweh Pascal Odinaka, popularly known as Poco Lee, to February 2027.

The case came up on Tuesday at Snaresbrook Crown Court, but proceedings could not go ahead because the charge sheet was unavailable.

According to BBC News Pidgin, Poco Lee did not appear in court and consequently did not enter a plea.

The report stated, “In court, Poco Lee did not appear because the charge sheet was not available. As a result, he did not enter a plea.”

Snaresbrook Crown Court has now fixed February 8, 2027, for the plea and trial preparation hearing, when Poco Lee is expected to indicate whether he is guilty or not guilty of the charges against him.

“However, the pre-trial hearing will now take place on 8 February 2027, and he is expected to enter his plea at that time.”

“The trial has also been scheduled for 8 March 2027,” the BBC report stated.

The development followed Poco Lee’s earlier appearance before the court, after which he was granted bail on September 11.

Some Nigerians reportedly attended Tuesday’s proceedings in support of the entertainer, with the court gallery said to have reached capacity while others waited outside.

Following Poco Lee’s first court appearance, reports circulated that he had been granted bail, while videos emerged online showing the entertainer speaking about his experience in the UK.

Snaresbrook Crown Court subsequently confirmed the bail decision to the BBC, with the report stating that Poco Lee remained on bail.

Poco Lee studied Microbiology at Lagos State University (LASU) and rose to prominence around 2018 after videos of his legwork dance performances went viral.

World.title: ‘They are politically lazy’ – Wike tackles APC govs over Rainbow Coalition pushback
World.content:
Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has described governors of the All Progressives Congress as “politically lazy” following their opposition to his Rainbow Coalition ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The governors, led by their chairman and Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, had said they would not participate in, support or endorse any alliance that could undermine President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid or affect APC candidates at any level.

But Wike, in an interview on Arise TV’s Prime Time on Tuesday, dismissed the concerns, arguing that his decision to support Tinubu did not mean he had abandoned his political party or agreed that other parties should not field candidates.

“They are politically lazy. When you have your local problems, don’t use Mr President as your excuse,” Wike said.

The minister maintained that the disagreements surrounding his political activities did not start with his decision to support Tinubu, recalling that he had faced opposition even when he was serving as governor of Rivers State and later as FCT minister.

“This thing did not start today. It started at ministerial position. They were not happy that I was Minister of FCT. Also, they were unhappy when I was governor,” he said.

Wike said his knowledge of the political situation was greater than that of those criticising his activities, suggesting that his critics would understand his position better if they had access to the information available to him.

“If they know what I know, they would not come out to shout,” he said.

The former Rivers State governor also insisted that his support for Tinubu remained unchanged, arguing that supporting the President was separate from the activities of his political party.

“I have said I will support the President and I am still supporting him. What has that got to do with my party?” Wike asked.

The minister further cited the political activities of governors such as Anambra State Governor Chukwuma Soludo, Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke and Abia State Governor Alex Otti to argue that support for a presidential candidate should not prevent political parties from presenting candidates at other levels.

“Take Soludo, Adeleke and Otti. Does it mean that their parties will not present other candidates? This thing they are saying does not have any basis,” he said.

Wike also recalled the 2023 presidential election, saying his decision to support Tinubu was based on his belief that it was the South’s turn to produce the President after the Muhammadu Buhari administration.

“Recall that in 2023, as far as the President is concerned, it is my belief that it was the time of the South and so it would be unfair that it goes back to the North,” he said.
