World.title: State of U.S. democracy reaches new low, report finds
World.content:
State of U.S. democracy reaches new low, report finds

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP

U.S. democracy has reached its lowest levels in 50 years, according to a new global report that tracks democratic performance around the world.

For several years, Dr. Seema Shah, who heads the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance's democracy assessment team, said their researchers have observed a global pattern of democratic decline: "Severe drops in scores that measure freedom of expression, freedom of the press, credible elections, effective parliament," she said.

Shah says that in the 50 years of compiling this survey, she's seen undemocratic trends like this correcting themselves.

But not this time.

Sponsor Message

"It's getting worse and worse," Shah says. "So that's really worrying, especially because we also see that people are more willing in some cases to consider non-democratic leadership or non-democratic governance."

The organization's annual Global State of Democracy report, which tracks democratic performance across 174 countries and draws on data going back to 1975, was released Tuesday. The latest report focuses on changes in democratic performance between 2020 and 2025.

And Shah says one country stood out for how far its democracy has declined. "The clearest example, unfortunately, is the United States," she says.

The report says that in 2025, "President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies. … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation."

Shah says the U.S. has historically served as a bastion of democratic governance, with strong performance in the rule of law and judicial independence and a prominent role in promoting democracy around the world. "But that's no longer the case," says Shah.

"Inside the U.S. and outside the U.S., we're seeing in the U.S. administration policies harming domestic democracy...but also really weakening global norms and actually providing fodder for other non-democratic leaders."

Sponsor Message

Democracy, she notes, is no longer the central focus of U.S. foreign policy.

Democratic values are also no longer the basis for new alliances globally, Shah says, noting that the democratic aid the U.S. used to provide to developing countries has been dismantled.

President Trump has hinted at this himself. At a summit last year in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, he criticized previous U.S. administrations as "interventionist" and said the U.S. would no longer give other countries "lectures on how to live."

Domestically, Shah says, the U.S. has seen declines in nearly half of the 30 indicators the organization measures. She says they've hit their lowest levels in 50 years of gathering data on democracies.

And it's not just the U.S. seeing these declines.

The organization's survey shows that 57% of countries surveyed showed declines in at least one key indicator of democratic performance, with the rule of law serving as the weakest-performing area of democracy globally.

But what about countries that have seen a resurgence of democracy — places like Poland, Hungary and Syria in recent years?

"What the research shows is that, depressingly, in 90% of cases, a democracy that has suffered decline and then comes back and what's called a U-turn in 90% of the cases, they suffer another democratic decline within five years."

Shah says candidates promising change typically find that when voters give them power, they often are not able to deliver on those promises because remnants of the old guard often prevent those changes.

"And unless," she says, "you're willing to break your own democratic laws to get them out, what can you do?"

World.title: Family income rose and poverty fell in 2025 — but safety net cuts could erase gains
World.content:
Family income rose and poverty fell in 2025 — but safety net cuts could erase gains

toggle caption Patrick T. Fallon/AFP

The average American family made more money last year than in 2024, while the number of people living in poverty fell slightly, according to a new report from the Census Bureau.

The annual snapshot of last year's family income, poverty and health coverage comes as Americans are currently wrestling with stubborn inflation that's been rekindled by the war with Iran. Prices have been climbing faster than average wages for the last five months.

In 2025, by contrast, families saw real improvements in their purchasing power. The average family's income rose 2.6% last year, after adjusting for inflation, to $87,460. Families at the top of the income ladder saw bigger gains than those at the bottom.

Analysts say those gains could be eroded by cuts to the social safety net. In 2025, programs such as Supplemental Nutrition Assistance (SNAP) helped keep many families out of poverty, as measured by a special yardstick that includes government aid. Some of those programs are being scaled back as part of the sweeping tax cut package passed by the GOP Congress last year. Results of those cuts are likely to be reflected in future Census tallies.

Sponsor Message

Health insurance coverage held steady in 2025 but is expected to fall now that enhanced subsidies for Obamacare coverage have lapsed. Stricter work requirements for Medicaid are also set to take effect next year.

"Things like SNAP and Medicaid made a really big difference in lowering poverty and expanding health coverage," says Sharon Parrott, president of the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. "Instead of building on that improvement and recognizing the record of success of things like SNAP and Medicaid, Republican policymakers enacted very deep cuts, historically large cuts that right now are taking food assistance and health coverage away from people, putting upward pressure on poverty, increasing the ranks of the uninsured, and really taking us in the wrong direction."

The share of people living in poverty declined last year to 10.2% from 10.7% in 2024. In 2025, 34.5 million people in the country fell below the poverty line, compared to 36 million the previous year.

A supplemental measure of poverty, which accounts for taxes, government benefits and additional expenses showed somewhat higher levels of poverty — 13.1%. This figure was little changed from 2024.

While average family income rose last year, some families did better than others. Families in the top 10% of income saw gains of 1.7%, while those in the bottom 10% saw little change. On average, African American families saw the largest increase in income last year — 4.8% — but at $59,980, the median income among Black families remains far lower than for white ($91,930) or Asian ($126,300) families.

Sponsor Message

"2025 becomes a benchmark of sorts," Parrott says. "We saw these modest gains. We saw some improvement in poverty. We saw health insurance hold steady at relatively low rates. And we saw real wage gains. And on almost every measure, things are worse today."

World.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close it, as judge again keeps Trump's name off
World.content:
Kennedy Center board votes to close it, as judge again keeps Trump's name off

toggle caption Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

The Kennedy Center's board of directors on Tuesday voted to close the historic arts center in a meeting that began just minutes after a federal judge once again stopped a plan to put President Trump's name on the building.

The president immediately vowed to cancel a planned renovation of the facility unless the decision about adding his name is reversed by a higher court.

Trump wrote: "The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name. If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place."

Sponsor Message

The plaintiff in the federal suit, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Democrat of Ohio, filed Trump's statement with the federal judge.

Administrators of the Kennedy Center told the board in recent days that the physical plant of the complex's main building is unsafe, and that the center's finances are "within weeks" of bankruptcy .

Kennedy Center officials did not reply to NPR's requests for comment.

Limited offerings will remain

Even before Tuesday's vote, the Kennedy Center was down to a skeletal version of itself. Ticket sales had plummeted, and many prominent artists had canceled planned appearances, saying that the center had become politicized under Trump. There were very few events on the calendar. Most of the administrative staff had already either been fired or had left.

The board has been signposting its desire to close the center's main venues for months. A small, fairly recently opened extension called the REACH will remain open, in part to fulfill the Congressional mandate of making the living memorial to President John F. Kennedy open and accessible to the public.

Additionally, the board wrote in documents filed with the federal court that it intends to make allowances for two of the center's signature programs, as well as for the National Symphony Orchestra, whose budget is tethered to the Kennedy Center.

Sponsor Message

A proposed resolution by the board, included in those documents, pledges "continued programming in the REACH and offsite," as well as continued support for "the National Symphony Orchestra, and continuing the Center's longstanding tradition of presenting the Kennedy Center Honors and Mark Twain Prize."

That, the resolution adds, will enable enough "engagement" with artists, donors and patrons so that "a two-year closure of the main building will not unduly affect its ability to ramp up programming in a revitalized main building in 2028."

Need for Congressional approval

A lengthy memorandum circulated to the board before the vote, which NPR obtained on Monday, deals strictly with the physical plant. It does not detail any plans of how programming will "ramp up" in the years to come. Marquee artists of the caliber previously presented by the Kennedy Center usually schedule their performances years in advance .

But the board had doubled down on its argument that only Trump can "save" the Kennedy Center. Most of the current Kennedy Center board members are Trump allies who were picked by the president, who now also serves as the arts institution's chair. Those members include individuals like former attorney general Pam Bondi, Fox host Laura Ingraham, and Dana Kraft, the wife of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft – people very close to Trump.

This board has no known experience in the administration of a performing arts institution. The last president of the Kennedy Center, former Ambassador Richard Grenell, tried to insist that every performance be revenue-generating or at least revenue-neutral. Its current executive director and chief operating officer, Matt Floca, was elevated from his position as head of facilities for the Kennedy Center. Unlike his peers at similar centers across the country, Floca has no prior experience in artistic direction, fundraising or arts administration.

Tuesday's board meeting began just minutes after a federal judge, Christopher Cooper, ruled that the board cannot put President Trump's name back on the building, or rename the physical grounds of the arts center as the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

Sponsor Message

In a 22-page decision, Cooper referred to an earlier ruling, as well Congress' mandate regarding the living memorial to John F. Kennedy. "Simply put," he wrote, "Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing. The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted."

The ruling came as part of the ongoing federal lawsuit filed by Rep. Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board. She originally sued last December to stop the board from renaming the arts institution as "The Trump Kennedy Center."

Beatty's lawsuit does not address the renovation plans.

In his decision, Cooper left open for now the possibility of whether or not the board can name its planned $100 million fundraising campaign "The Trump Kennedy Center Fund," or include any such plaque or other signage at the center eventually. The board has said that using Trump's name is crucial to its efforts to raise money for the center. In his decision, Cooper wrote: "The fund has raised nothing yet."

The board has placed Trump at the locus of its efforts, arguing both publicly and in court that the president is the only person who can fundraise at such a massive scale or successfully oversee such an extensive renovation project – and, as such, deserved public credit in the form of signage on the front of the arts complex.

In a statement emailed to NPR Tuesday afternoon, Rep. Beatty wrote: "The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy – and no one else. But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial. The Court just rejected this proposal for the second time. This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop."

World.title: Prosecutors won't seek the death penalty for Nick Reiner
World.content:
Prosecutors won't seek the death penalty for Nick Reiner

toggle caption Chris Torres/Pool EPA via AP

Prosecutors say they will not seek the death penalty for 33-year-old Nick Reiner. Reiner was previously indicted on charges of killing his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner.

"In deciding whether or not the DA's office was going to seek the death penalty, we have gone through a rigorous review, where we look at the aggravating factors as well as the mitigating factors," said Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman at a press briefing Tuesday morning. "After a careful and thorough review of all these factors, the district attorney's office will not be seeking the death penalty in this case."

Sponsor Message

A Los Angeles County grand jury indicted Reiner in July on two counts of first-degree murder. He was first charged with first-degree murder last December, two days after the lethal attack on his parents in their Los Angeles home.

In addition to the double murder charges, Reiner's indictment includes special allegations that he was "lying in wait."

He has pleaded not guilty.

If convicted, Reiner now faces a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Hochman said prosecutors decided against capital punishment after discussions with law enforcement, and consultation with Nick Reiner's siblings, Jake and Romy Reiner.

At a pre-trial hearing, also on Tuesday, regarding whether to unseal grand jury indictment transcripts, Hochman shared statements on behalf of Jake and Romy Reiner. The siblings requested that the transcripts remain sealed to prevent further trauma.

Hochman said that due to the volume of discovery — the information and document gathering before trial — and ongoing legal proceedings, a trial is not anticipated to begin until at least next year.

"The brutal murders of Rob and Michele Reiner are ones that will never leave us," Hochman said. "We will be presenting the evidence that we believe will convict Nick Reiner beyond a reasonable doubt of all the charges he's been filed — that we have filed against him, or that the grand jury has filed at this point — as well as the special allegations."

Sponsor Message

On Monday night, Rob Reiner was honored at the Emmy Awards with a special tribute from Jamie Lee Curtis. He posthumously won an Emmy earlier this month for an appearance on The Bear.

World.title: Stephen Harper says Canada had 'no choice' but to walk away from U.S. trade talks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper, who led Canada's Conservative Party for over a decade, backed the federal government's decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States "to see a trade war commence in earnest."

Harper delivered the closing keynote to hundreds of the world's wealthiest investors gathered in downtown Toronto for the first-of-its-kind Canada Investment Summit.

"This had to be a very difficult decision, but I do believe that our government had no choice but to take this path," Harper said.

Harper, who has described himself as "probably the most pro-American prime minister in Canadian history," acknowledged his own long-held admiration for our southern neighbours.

But Canada needs to remain committed to retaining its economic diversity, Harper argued, not allowing U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to "hollow out" the country's industrial capacity.

"It is clear that the current U.S. administration views our level of economic integration as incompatible with our separate sovereignty," Harper said. "Thus to maintain that sovereignty, we must pursue diminished reliance on the United States."

"I do find this all very sad, just as equally necessary."

WATCH | Harper's full speech at Canada Investment Summit: FULL SPEECH | Harper backs Carney's decision to walk away from U.S. trade talks | Duration 14:40 At Prime Minister Mark Carney's Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper said he believes the Carney government 'had no choice' but to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States and that Canada 'must pursue diminished reliance' on our southern neighbour.

Within Canada's departure from its previous relationship with the U.S., Harper said the country is discovering an opportunity to rediscover its true potential.

"Leadership is defined by taking accountability for what you can control," he said, and Canada cannot only blame external factors for the headwinds it faces.

Harper argued Canada needs to become "more internally competitive, more externally connected and more truly sovereign than it has been."

Harper's remarks formally wrapped the multi-day investment summit which was spearheaded by Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The summit brought together hundreds of business leaders, foreign investors and current and former politicians in the hopes of attracting $1 trillion worth of investments over the next five years to fund big projects across Canada.

Harper attended the summit as the chair of the Alberta Investment Management Corporation (AIMCo), a position he has held since 2024.

The former prime minister told the room of investors that Canada's resource development is its "competitive advantage," and said becoming an energy superpower is "critical to our prosperity and indeed to our survival as a country."

'I wish I had thought of it,' Harper says of summit

Harper faulted the Liberal government that followed his election loss in 2015, saying until that point, "Canada was poised to become that energy superpower."

He said Canada missed that potential "because of deliberate policy choices that followed over the next decade."

"But there is no point bemoaning what is passed," Harper continued. "Especially because the opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again."

Harper congratulated Carney's Liberal government on its efforts to fast-track major project approvals, in particular in Alberta's oilsands. He also commended Ottawa for holding the investment summit.

"It is such a great innovation that I wish I had thought of it," Harper said to a chuckling audience.

Amid the congratulations, Harper was clear: "More does need to be done."

He called for a removal of burdens and restrictions in Canada "that do not exist elsewhere," and for the government to reform its regulatory reviews and permitting processes to provide investors with a degree of certainty, "as we had set up a decade ago."

Harper warned that if the government doesn't clear those hurdles, the U.S. will continue to be Canada's sole customer and "they will not lack the urgency that we have lacked here in Canada."

"That is why I have to say that I am very encouraged by the detailed comments the prime minister made today on doing just some of these things, and I welcome them," Harper said.

"I believe that Canada's new government is committed to further reforms in these areas and committed to their urgency."

Harper's change of tune

Harper's closing keynote endorsing the summit and aspects of the current government's direction is especially notable given the former Conservative prime minister has not always appeared so onside with Carney.

Just last year, Harper accused Carney of inflating the role he played as Bank of Canada governor during the 2008 financial crisis, a crisis managed by Harper's government.

"I have listened, with increasing disbelief, to Mark Carney's attempts to take credit for things he had little or nothing to do with back then," Harper wrote in a fundraising letter at the time.

Carney was Bank of Canada governor between 2008 and 2013, serving under Finance Minister Jim Flaherty. Carney's campaign website stated that he "guided Canada through one of the most turbulent economic periods in modern history, protecting jobs and helping ensure that Canada came out stronger."

During the 2025 election, Harper endorsed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre "without hesitation, without equivocation, without a shadow of a doubt," for prime minister over Carney.

But over the past year, Harper returned to the limelight, delivering a number of speeches calling for Canadian unity and to reduce the country's dependence on an American neighbour that has become "hostile."

In February, Harper said Canada should consider tariffing U.S. goods because a one-sided tariff arrangement could decimate the manufacturing sector. Carney's government mounted counter measures including tariffs against the U.S. after trade talks fell through in August.

World.title: Family of missing B.C. mountaineer believes she fell while descending the Matterhorn
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The family of famed Canadian skyrunner and mountaineer Kalie McCrystal, who went missing on the Matterhorn in the Alps more than two weeks ago, say she "remains among the mountains where she felt most at home."

Her mother and sister say in a statement that everything they know after an extensive search suggests she fell while descending the mountain.

The statement that was shared by British Columbia provincial legislator Amelia Boultbee, a friend of McCrystal, praises search and rescue crews for their efforts and says the family is confident everything possible has been done to find her.

McCrystal was last seen Sept. 1 while attempting to break a mountain-running record in the Alps along the Switzerland-Italy border, climbing the 4,481-metre-tall Matterhorn.

The family statement says friends and loved ones from around the world mobilized and went to remarkable lengths to help find McCrystal and bring her home.

They say not finding her was not the outcome they were hoping for and is difficult to accept.

The statement describes McCrystal as a special person who moved through life with equal parts determination and fun and says her absence will leave a hole in communities in skyrunning, Squamish and beyond.

"While we desperately wish we could have found her, we find peace in knowing that she was doing what made her feel most alive until her very last moments, and that she remains among the mountains where she felt most at home," the statement says.

World.title: Alberta NDP flies the anti-separatist flag to snatch a UCP riding in Calgary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In among all the splashes of Alberta NDP orange and UCP blue, there was plenty of red adorning the front yards of many homes ahead of this week’s Calgary-Shaw byelection.

No, sorry, I’m not talking about Alberta Liberal Leader John Roggeveen and the 3.8 per cent vote share he snagged.

The red refers to the many Canadian flags homeowners have newly erected, and the pro-unity, anti-separatist lawn signs that have sprung up throughout Alberta.

The campaigning New Democrats sensed the kind of reception they’d get at those doors for their candidate Kyle Campbell, now the MLA-elect.

“If you were flying a Canadian flag or you had a forever Canadian sign … Yeah, we pretty much could mark you down as a supporter,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters on Tuesday, the day after his party’s victory in what was previously a UCP riding in Calgary’s deep suburbs.

Campaign signs line a street in the southwest community of Somerset. Residents of Calgary-Shaw converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. (Ryan McLeod/CBC)

It’s often too easy and too foolish to treat the results of a single byelection as a predictor of a general election a year away, although darned if the partisans like Nenshi won’t try.

We’re likely on firmer ground trying to discern what a byelection says about the mood heading into the referendum about Alberta separation that’s set for five weeks from now.

Polls have consistently indicated that Albertans, especially in big cities, resoundingly support the “stay” option and oppose holding a future referendum for independence.

Now, another indication, in the form of voting results. At least in Calgary-Shaw, the public mood has turned against Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservatives, who thrust the province deeper into the unity debate by crafting and scheduling the Oct. 19 vote.

Shaw residents converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. Of the 12 Calgary ridings that Smith’s party took in 2023, Shaw had the third-widest victory margin, a fact that might bring worry to UCP cabinet ministers and backbenchers in the city.

The win in Shaw was somewhat of a surprise to the NDP, judging by, among more publicly available factors, the fact Nenshi said his party’s relatively modest win margin “exceeded my wildest expectations.”

After all, the Opposition party had long been trailing the UCP in public opinion, and Nenshi lagged behind Smith, including in the city he formerly served as mayor. Most voters may have been squarely against separation or even the debate itself, but that dissatisfaction hadn’t been washing up on United Conservative shores. Not yet at least.

Premier Danielle Smith has stated she supports Alberta staying in Canada, and only put the unity question to a referendum because petitioners wanted it. (Joshua McLean/CBC)

Smith and her Shaw candidate Mike Derry might have said repeatedly that they endorse staying in Canada, but Campbell and Nenshi spent much of the campaign trying to remind voters how responsible the UCP government is for the referendum — and that senior organizers in the party favour separation.

How thoroughly did the New Democrats wrap their campaign identity around federalism? After Campbell’s victory speech at a southwest Calgary bar, supporters spontaneously broke into a rendition of O Canada.

After the verdict that got his backers singing, a jubilant Nenshi called the byelection an “earthquake.”

“This means that 35 days from today, we send Danielle Smith and her separatist pals packing, and within a year from now, we give Albertans the NDP government they deserve,” he said.

Sure, Alberta would have a Premier Naheed Nenshi if Shaw’s 18-point swing from UCP to NDP gets translated to the rest of the province in the fall 2027 election.

In the same way that a stunner of a federal Conservative victory in a 2024 byelection in the Toronto riding of St. Paul’s led to Prime Minister Pierre Poilievre in 2025. Or didn’t.

In mid-2024, the Pierre Poilievre Conservatives stole a federal byelection in downtown Toronto, flipping a seat that had been Liberal for three decades. One year and one prime ministerial resignation later, the Liberals took the riding by 28 percentage points, and Mark Carney secured a fourth straight Liberal government term.

Ample time to interpret message

That Toronto byelection sent a political message of sorts that ultimately led to Justin Trudeau’s resignation. There’s ample time and opportunity for Alberta’s premier to interpret the message that voters sent her in the sort of suburban seat her party can’t afford to lose in a general election.

Barring another political “earthquake” on Oct. 19, independence referendums will be a distant memory come next fall. Alberta politics could change a lot before then; heavens knows they’re prone to turbulence.

Smith could pivot her agenda farther away from the independence question. She could give her Opposition less room to cast her as an agent of disunity, and themselves as the exclusive guardians of Alberta’s place within Canada.

It’s also possible United Conservative members give their federalist leader new marching orders on that same matter, and urge her at a November convention to get in line with many party activists and take a more pro-separatist stance.

The future could also be determined by what Calgary-Shaw and other ridings look like in the next election. Alberta’s electoral boundaries are getting revised by an unorthodox UCP-led advisory panel , with the prospect that the cities’ suburban ridings are spliced with more UCP-friendly rural areas.

The October referendum seems to have left its striking imprint in one riding. The boundary revisions will be but one of many factors that will colour in the map when all Albertans get to vote next year.

World.title: Remaining supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran tour amid backlash over Macklemore ousting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hours after singer Ed Sheeran addressed the backlash over rapper Macklemore being ousted from his tour for pro-Palestinian comments onstage, his remaining supporting acts have all quit Sheeran's tour.

Sheeran said in a statement Tuesday that he is "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," calling the suffering on "both sides" a "human tragedy," but defended his choice not to take a public stance.

After he put Macklemore's removal solely on venues and promoters, supporting acts Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Beoga and Finneas announced that they were withdrawing from Sheeran's tour to stand in solidarity with Palestinians — meaning the tour now has no openers.

Sheeran said upcoming venues contacted him after his shows at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium earlier this month, saying they would pull his performances if Macklemore, 43, was not removed as his opening act, because of "how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance," the singer said.

Videos from the performances, which have drawn criticism from pro-Israel groups, show the rapper repeating "Free Palestine" to a cheering crowd and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank. In his speech at the second show on Sept. 5, he addressed Jewish audience members, saying, "criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way is a criticism of you.

"My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality."

In his statement, Sheeran said, "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.

He added that while he tried to "build a bridge," the venues would not change their minds.

Sheeran's band, openers leave

Rowe, one of the co-openers for the remaining U.S. shows, said Sheeran was a friend who had changed his life. But the Irish artist cited his country's history with "genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," as one of the reasons he's dropping out of the tou r.

"I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland."

The sentiments were echoed by Beoga, an Irish band who said they would no longer be serving as Sheeran's backing band for the remaining U.S. tour dates.

"To play in venues that silence anyone advocating for a Free Palestine is simply not an option for us," the band wrote on Instagram.

"As founding members of the Irish Artists For Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be."

Danish artist Lukas Graham, who would've opened in the U.S. alongside Rowe, said on Instagram that it's a "difficult decision" to leave the tour, but that "we should be able to talk about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up.

"Money doesn't give the right to own the conversation."

Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, shared on Instagram that he would be dropping out of upcoming tour dates with Sheeran in South America.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," he wrote .

Macklemore said in a statement Monday that although Sheeran is "a friend" it doesn't "change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened."

"He told me that the words 'Free Palestine' and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with. I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn't get past his public facing, 'I don't take sides.'"

WATCH | Supporting acts quit Sheeran tour after Macklemore ousted: Supporting acts quit Sheeran tour after Macklemore ousted over pro-Palestinian comments | Duration 4:42 Hours after singer Ed Sheeran addressed the backlash over rapper Macklemore's removal from his tour following pro-Palestinian comments onstage, the remaining supporting acts have also quit Sheeran's tour. Sarah Galashan breaks down the latest.

During his set, Macklemore also displayed images of the devastation in Gaza while performing his song, Hind's Hall, about pro-Palestinian student protests, which references Hind Rajab, a child killed by Israeli forces in Gaza.

Amnesty International and a United Nations commission have said Israel's actions in Gaza constitute a genocide. Israel has denied these allegations.

'I have my personal views'

Billionaire Robert Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, was one of the people behind the call for Macklemore's removal, Sheeran confirmed.

Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel, said in a statement shared with CBC News Monday that his stadium would "not provide a platform for hate speech," stating Macklemore spread divisiveness through "selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas."

Backlash against Sheeran was swift online following Macklemore's exit, with critics slamming Sheeran's apolitical stance.

"I am not complicit," Sheeran said in his statement. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."

Ed Sheeran performs in Brooklyn, New York, in September 2025. (Andy Kropa/The Associated Press)

Sheeran said he refrains from weighing in on global events because his audience "includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."

But children's content creator Ms. Rachel, pointed out Tuesday the hypocrisy behind Sheeran participating in charity efforts for Ukraine while considering "Palestine too dangerous and political."

"Imagine being a Palestinian kid and seeing he did a concert for Ukraine but when over 20,000 Palestinian children are killed he's silent," she wrote in an Instagram post . Sheeran was one of the artists who performed at the "Concert for Ukraine" benefit concert in Birmingham, England, in 2022.

The situation has put a renewed spotlight on how artists who speak up about Gaza often face increased scrutiny. Actors have been dropped from projects or agencies for taking public pro-Palestinian stances.

It's unclear if Sheeran's tour will continue its remaining U.S. dates without openers or seek new ones. The U.S. run ends at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Fla., a venue which hosted two Kanye West shows earlier this summer despite calls for cancellation over West's well-documented history of virulent antisemitic statements.

World.title: PM's European address will find an eager audience in a continent rattled by Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of the drawbacks of giving a historic speech like the one that Prime Minister Mark Carney gave in Davos , Switzerland, in January is that people expect an encore every time you speak.

The Carney government has been at pains to lower expectations for anyone who's hoping for another worldwide viral moment when Carney addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday morning.

There will be nothing that will really surprise those who've been following the prime minister's publicly expressed thinking, or the progress of the growing rapprochement between Canada and the European Union, one senior government official told CBC News.

And yet neither the Canadians nor the Europeans are downplaying the large expectations they have for an expanded EU-Canada alliance that goes far beyond the current Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).

Carney 'nailed it' at Davos: EU committee chair

"Europeans looked very positively on him and on that speech in Davos," said Sven Simon, chair of the European Parliament's committee on constitutional affairs. "He nailed it. He put it really in the right direction. I think in those uncertain times, we, both the Europeans and Canadians, have a huge interest in closer co-operation."

Carney himself, while stressing that this trip is not the grand finale of a grand bargain, told Bloomberg News that he expects great things in the future.

"It's an exciting time. Look, it's not going to be solved this week in Strasbourg. This, to be clear, it's the start of a process, but it's the start of a high-ambition process."

WATCH | Power & Politics speaks with EU ambassador to Canada: How much is Trump driving Canada-EU politics? | Duration 8:08 Power & Politics sits down with the EU Ambassador to Canada Geneviève Tuts as Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to address the EU Parliament next week. Tuts says it's ‘even more relevant’ to deepen Canada-EU ties in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump's latest moves.

All indications are that both sides are heavily focused on the Canada-EU Summit scheduled for Oct. 29-30.

"I think that there is a significant step to be done in October because both parties would like to enhance or to elevate their relationship," EU Ambassador to Canada Geneviève Tuts told CBC's Power and Politics .

"We want to reimagine the relationship between the EU and Canada."

Rattled Europeans

Hans-Gert Pöttering, a former president of the European Parliament who visited Canada last week, told CBC News that the Trump administration's treatment of Canada had shocked Europeans.

"There is somebody who wants to make Canada the 51st state of the United States. And all these crazy ideas, I think are the basis that we see how important Canada is for us," he said.

Both Canadian and European officials often say they want to work with "like-minded" allies, and for the Canadians, "like-minded" has increasingly come to mean "European," while for Europeans, it increasingly means "Canadian."

Both sides have poured cold water on any talk of Canada joining the EU. The Canadians say they aren't interested in the basic formula of EU membership under which countries give up some sovereignty in return for access.

WATCH | Carney says Canada not seeking EU membership: Carney shuts down rumours of Canada seeking EU membership | Duration 2:22 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada plans to begin discussions for a 'unique alliance' with the European Union — but not membership — as he gears up to address the European Parliament on Sept. 17. Reporting from the Wall Street Journal said Carney suggested that Canada could take on a title of 'associate member' within the European bloc of 27 countries, a move panned by Conservative critics and one former Liberal leader.

Canada is engaging with Europe in order to strengthen its sovereignty, not to dilute it, a senior official told CBC News.

The same official said that reporting in the Wall Street Journal that suggested Canada was looking to reproduce arrangements that non-EU members such as Norway have with the union — which do involve some concessions on sovereignty — are false.

No name yet to define the relationship

European officials also say they envision an alliance between the EU and Canada, rather than an amalgamation. But the partnership they envision would go further than the current relationship with the United Kingdom.

Germany's David McAllister, who chairs the foreign affairs committee of the European Parliament, told CBC News that neither side had yet paid much attention to labels — but stressed the EU is not trying to get Canada to surrender sovereignty

On the contrary, McAllister, who trained in Manitoba at CFB Shiloh as a young soldier in the German Army, said Europe was willing to collaborate with Canada to protect itself from U.S. threats.

"We in Europe understand that threats and economic pressure against an ally simply damaged the trust which we need among transatlantic allies," he said. "That's why the U.S.-Canadian dispute, which President Trump is responsible for, has received such wide media coverage all over Europe."

On the trade front, 99 per cent of commerce between Canada and the European Union is already tariff-free. Both sides speak about the importance of getting 10 holdout countries, including France and Italy, to ratify CETA, but that's mostly symbolic.

Canada is also already integrated into two vital pan-European projects: the Security Action for Europe ( SAFE ) program that provides low-interest loans for joint military procurement and the Horizon program that funds scientific research.

Untapped possibilities

But both sides say there are areas of co-operation that remain under-exploited or even unexplored.

There have been signs of openness to increased labour mobility, although it's very unlikely that would go as far as the full freedom of movement that exists in the EU.

Two areas appear to be of greatest interest. The first is to use the free trade framework that already exists to build a genuine synergy between Canada's natural resource and energy wealth, and Europe's large market and manufacturing capacity, to the benefit of both economies.

WATCH | Is joining the EU possible? Fact check: Could Canada join the EU? | Duration 1:55 Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada is 'not looking to be a member of the European Union.' But if we did want to join the EU, is that even possible? Here are the facts.

CETA "is actually a fantastic framework, but we are not fully using it either in Europe or in Canada," said Tobias Cremer, who sits on the foreign affairs and defence committees of the European Parliament.

"A lot of our especially medium- and small-sized companies don't even know the potential we have. Canada has all this potential, but the infrastructure for instance isn't actually set up yet to go across the Atlantic."

Both Carney and the Europeans often point out that Europe — large and rich but resource poor — and Canada — lightly populated but resource and energy-rich — complement one another naturally. That is not always as evident in the U.S.-Canada relationship where, in any case, the current U.S. administration views Canada more as a rival than a partner.

A second avenue is to combine forces in sovereignty-protecting projects that would be difficult for Canada to do on its own.

In his interview with Bloomberg, Carney said that "sovereignty is determined by where you stand in a series of strategic capabilities in space, obviously in AI, in sovereign computing, in critical minerals, in energy."

Carney also mentioned financial payments as a potential vulnerability, one of "those interconnections, that integration [that] can be used as leverage against you."

China has long viewed dependence on the U.S. dollar and the U.S.-based SWIFT system for international payments as a weakness, and sought to "de-dollarize" not only its bond holdings but also its trade with other countries. India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. have all set up new facilities for trading payments to avoid the dollar and go around U.S. banks, and increasingly, traditional U.S. allies are thinking along the same lines.

The U.S. would likely perceive any move by Canada and Europe to cut SWIFT out of their trading arrangements as another threat to a U.S. dollar that is already losing ground as the world's go-to currency for trading and saving.

Planning and stockpiling together

Building sovereign resilience could also involve holding shared stockpiles of essentials. The pandemic, as well as transportation bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz and Suez Canal , and the trade disruptions of the Trump era have moved governments away from the just-in-time delivery mentality of a decade ago to one of planning and hoarding.

"We're hearing talk in Canada about stockpiling raw materials," said Mark Camilleri, Brussels-based president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association. "Maybe there's a way that we can work together in a trusted manner, in a more efficient way, in what's becoming a very inefficient world."

Canada is sending a message to the Trump administration, says Brian Clow, former prime minister Justin Trudeau's chief adviser on the Canada-U.S. relationship: "We can sell elsewhere. We can have security partnerships elsewhere."

"Both Europe and Canada are under attack, frankly, by the United States on our economy, on our sovereignty, and that is pushing us closer together," said Clow.

For the Carney government, Europe is not only a place to trade, but also a potential replacement partner with which to integrate sovereign networks, launch satellites, stockpile critical minerals and build a strong defence manufacturing base, or as Carney put it to Bloomberg, a place to "deepen co-operation with like-minded partners so you have sovereignty, so you have resilience, so you have independence.

"No country can do that alone."

World.title: Athlete who won Hyrox competition while leaking diarrhea unleashes 'biohazard' debate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Popular indoor fitness competition Hyrox has said it has changed its protocols after allowing an Australian athlete to keep competing — and win — despite suffering from what appeared to be diarrhea.

The graphic images of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.

"It's a biohazard, how they let the competition go on is beyond me," an observer wrote on Reddit.

"Think about how disgusting it is, especially when we use the exact same track," a race participant told the South China Morning Post.

Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23.

A screen grab of an Instagram post by BoxRox, a digital publishing platform for fitness events, celebrates Wietrzyk as the pro women's champion at Saturday's Hyrox competition in Beijing. (@BoxRox/Instagram)

"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.

As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.

"Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not," co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement Monday.

"As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again," he added.

The Hyrox official rulebook already had some penalties in place for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited, but until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.

As some people have pointed out in the comments on Hyrox's Instagram apology, perhaps it's "unbelievable that this even needs a rule."

"That’s not a rule. That’s basic human decency," someone commented.

Participants compete in the 'sled push' event during the Hyrox fitness race in Bangkok on March 21, 2026. (Amaury Paul/AFP/Getty Images)

So, what happened?

Hyrox, a structured indoor activity divided into eight segments, each involving a one-kilometre run followed by a fitness exercise, attracts tens of thousands of participants to its biggest events.

The event was developed in 2017 by German entrepreneur Christian Toetzke and Moritz Fürste, who won field hockey gold medals for Germany in the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics. It's since become a global phenomenon, was accepted as a format in World Triathlon this year (under the name Hyathlon) and has its sights set on the Olympics.

And Wietrzyk is the women's pro world record holder after her performance at the Warsaw Major in April. While she hasn't made an official statement about what happening in Beijing, several reports claim Wietrzyk was suffering from food poisoning.

A spectator at the event told the South China Morning Post that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.

Hyrox China, in a statement posted on the social media platform Weibo, said a competitor experienced a "sudden medical issue." The statement explained that organizers later disinfected contaminated areas, removed any contaminated equipment and replaced the carpet in the venue.

WATCH | Ont. teacher places 2nd in Hyrox: 60-year-old teacher places 2nd at Hyrox world championship | Duration 6:31 By day, Annette Barry is a St. Thomas, Ont., high school teacher. In her spare time, she does Hyrox — a growing sport that combines running and functional exercise. Barry placed second in her age category at the Hyrox World Championships in Stockholm.

As the TaiPei Times reports, Hyrox China did not apologize, but "admitted in an earlier statement to 'shortcomings' in the regulations which had prevented judges from intervening immediately during the competition."

Wietrzyk's coach, Chris Bayens, defended her in a statement posted to Instagram Sunday, urging people not to judge her "intent, clarity, or morality."

"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," Bayens wrote.

"What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time."

CBC News has reached out to Hyrox, Wietrzyk and her coach for comment, but not yet heard back.

Poop incidents are common

As many high-intensity athletes likely know, shit happens. Sometimes literally. There's even a term for it: runner's diarrhea, which Healthline describes as an inflammation of the colon caused by the intensity of workouts that can lead to frequent bowel movements.

According to a 2014 study, anywhere from 30 to 50 per cent of athletes report g astrointestinal problems. More recently, a 2025 literature review published in the World Journal of Gastroenterology concluded that high-intensity or prolonged exercise may contribute to symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

There are many well-documented and highly public cases where athletes have soiled themselves mid-competition. Just this past June, for instance, South African runner George Kusche won the Comrades Marathon with feces dripping down his legs.

Meanwhile, U.S. athlete Taylor Knibb won the 2024 T100 World Championship in Dubai, but made headlines for telling a cameraman, "I just shit myself. So can you not get my ass?"

WATCH | Athletes train for Ottawa Hyrox: Hyrox is coming to Ottawa and athletes are training at this 24/7 pop-up gym | Duration 3:36 Ottawa is set to host its first ever Hyrox fitness racing event from May 14 to 17, with 14,000 athletes registered to compete. CBC's Sannah Choi met with Hyrox athlete Kenny Caceros, who competed in the 2025 World Championships and has opened the Hybrid Training Pop-Up. It's a local gym where people can train 24/7 for the race.

In 2021, another U.S. athlete, Addi Zerrenner, went viral after soiling herself three times while running the California International Marathon, and told Business Insider, "I'm finally having the true marathon experience."

And U.K. runner Paula Radcliffe famously won the 2005 London Marathon after having to stop at 22-mile mark to defecate on the sidelines, calling it "an embarrassing necessity."

But, as many observers have noted, these incidents have all occurred outdoors.

Meanwhile, another Hyrox competitor, Malaysia's Zarif Zakaria, posted on Threads that he was recently disqualified from the Aug. 13 competition in Bangkok for using the bathroom — before the race. He claimed it's because it meant he had a late start.

"How come people can race while having diarrhea and not get DQ’d?" he posted Monday.

"Maybe it's time for me to retire from HYROX."

World.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge again blocks efforts to add Trump name to it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The board of the Kennedy Center voted on Tuesday to close over financial issues and a dispute over putting President Donald Trump's name on the iconic performing arts venue, the president confirmed on social media Tuesday.

"The closing will take place immediately," he wrote, "however the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name."

He adds that if the ruling is "a negative one," the renovation will not take place.

Trump's post followed an earlier ruling by a federal judge who blocked the Kennedy Center from returning Trump's name to the performing arts venue, saying it would violate an earlier ruling that his name was illegally added to the building when an inscription on the facade was approved that acknowledged his role in renovating and restoring the building.

Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that, "Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."

The Trump-aligned board at the Kennedy Center voted in August to inscribe the president's name on the venue's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts restored and renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

And if the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, it had voted for another inscription to be added reading: "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."

The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would have also been renamed in Trump's honour, as part of the board's vote.

A woman holds protest signs outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, Aug. 26. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

Fate of building in limbo

Tuesday's developments left uncertain the fate of one of the nation's most prominent cultural institutions, where presidents, lawmakers and celebrities across the political spectrum have gathered for decades to recognize and celebrate the best in American arts and culture.

The venue's leaders have argued that the massive building, which began construction in 1965, was in dire need of renovations. A partial ceiling collapse in the building's main hallway earlier this month intensified those calls.

"The building is not currently built to last, the chairman knows that because he is among the best builders in the world," Kennedy Center board member Brian Ballard said in a statement, referring to Trump.

But Trump's insistence on a physical recognition of his role in the work on the building — reminiscent of his tendency as a real estate developer to put his name on buildings — has been a persistent sticking point, alienating many of the institution's longtime supporters and facing repeated legal roadblocks.

The Justice Department said it would appeal the decision.

WATCH | Vote to close: Kennedy Center board votes to close after failed efforts to add Trump name | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 3:50 The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted to close most of the performing arts venue just hours after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning President Donald Trump's name to the building.

Months-long saga

Cooper had ruled in May that only Congress can approve changes to the Kennedy Center's name. In an emergency hearing on the matter in August, the administration argued it was no longer attempting to rename the building and that the vote was simply a recognition of Trump's effort to secure money for much-needed renovations.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose wife sits on the Kennedy Center board, compared the move to the way hospitals and colleges recognize high-dollar donors.

But a lawyer for U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, argued the changes amounted to "déja vu" and violated Cooper's earlier ruling.

"The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else," Beatty said in a statement Tuesday.

"But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial. The court just rejected this proposal for the second time. This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop."

Tuesday's ruling is the latest twist in the months-old naming saga that first saw the board installing Trump's name above Kennedy's. After Cooper shot down that move, an elevated tarp was erected, which obscures Trump's name and most of Kennedy's.

World.title: IN PHOTOS | Tom Hiddleston, Penélope Cruz promote films at TIFF

Film fans and stars are flocking to Canada's largest city for the Toronto International Film Festival. The 51st edition of TIFF, which runs for 11 days until Sept. 20, features nearly 300 titles and big-name actors, including Javier Bardem, Cynthia Erivo and Seth Rogen, among others.

Each day, we will feature highlights from red carpet premieres, fan excitement and other festival moments, so keep scrolling.

Day 6: Sept. 15

Tom Hiddleston attends the Canadian premiere of Tenzing, a story about the Himalayan Sherpa mountaineer who helped lead the first successful summit of Mount Everest in 1953. The film also stars Willem Dafoe (second photo), Caitriona Balfe, Thinley Lhamo (third photo, centre) and Genden Phuntsok.

(Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)

(Joel C Ryan/Invision/The Associated Press)

(Arturo Holmes/2026 Getty Images)

Penélope Cruz, Javier Ambrossi (second photo, left) and Javier Calvo (second photo, right) promote the Spanish-language film, La Bola Negra, which follows the interconnected lives of three men as they experience love and loss.

(Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

(Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

Aimee Lou Wood, left, and Johnny Flynn attend the red carpet premiere of their film, The Idiot(s) at the Princess of Wales Theatre.

(Arlyn McAdorey/Reuters)

Oscar winner Kenneth Branagh poses with fans at the premiere of his film Atonement, a story of trauma and forgiveness following a horrifying event during the Iraq War.

(Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)

Ink, directed by Danny Boyle, gets its Canadian premiere at TIFF at the Princess of Wales Theatre. The film stars Guy Pearce (second photo), Jack O'Connell and Claire Foy, and is about Rupert Murdoch's meteoric rise with The Sun newspaper and its influence on tabloid culture.

(Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

(Robin Marchant/Getty Images)

Actor Anna Díaz smiles on the red carpet during the North American premiere for Hombre al agua at Scotiabank Theatre.

(Mark Blinch/Reuters)

Actor Diego Luna waves to fans during the the red carpet for Hombre al agua.

(Mark Blinch/Reuters)

Day 5: Sept. 14

TIFF is now at the half-way point. But the stars are still out in full force today.

Oscar-winning married couple and stars of the psychological thriller, Bunker, Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz (second photo) attend the film's premiere at Roy Thomson Hall.

(Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)

(Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)

Director Hirokazu Kore-eda attends the premiere of his film Look Back, which explores the life-long friendship and shared creative journey of two young manga artists.

(Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)

Director Takashi Miike, centre, and stars Shotaro Mamiya, left, Shun Oguri, right, and Lily James (second photo) attend the premiere of Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.

Orlando Bloom as well as sisters Kate (in second photo) and Rooney Mara are among the celebrities in town to promote their film. In their case, it's the buzzy Bucking Fastard, the tale of sisters Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who speak in unison, dress alike and fall for the same man played by Bloom.

(Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Taraji P. Henson attends the premiere of Darlene Love: I Know Where I've Been, at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.

(Arturo Holmes/Getty Images)

Alden Ehrenreich on the red carpet for the premiere of the thriller A Talent for Murder at Roy Thomson Hall.

Day 4: Sept. 13

Léa Seydoux (first photo) and Lily-Rose Depp (second photo) attend the premiere of their film, Alpha Gang, which is about aliens that come to Earth to conquer it, and find that the human world has a plague they weren’t ready for.

Cynthia Erivo poses with fans at the premiere of Prima Facie at Roy Thomson Hall. In the film, she plays a British defence lawyer, who primarily defends those accused of sex crimes.

Day 1: Sept. 10

Workers roll out the red carpet ahead of Thursday's opening film Being Heumann by Oscar-winning director Siân Heder, as well as the Canadian premieres for Fjord, The Housewife and Stuffed.

And the film's director and co-writer Theo Rhys meets fans at the premiere.
