World.title: Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands
World.content:
Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands

14th Monday, September 2026 - 22:06 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicolás Aguilera/AFP

Two private Argentine pollsters released findings this week pointing to an adverse reception of President Javier Milei's shift on the Falklands, even though the sovereignty claim commands broad consensus in Argentine society.

The consultancy Analogías, which surveyed views of the national government between September 5 and 8, reported that 61% of respondents expressed distrust of the president's new position: 49.8% said they did not believe him at all and 11.2% believed him little. The firm did not publish technical details such as sample size or margin of error.

Monitor Digital, which analyzed 89,900 mentions of the government on social media, ranked the Islands as the second axis of the official digital conversation, clustered around terms such as sovereignty, measures, the United Kingdom and the United States. Its director, Diego Corbalán, told Perfil the volume did not translate into support: “In some way the government managed to place the issue, but it is not clear that all of it works to its benefit.”

The same study played down the reach of the matter beyond political circles. Across nearly a thousand Google trends recorded in the week after the September 3 televised address, the cluster associated with the Islands appeared only at 27th place, with some 50,000 searches, and the foreign policy category accounted for 0.8% of the total, far below sports and entertainment.

The sequence began with that address, in which Milei asserted sovereignty over the archipelago and announced measures against oil development. The following day the government confirmed sanctions against individuals and companies linked to that activity, and this week it is preparing to send Congress a National Sovereignty Defense bill.

The announcements followed the World Cup episode in July, when National Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva endorsed a ban on flags and shirts referring to the Islands during the semifinal between Argentina and England. The players themselves defied the measure by displaying a banner at the end of the match, and the episode led to the suspension of debate on the land ownership bill in the Senate.

On Sunday the government distributed to the press an institutional video by Santiago Oria, director of audiovisual production at the Presidency, combining statements by Milei, remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump on a possible review of Washington's neutral position, and footage of the match against England, set to terrace music. Milei and La Libertad Avanza figures shared the piece.

Corbalán criticized the strategy in political terms: in adopting it, he said, the libertarians “embrace the whole Kirchnerist populist mode,” which he described as chauvinism.

Islanders confirmed their status as a British Overseas Territory in the 2013 referendum, with 99.8% of the vote.

World.title: Is Mexico’s soccer league a monopoly? Antitrust officials are looking to find out
World.content:
The National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has unilaterally opened an investigation into Liga MX, Mexico’s top professional soccer league and a massive cultural touchstone that captures the country’s passion for the sport.

An internal CNA document says the investigation aims to identify “the possible commission of relative monopolistic practices in the market of ‘affiliation, organization and access’ to professional federated football competitions in Mexico, as well as similar or related services.”

⚽ ¿Cómo investigamos el funcionamiento de un mercado?

José Manuel Haro Zepeda, titular de nuestra Autoridad Investigadora, explicó en @MVSNoticias las herramientas con las que contamos para analizar la organización y acceso a competiciones de fútbol profesional en México. pic.twitter.com/r2qgofrR9M — Comisión Nacional Antimonopolio (@AntimonopolioMX) September 15, 2026

In short, the CNA wants to know if a small group is violating the Federal Law of Economic Competition by unfairly controlling who can join, who can compete and how tournaments are organized, to the exclusion of other interested parties.

“After analyzing the events that occurred in recent months, the Investigating Authority determined that it has sufficient evidence to formally open an investigation on its own initiative for possible monopolistic practices in the professional soccer market in Mexico,” the CNA said in a public report.

The recent events referred to are likely related to a Liga MX decision in July to scrap promotion/relegation between the top-flight Mexican soccer league and the second-tier Liga Expansión. Liga MX also announced the end to payouts to the second-tier sides.

Promotion and relegation were scrapped in 2020 to insulate the clubs from the financial impacts of lost revenue during the enforced lockdown ordered due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed the decision, even filing a suit with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that the 2026-27 campaign was the earliest point at which promotion/relegation ought to be reinstituted.

Critics have also identified the league’s policy regarding possession of television broadcasting rights by teams as a monopolistic practice.

The commission has sought to make clear that there are no defendants identified as yet and it hasn’t been determined exactly who will be investigated. Instead, the probe will simply review whether competition law is being followed.

The investigation can last up to 120 business days, but can be extended up to three times longer if necessary. During that time, the CNA can request documents, visit offices, summon people to testify and conduct inspections.

If guilt is determined, the Liga MX and its member teams could face a penalty of up to 10% of their annual income and would be required to correct any monopolistic practices detected.

With reports from ESPN, El Economista, El Universal and SportCa

World.title: Should you be worried about the presence of brain-eating amoeba in Yucatán water bodies?
World.content:
A man died of Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) in a Mérida hospital last week, most likely from contact with the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri, the Yucatán Health Services (SSY) reported on Monday.

The SSY confirmed the presence of N. fowleri in an artificial lake at the La Isla shopping center in Mérida, where the 34-year-old man worked as a water sports instructor.

FAMILIARES DESPIDEN A CARLOS, INSTRUCTOR QUE F4LL3C10 POR AMEBA COME CEREBROS#Video | Familiares y amigos despidieron con tristeza a Carlos, el joven instructor de wakeboard de 33 años que perdió la v1d4 tras contraer una agresiva infección por la ameba ‘Naegleria fowleri’ en… pic.twitter.com/f57zIqs8Ly — Yucatán Ahora (@yucatanahora) September 15, 2026

“It is a serious and extremely rare disease; this is the first case registered in Yucatán,” the SSY said in a statement.

The microorganism is most commonly found in stagnant, warm waters between 35°C and 46°C. It enters the body when contaminated water is forcefully inhaled through the nose, although it can also occur while swimming, diving or submerging one’s head in lakes, rivers or poorly chlorinated swimming pools.

PAM is not transmitted from person to person and is not acquired by drinking contaminated water, the SSY emphasized.

People living in the Yucatán capital have expressed concern about the water quality in nearby cenotes, where swimming is common. However, experts suggest that natural freshwater bodies are cooler, at between 24°C and 26°C, making the presence of N. fowleri far less likely.

The development of microorganisms in pools can be avoided through chlorination and pH management, and in larger water bodies through adequate water movement, which promotes aeration. Regular cleaning and maintenance can also help avoid the accumulation of sediment, organic matter, algae and biofilms in stagnant water, conditions that attract N. fowleri.

The first symptoms of PAM are usually severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting. According to initial reports, the victim presented with severe symptoms of central nervous system infection and was taken to a hospital in the city, where he died.

Health authorities ordered the temporary closure of the water feature at La Isla while samples were tested at the Hidalgo State Public Health Laboratory, which confirmed the presence of N. fowleri. Meanwhile, cleaning efforts and technical inspections were carried out at the site.

Epidemiological investigators are conducting interviews to locate other individuals who may have come into contact with the water.

The SSY said it plans to investigate the companies responsible for water quality and lake maintenance for their compliance with Mexican rules and regulations.

“Anyone who has violated health regulations will be sanctioned,” the SSY stressed.

According to the SSY statement, once the responsible company demonstrates through laboratory tests that the lake water is suitable for recreational use in accordance with legal standards, a new verification and sampling of the water will be conducted and a decision will be made on whether to lift the temporary closure.

With reports from Reportur, La Jornada and Diario de Yucatán

World.title: 139 US troops cleared to enter Mexico for joint training in Chihuahua
World.content:
More than 100 U.S. soldiers will travel to Mexico this month to participate in joint training exercises with Mexican military personnel in the northern state of Chihuahua.

The federal Senate on Monday granted President Claudia Sheinbaum the authority to allow the entry into Mexico of 139 U.S. Army troops, who are scheduled to land at the Santa Gertrudis Air Force Base south of Chihuahua city this Sunday.

The granting of that authority comes amid security-related tension in the Mexico-U.S. relationship.

Among the causes of that tension are the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the knowledge or authorization of the Mexican government; U.S. prosecutors’ drug-trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya and other current and former officials; and suggestions from Trump administration officials that the U.S. could take unilateral action against Mexican drug cartels on Mexican soil.

While each of those developments has drawn the ire of Sheinbaum, the president remains committed to cooperating with the Trump administration on security on the proviso that Mexican sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected. One example of that cooperation is a joint anti-drone operation that is currently taking place on the border between Tijuana and San Diego.

U.S. soldiers have previously traveled to Mexico to undertake joint training exercises with Mexican personnel. However, the U.S. contingent set to arrive in Chihuahua on Sunday is larger than previous ones that have come to Mexico.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming military collaboration on Mexican soil.

Where will the joint training exercises take place?

The joint training exercises will take place at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento (National Training Center), located in Santa Gertrudis in the municipality of Saucillo, Chihuahua. The CNA is the Mexican military’s largest training facility.

Among the simulated combat exercises U.S. and Mexican military personnel will conduct are the destruction of sniper positions; the seizure of an airfield; an air assault; the destruction of a fuel-supply point; and the capture and extraction of a target using live fire.

The U.S. soldiers will stay at the CNA during their time in Mexico.

What is the objective of the training exercises?

The Senate said in a statement that the aim of the joint training exercises is to “strengthen operational capabilities between the United States and Mexican Armed Forces through the planning and execution of military operations under the principles of respect, sovereignty and territorial integrity; shared responsibility; mutual trust; and collaboration without subordination.

The Senate said that the joint training “will not only have a positive impact on strengthening individual and collective preparedness, but will also contribute to the improvement of bilateral military cooperation mechanisms.”

How long will the US soldiers remain in Mexico?

The U.S. troops will arrive in Chihuahua on a U.S. Air Force plane on Sept. 20 and return to the United States on Sept. 30. Therefore, the soldiers will be in Mexico for a total of 11 days.

The Senate noted that the U.S. troops will enter Mexico “with weapons.”

Which division of the US army to the soldiers belong to?

The 139 soldiers coming to Mexico belong to the 101st Airborne Division of the U.S. Army. The division, known as the “Screaming Eagles,” is the only air assault division of the United States Army. It is based at Fort Campbell, Kentucky.

With reports from La Silla Rota, El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Tehran’s Azadi Tower bears Mexican flag in first-ever Independence Day tribute
World.content:
For the first time, Iran lit one of its most recognizable landmarks in the green, white and red of the Mexican flag, turning Tehran’s Azadi Tower into a striking Independence Day tribute Tuesday night.

The Azadi Tower illumination marked the 216th anniversary of the Grito de Dolores — the 1810 call by priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla that launched Mexico’s war for independence from Spain.

La emblemática Torre Azadi, símbolo de Teherán, se iluminó con los colores de la bandera mexicana para conmemorar el 216° aniversario de la Independencia de México. La Embajada de Irán en México destacó el acto como un gesto de amistad entre ambos pueblos. Más en La Jornada:… pic.twitter.com/tfgRRj5ddy — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) September 15, 2026

“Today, Mexico is not in Mexico. It is in the heart of Iran,” the Iranian Embassy in Mexico posted Sept. 15 with a video of the glowing monument.

The display marked the first time Iran has illuminated a monument in honor of Mexico, according to the newspaper El Universal.

Those colors, however, are not inherently unusual at Azadi Tower, since green, white and red are also Iran’s national colors. For example, on Feb. 10, 2024, it was lit up in that way for the 45th anniversary of the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Speaking to HispanTV from Tehran, Mexican Ambassador Guillermo Puente Ordorica called the lighting “a great gesture of friendship” that Mexicans will cherish.

Built in 1971, the 45-meter Azadi Tower was originally called Shahyad Tower, then renamed Azadi (Persian for “freedom”) after the 1979 revolution. The tower and its surrounding square are often the site of major public gatherings.

Beyond Iran, Mexican communities and diplomats marked Día de la Independencia across several continents.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani was grand marshal Sunday at a Mexican Independence Day parade in Brooklyn, wearing a tricolor sash and carrying a Mexican flag. He said he was proud to be the first New York City mayor to march in the parade with “a community that has fostered cultural pride for generations.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@nycmayor)

Mamdani’s remarks came just days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance criticized a protester carrying a Mexican flag at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, calling him an “idiot” and telling him, “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

Elsewhere, Mexico’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, Alejandro Gertz Manero, led a Grito ceremony in London, where festivities included music, food, dance and other traditions.

In Madrid, the Mexican Embassy hosted a public Grito in Chamberí Square, followed by folk ballet, mariachi and a circus performance.

Mexican celebrations were also reported in Krakow, Rome, Vienna, Beijing, Seoul, Barcelona, Budapest and Kansas City.

With reports from El Universal, La Jornada and Madrid Gazette

World.title: New US-Mexico water agreement means reduced allotments but a heathier Colorado River
World.content:
A long-running dispute between Mexico and the United States over Colorado River water-sharing has been resolved — at least for the next two years — with Mexico getting significantly less water as a result.

The U.S. is also receiving less water as part of a joint effort to mitigate ongoing drought conditions and low reservoir levels in the Colorado River basin.

In fact, under the new agreement, formally called Minute 334 and finalized by the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC) on Sept. 2, Mexico’s 16.7% (250,000 acre-feet) annual reduction of its previous typical water allocation is equivalent to water-use reductions imposed on U.S. Lower Basin states (Arizona, California and Nevada).

The agreement also implements a strategy to manage the salinity of Colorado River water as it reaches Mexico. Consultations regarding possible further cuts are contemplated for 2028 if conditions worsen.

Minute 334 was signed by Mexican IBWC Commissioner Adriana Reséndez and her U.S. counterpart, Chad McIntosh, with the participation of Mexican IBWC Secretary Manuel Morales. The U.S. Department of the Interior confirmed the approval of both governments.

“This Minute makes sure water is shared fairly among our users and protects the health of the Colorado River during these difficult times,” McIntosh said in a news release. “Both countries deserve a lot of credit for agreeing to these water reductions and other measures.”

Reséndez insisted on proportionality between the two countries, defending Mexico’s position even as it has struggled to meet its obligations in the original 1944 treaty.

When the most recent five-year cycle of that treaty came to an end on Oct. 24 last year, Mexico still owed 865,136 acre-feet of water, though the terms of the treaty grant Mexico five years to catch up.

The reduction agreed to in Minute 334 is equivalent to one-sixth of Mexico’s annual allocation established in the treaty, about 1.85 billion cubic meters.

The two nations also agreed to cooperate on managing the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, which has been transformed from a lush 2-million-acre wetland into a mostly dry salt flat due to decades of intensive upstream dam construction and water diversions.

With reports from El Universal, WaterWorld and The Colorado Sun

World.title: MND Local: WTA Tennis, an international film fest and more events in Guadalajara
World.content:
Late September in Guadalajara brings an action-packed calendar. Upcoming events include a World Migrant Day celebration benefiting a local nonprofit organization, an international film festival and the 2026 Guadalajara Open, an important stop on the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) professional tour.

Top female tennis players to compete at the Guadalajara Open this week

Following hard on the heels of the U.S. Open in New York City, Zapopan welcomes a select group of the WTA’s brightest stars to the Guadalajara Open this week.

The annual event, played at the Panamerican Tennis Center in Parque Metropolitano, attracts a diverse group of top female tennis players from around the globe. The field will compete in singles and doubles for a US $1.2 million purse and a top singles prize of US $185,500.

Confirmed players for this year’s event include world number 11 Marta Kostyuk of Ukraine and world number 14 and defending champion Iva Jovic of the United States.

Kostyuk returns to Mexico as one of the hottest players on the WTA tour during the 2026 season, having reached the semifinals of Wimbledon and Roland Garros, in addition to claiming two titles on clay last spring. She last competed at the Guadalajara Open in 2023, where she reached the second round.

Latin American tennis will also be well represented, with Colombian veteran Camila Osorio and Mexican No. 1 Renata Zarazúa scheduled to compete.

For details, visit the tournament website.

Dates: Sept. 13-19, 2026.

Sept. 13-19, 2026. Location: Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco.

Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco. Cost: Individual tickets start at 866 pesos, not including fees. Tournament packages are available on Boletomovil.

Aeroméxico to launch nonstop service from Guadalajara to Paris in 2027

Savoring the perfect pain au chocolat is about to get a little easier for Francophile Tapatíos. Starting April 13, 2027, the city will have its second direct European flight route, as Aeroméxico launches nonstop service between Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo International Airport (GDL) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).

The route will run three times per week on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays, departing Guadalajara at 1:55 p.m. and arriving in Paris at 9:25 a.m. the following day. Return flights will operate on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays, departing Paris at 11:40 a.m. and arriving in Guadalajara at 4:10 p.m. the same day.

“Adding Guadalajara–Paris … strengthens our network, offers customers more travel options and further consolidates our position as the leading airline between Mexico and Europe,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeroméxico, told Aviacionline last week.

Celebrate World Migrant Day with the Rhizome Center

Later this month, Guadalajara residents will have the opportunity to celebrate World Migrant Day at a community celebration featuring local food, culture and a social cause.

Hosted by The Rhizome Center, this year’s festival, “Many Journeys. One Community,” is both a fundraiser and an opportunity to raise awareness about the organization’s work. During the event, guests can sample food from 15 migrant kitchens, enjoy live French, Cuban and Syrian music, listen to storytelling, and meet artists sharing their craft and culture.

The Rhizome Center was founded in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term, with a mission to provide direct support to deportees and refugees sent to Mexico.

Since his return to office, the need has grown. Many deportees arrive with no resources or documentation to regularize their status in Mexico. Filling that void, the organization provides legal aid, crisis assistance, counseling and other services.

Run by executive director and founder Tran Dang, The Rhizome Center derived its name from plant rhizomes — the underground roots that provide essential nutrients — symbolizing humanity’s resilience and interconnectedness across borders.

For more information about The Rhizome Center for Migrants and details on how to support the cause, visit the group’s Instagram account. Donations are accepted via PayPal and Zelle.

Date: Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. Location: Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara.

Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara. Cost: General admission is 375 pesos. VIP tickets are 500 pesos per person and guarantee a seat.

The MUBI film fest lands in Guadalajara next weekend

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MUBI México (@mubimexico)

Global distributor, producer and streaming service MUBI recently added film festivals to its portfolio and announced a Guadalajara edition from Sept. 18-20. The festival will screen independent feature films and shorts, alongside filmmaker Q&As, workshops, installations and DJ sets.

Anticipated films on the schedule include:

“Her Private Hell” by Nicolas Winding Refn

“Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?” by Garth Jennings

“Hope: The First Impact” by Na Hong-jin

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” by Jane Schoenbrun

“Rose” by Markus Schleinzer

For moviegoers seeking nostalgia, Ridley Scott’s 1991 feminist classic “Thelma & Louise,” starring Susan Sarandon, Geena Davis and Brad Pitt, is also on the schedule.

For full program details, visit Mubi Mexico’s website. In addition to Guadalajara, MUBI Fest 2026 made stops in Mexico City, São Paulo, Bogotá and Buenos Aires this year.

Dates: Sept. 18-20.

Sept. 18-20. Location: FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan.

FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan. Cost: Tickets available on the MUBI website.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico City-area airports to halt takeoffs and landings for 4 hours tomorrow
World.content:
Takeoffs and landings at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) will be suspended for four hours on Wednesday, Sept. 16, to ensure that military aircraft can operate safely in the capital’s airspace while the annual Independence Day parade takes place below.

The Mexican Navy, which operates the AICM, announced the suspension in a statement.

El AICM suspenderá operaciones aéreas por desfile del 16 de septiembre. ➡️ https://t.co/T6iEPTFtOa @aeropuertos_GAM pic.twitter.com/wJK8Khf3YB — Aeropuerto Internacional Benito Juárez CDMX (@AICM_mx) September 14, 2026

“To ensure the safety of the military air maneuvers that will be carried out to commemorate the 216th anniversary of the start of Mexico’s independence, and as directed by the aviation authority, the Mexico City Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) will suspend aircraft takeoffs and landings on September 16 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.,” the navy said.

“According to NOTAMs [Notices to Airmen] A8260/26 and B1724/26, … issued by the Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) and disseminated through the Mexican Airspace Navigation Services (SENEAM), the airport will be closed to all types of flights during the specified hours.”

The Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) in México state will also suspend takeoffs and landings between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Wednesday. Military aircraft that will conduct flyovers as part of the Independence Day festivities will take off from the Santa Lucía Air Force Base, which adjoins AIFA.

The navy advised air passengers who have a flight scheduled for Wednesday to ask their airlines about the status of their flights as “this event will result in some adjustments to scheduled times.”

The Independence Day parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Wednesday with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central square — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes (Palace of Fine Arts), continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Following a higher soda tax, is a salty foods tax coming next?
World.content:
Lawmakers from Mexico’s ruling party Morena, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Green Party (PVEM) have submitted a congressional proposal to apply a Special Tax on Production and Services (IEPS) to certain processed foods with excessive sodium content, such as cured meats, instant soups, sauces and dressings.

The initiative seeks to expand a tax strategy that has been applied since the 1980s to products considered harmful to health, such as sugary drinks, tobacco and high-calorie foods.

The bill’s proponents estimate that a tax on products with high sodium levels could generate approximately 12 billion pesos (US $116.6 million) in additional federal revenue, while helping reduce the prevalence of diseases associated with excessive salt consumption.

The focus would be on processed products exceeding technical criteria for sodium content, particularly front-of-package warning labels under NOM-051, which indicate “Excess Sodium.” This means that the potential measure would not penalize the domestic use of salt, nor would it, in principle, indiscriminately cover all salty foods.

The initiative follows growing concerns regarding average sodium intake in Mexico.

According to the NGO El Poder del Consumidor (The Power of the Consumer), the Mexican adult population consumes an average of 3.3 grams of sodium per day, far exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendation, which advises against exceeding 2 grams daily. Excess sodium consumption is related to cardiovascular diseases – the leading cause of death in Mexico – and hypertension.

Meeting the WHO’s target of a 30% reduction in sodium intake by 2030 could save an estimated 7 million lives globally and annually prevent approximately 5% of deaths in Mexico from cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and stomach cancer.

Dr. Jorge Vargas, a researcher at El Poder del Consumidor, told the news outlet Infobae that “the fact that Mexico is finally considering a sodium tax is positive news,” but cautioned that the technical design would be a decisive factor in determining whether the tax alters consumption habits and drives companies to reduce the salt content of their products. He also urged lawmakers to review the results observed in other countries before voting on the initiative.

The proposal follows a recent IEPS increase targeting domestic sugar consumption, which, according to the government’s 2027 budget proposal, is forecast to bring in over 76.92 billion pesos ($4.5 billion) next year from soft drinks alone.

With reports from El Universal and El Financiero

World.title: The Dangote Refinery Share Offer Is Cheap to Enter and Expensive to Own
World.content:
Nigeria · Markets

Key Facts — What is being sold A 3.3 percent stake in the Dangote refinery outside Lagos, raising about US$1.6 billion.

— Why that is notable It is the largest share sale ever held in Africa, and it opened on 14 September.

— The smallest ticket Ten shares cost 5,250 naira, about US$4, which is well under a tenth of the monthly minimum wage.

— What the refinery does It turns crude oil into petrol and diesel, and it already runs at 700,000 barrels a day.

— What analysts object to Not the access, the price. One Nigerian mid-cycle valuation lands at a third to two thirds of the offer.

— For a foreign buyer One document, the certificate of capital importation, decides whether the money can leave again.

Aliko Dangote is selling 3.3 percent of the largest refinery ever built on one site, and he is selling it to anyone who wants ten shares. The question is not whether ordinary people can afford to get in. It is what they are paying for.

The Dangote Refinery Share Offer Is Cheap to Enter and Expensive to Own

The Dangote refinery share offer opened on Monday and runs to 13 October. It is the largest share sale Africa has held, and the smallest way in costs less than a sandwich.

The Mechanics

The company is issuing 4.1 billion new ordinary shares at 525 naira each, about 40 US cents. That raises roughly 2.15 trillion naira, or US$1.6 billion, and could reach US$2.1 billion if an over-allotment option is used.

The stake on sale is 3.30 percent. Aliko Dangote keeps 84.34 percent afterwards.

The implied value of the whole company is around US$47 billion to US$49 billion. Nigeria’s securities regulator approved the offer on 4 September.

The minimum subscription is ten shares, which is 5,250 naira or about US$4. Nigeria’s monthly minimum wage is 70,000 naira, about US$53.

So the entry ticket is roughly seven percent of a month at the legal minimum. The stated target is up to ten million retail buyers.

What the Refinery Is

The plant sits in the Lekki free zone outside Lagos and turns crude oil into petrol, diesel and jet fuel. Its nameplate capacity is 650,000 barrels a day, debottlenecked to 700,000.

It reached that full rate during 2026. An expansion to 1.4 million barrels a day has been announced at a cost of about US$46 billion.

Jamnagar in India is currently the world’s largest single-site refinery, at 1.24 million barrels a day. If the expansion is completed, the Nigerian plant overtakes it.

Company statements have put the date variously at 2028, 2029 and 2030. That is a wide range for a stated plan.

The most recent company briefing said 2030. The honest way to write it is before the end of the decade.

The Real Argument Is About Price

The criticism that has actually been made by named Nigerian analysts is about valuation. Nobody credible is arguing that the Dangote refinery share offer is out of reach.

BusinessDay’s editorial board put mid-cycle fair value at 176 to 324 naira a share, roughly US$0.13 to US$0.24. The offer price is 525 naira, about US$0.40.

Their arithmetic compares the refinery at about 9.5 times enterprise value to earnings against Marathon Petroleum at 8.21 and Valero at 8.50. The industry median is 7.52.

They also note that the plant cost about US$27,143 per barrel of daily capacity to build. The offer values it at US$70,308 per barrel, a premium of about two and a half times.

Samson Esemuede, chief investment officer at Zrosk, made the point about sentiment. Psychology is important, he said, but he cannot bank on psychology.

The first-half margins that support the price were inflated by a supply shock in the Gulf. Refining is a cyclical business and those margins are not a baseline.

A tax change also lands in January 2028. The effective rate rises from 13.6 percent to a blended rate near 25 percent.

On current earnings that removes about a tenth of profit. It is a known change with a known date.

How a Foreign Buyer Actually Does It

Two routes exist. The first is to build the local infrastructure.

That means a non-resident bank verification number and a custodian account at a Nigerian bank. A linked share-depository account is needed as well.

Money is then wired to the custodian, converted to naira, and the custodian issues a certificate of capital importation. That certificate is the legal basis for taking dividends and sale proceeds back out of the country.

Without it, a foreign holder is stuck with the parallel market. It is the single most important piece of paper in the transaction.

The second route uses an international broker distributing through a Nigerian regulated house. On that path no Nigerian bank account or local depository account is needed, and the platform handles the importation paperwork.

The shares list on the main board of the Nigerian Exchange in Lagos. There is no depositary receipt, and no American listing before 2029 at the earliest.

Dangote has said dividends will be paid in US dollars. That is a stated intention rather than a covenant, and it is not the same as a guarantee.

What Could Go Wrong

The free float is about 3.3 percent, which means thin trading and sharp moves. Minority holders have no influence over a company that remains 84 percent owned by one man.

Crude supply is a live issue. Dangote has publicly complained about shortfalls in domestic supply, and the state oil company denies them.

There is also an open fight over fuel pricing. Marketers rejected dollar-based pricing and asked the president to intervene, while the state oil company has accused the refinery of monopoly behaviour.

Currency is the last one. The official rate was 1,326 naira to the dollar on Tuesday.

The parallel market sat at 1,385 to 1,410. That is a gap of about six percent between the two.

Earlier investors are already underwater. A July private placement priced around 473 naira, about US$0.36, carries a one-year lock-in.

Those shares come free from mid-2027. Holders sitting on a loss may want out when they do.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to take part?

The minimum subscription is ten shares at 525 naira each, so 5,250 naira, about US$4. Nigeria’s monthly minimum wage is 70,000 naira, roughly US$53, so the smallest ticket is about seven percent of that. The offer opened on 14 September 2026 and closes on 13 October.

Can someone outside Nigeria buy in?

Yes, by two routes. One is to open a custodian account at a Nigerian bank with a non-resident bank verification number and a linked depository account, wiring in foreign currency so the custodian can issue a certificate of capital importation. The other is through an international broker distributing via a regulated Nigerian house, which handles that paperwork. The certificate is what allows money to leave Nigeria again.

Is the refinery really the world’s largest?

Not yet. It currently runs at 700,000 barrels a day, behind Jamnagar in India at 1.24 million. An announced expansion to 1.4 million barrels a day would make it the largest single-site refinery in the world, and company statements have put that at some point before 2030.

What do critics say?

They are arguing about price, not access. BusinessDay’s editorial board puts mid-cycle fair value at 176 to 324 naira, about US$0.13 to US$0.24, against an offer price of 525 naira or US$0.40, and notes the offer values the plant at roughly two and a half times what it cost to build per barrel of daily capacity.

Sources: Channels Television on the launch of the offer, Nairametrics on the valuation test facing the offer, BusinessDay editorial on the pricing, BusinessDay on how to participate, CNBC Africa on Africa’s biggest share sale, Vanguard on the naira exchange rate for 15 September 2026

World.title: M23 Parallel Administration Now Taxes Eastern Congo, Aid Agencies Included
World.content:
DR Congo · Analysis

Key Facts — Who M23 are A Rwanda-backed armed group that seized Goma in January 2025 and Bukavu three weeks later.

— What they built A working administration with its own tax office, police, customs, courts and utility control.

— What it charges Fees on shops, trucks, borders and minerals, plus income tax on aid workers’ salaries.

— The aid agency price list Fifty US dollars for a seven-day permit, five hundred for six months of access.

— Where the money comes from Coltan from the Rubaya mine alone is estimated at around US$800,000 a month.

— Why it reaches your phone That coltan leaves through Rwanda and enters the global electronics supply chain.

The armed group that took the two largest cities of eastern Congo last year did not simply occupy them. It built a state inside them, and that state now sends invoices.

M23 Parallel Administration Now Taxes Eastern Congo, Aid Agencies Included

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The M23 parallel administration in eastern Congo has a tax office, and it expects to be paid. That is the finding running through a year of reporting and a United Nations investigation into how the group funds itself.

A Government Without a Country

M23 took Goma on 27 January 2025 and Bukavu about three weeks later. Between them the two cities hold several million people.

The M23 parallel administration was not the usual pattern of an occupying force living off looting. The group appointed governors, trained civil servants and took over the machinery that collects money.

Zobel Behalal, of the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime, calls it a de facto and deeply illegal parallel administration. He describes it as methodically consolidated rather than improvised.

United Nations experts reported in June that the group had created tax systems and taken control of revenue services. It also extended authority over the state electricity and water utilities.

The Price List

The clearest evidence of how this works is what humanitarian organisations are charged. M23’s directorate of finances issues visas for its own territory.

A seven-day permit costs fifty US dollars. Six months of multiple entry costs five hundred.

The group also demands income tax on the salaries of aid workers. A further tax applies to rented offices and guesthouses, and one large international organisation has paid.

A senior humanitarian official described the position as a sword hanging overhead. Refuse and lose access, pay and fund the group you are working around.

The reporting rests on nine anonymous sources across aid agencies, donors and embassies. That anonymity is easy to understand and it is still a limitation.

Where the Money Comes From

Mineral revenue is the part of the M23 parallel administration that can be counted. United Nations experts estimate the Rubaya coltan mine alone yields around US$800,000 a month.

The group charges four dollars a kilogram on coltan and two dollars on cassiterite at the point of sale. Loads are weighed at checkpoints west of Goma.

The payment is then made at a bank in Gisenyi, on the Rwandan side of the border. That detail tells you most of what you need to know about the route.

Everything else is taxed too. Trucks and motorbike taxis pay at checkpoints, shops and warehouses pay rates, and residents are asked for cash, labour or goods.

There is no published total across all of it. Anyone quoting one is estimating.

The Coltan Reaches Everyone

Global Witness traced at least 1,400 tonnes of coltan smuggled from Congo into Rwanda within a year of the Rubaya takeover. It identified more than 2,000 tonnes of conflict coltan in total.

Rwanda’s official coltan exports rose two and a half times between 2021 and 2025. Its cassiterite exports rose 58 percent in 2025 with no matching rise in its own production.

Coltan yields tantalum, which sits in the capacitors of almost every phone and laptop. This is the point at which a war in the Kivus becomes a supply-chain question for a company in Europe or Asia.

What Happened to the Banks

Commercial banks in Goma and Bukavu shut when the cities fell and have largely stayed shut. Equity BCDC says its branches closed for security reasons.

M23 filled the gap rather than leaving it. It reopened Cadeco, the state savings bank, and set up a regulator that functions as a central bank of sorts.

Who is to blame is contested. The group’s political leader says Kinshasa ordered the closures.

The Congolese government rejects that. It says no bank may legally operate in territory held by a sanctioned armed group.

Goma airport remains shut to commercial and humanitarian flights. A United Nations helicopter landed there in February, the first aircraft in over a year, and nothing has followed it.

The Talks That Have Not Stopped the Money

Congolese and Rwandan officials meet in Geneva on Tuesday and Wednesday under American, Qatari, Togolese and African Union mediation. The subject is the security commitments both sides made last year.

A separate track in Doha covers the government and M23 directly. Of eight protocols in that framework, two have been signed.

Fighting has continued throughout. M23 pushed west toward Walikale in the second week of September, and both sides used drones extensively in the Minembwe highlands.

Nothing in either negotiation currently addresses the M23 parallel administration itself. An administration that collects revenue is harder to dismantle than a front line.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is M23?

The March 23 Movement is a predominantly Congolese Tutsi-led armed group that resurfaced in 2021 and now operates under the Alliance Fleuve Congo, led by Corneille Nangaa, a former head of Congo’s electoral commission. United Nations experts estimate 14,000 to 18,000 Rwandan troops are deployed in eastern Congo alongside it. Rwanda denies backing the group.

Does M23 really tax aid agencies?

According to The New Humanitarian, yes. Its finance directorate charges US$50 for a seven-day visa and US$500 for six months of multiple entry, and demands income tax on aid workers’ salaries and tax on rented premises. At least one large international organisation has accepted the income tax demands.

How much money does the group raise?

No reliable total exists. The best-documented single stream is coltan from the Rubaya mine, which United Nations experts estimate at around US$800,000 a month, based on a levy of four US dollars a kilogram. Checkpoint fees, market rates and utility payments are documented but not quantified.

Is there a peace process?

Two, and neither has ended the fighting. Congo and Rwanda meet in Geneva under a mechanism created in December 2025, while a separate framework agreed in Doha in November 2025 covers the government and M23 directly. Only two of the Doha framework’s eight protocols have been signed.

Sources: The New Humanitarian on how M23 finances its war, The New Humanitarian on the taxes charged to aid groups, United Nations Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report of June 2026, Global Witness on smuggled coltan reaching world markets, Al Jazeera on Goma a year after the takeover, Al Jazeera on the Geneva talks between Congo and Rwanda

World.title: Senegal Debt Restructuring Was Unthinkable in February. Now Dakar Wants It Fast
World.content:
Senegal · Analysis

Key Facts — What happened Senegal has entered a G20 debt process after months of publicly rejecting the idea.

— Why it needs one Auditors found more than eleven billion US dollars of borrowing the previous government never disclosed.

— How deep the hole is Public debt reached about 119 percent of national output, or around 132 percent counting arrears.

— Who is pushing The World Bank president said on Tuesday he wants Senegal handled faster than any previous case.

— Why that is hard Zambia took roughly four years, Chad nearly two, and Ghana just over one.

— What is not included Nearly a third of the debt is in the regional CFA franc and is carved out of any treatment.

In February, Senegal’s finance minister said his government was against restructuring its debt and that this was not a matter of pride. By September the country had agreed to a process it spent the year refusing to name.

Senegal Debt Restructuring Was Unthinkable in February. Now Dakar Wants It Fast

Senegal debt restructuring was, until recently, the one thing Dakar insisted it would not do. On Tuesday the president of the World Bank said he wanted it completed faster than any comparable case.

The Reversal

Cheikh Diba, Senegal’s finance minister, put the old position plainly in February. We are against restructuring, he said, and this is not a matter of pride.

His argument was that Senegal debt restructuring was avoidable, and that active debt management could reach the same arithmetic. He pointed to more than 500 billion CFA francs, about US$890 million, of budget space freed during 2025.

Ousmane Sonko, then prime minister, had gone further the previous November. An internationally led restructuring, he said, would be a disgrace for the country.

By early September the government had reached a staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund on a three-year programme worth US$2.2 billion. It comes with a commitment to restore debt sustainability through an enhanced version of the G20 process.

Diba’s holding line is that this is not a restructuring in the classic sense of the term. The government is doing the thing while declining the word.

Why It Became Unavoidable

An audit under the current government found borrowing the previous administration had never disclosed. The Fund puts the concealed amount above US$11 billion, and some analysts nearer US$13 billion.

That is more than a quarter of the total, and it is what made Senegal debt restructuring unavoidable. Total government debt stood at about US$42 billion at the end of 2024.

Restated, public debt reached roughly 119 percent of national output, or 131 to 132 percent once state entities and arrears are counted. Those are not numbers a country grows out of.

The Fund’s managing director described it without much diplomacy. They slipped into this undisclosed debt situation, she said, and the Fund can work with the government’s commitment.

Dakar. Almost a third of Senegal’s debt is denominated in the regional CFA franc and sits outside any restructuring. (Photo: “2023-12-17 view from the Calao restaurant 2” by Tbo47, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

What Banga Actually Said

Ajay Banga spoke to Reuters in Washington on Tuesday, before a meeting with President Bassirou Diomaye Faye. He said the two would discuss ensuring the case goes through the G20 process at the fastest speed of any prior case.

He gave no timeline. He did give benchmarks, noting that Zambia took well over a year and Ghana completed in just over one.

Those benchmarks are generous to the framework. Zambia’s process, counted from application, ran closer to four years.

Chad was first into the framework in January 2021 and reached agreement in November 2022, about 22 months. It delivered reprofiling rather than any reduction in what was owed.

Ethiopia applied in February 2021 and had still not finalised by early 2025. The trend is improving, which is what makes Banga’s pledge more than a pleasantry.

Why This Case Is Different

The G20 Common Framework was built in November 2020 for low-income countries, to coordinate traditional lenders with newer ones, principally China. Senegal is middle-income, which the framework was not designed for.

The second difference is the perimeter. Nearly a third of Senegal’s debt is denominated in the CFA franc and held within the West African monetary union.

Restructuring that portion would destabilise a currency eight countries share. It is therefore carved out, leaving a treatable pool of roughly US$5 billion.

The third difference is the cause. Zambia, Chad and Ghana arrived through external shocks, while Senegal arrived through concealed borrowing.

What Is Still Unsettled

The Fund programme is a staff-level agreement, which means it still needs management and board approval. Until that happens no money moves.

Whether Senegal has made a formal request under the framework, in the technical sense, is not clear from the public record. Reporting says the country will use an enhanced version of it.

The framework’s usual complaint is that creditor groups negotiate one after another rather than together. That sequencing is what turned Zambia into a four-year exercise.

Senegal debt restructuring is now asking to be the exception to that pattern. The distance between February’s refusal and September’s request is the measure of how little room it had left.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the G20 Common Framework?

It is a mechanism created in November 2020 to coordinate debt relief for low-income countries across both traditional Paris Club lenders and newer bilateral creditors, principally China. Chad, Zambia, Ghana and Ethiopia have used it. Chad took about 22 months, Ghana just over a year, Zambia closer to four years, and Ethiopia had still not concluded four years after applying.

Why does Senegal need debt relief?

An audit under the current government uncovered borrowing the previous administration had not disclosed, estimated by the International Monetary Fund at more than US$11 billion, over a quarter of total debt. Restated public debt reached about 119 percent of national output, or around 132 percent including state entities and arrears.

Did Senegal not refuse to restructure?

It did. In February 2026 finance minister Cheikh Diba said the government was against restructuring, arguing active debt management would achieve the same result without the consequences. The previous November, then prime minister Ousmane Sonko called an internationally led restructuring a disgrace. By September the government had entered an enhanced G20 process alongside a US$2.2 billion IMF programme.

Is all of Senegal’s debt covered?

No. Almost a third is denominated in the CFA franc and held within the West African monetary union, and restructuring it would destabilise a currency shared by eight countries. That portion is carved out, leaving a treatable pool of roughly US$5 billion.

World.title: Munhumutapa Day Shut Zimbabwe for the First Time, on the President’s Birthday
World.content:
Zimbabwe · Politics

Key Facts — What was observed A new Zimbabwean public holiday on 15 September, closing offices, schools and consulates abroad.

— When it became law Six days ago. The statutory instrument was gazetted on 9 September 2026.

— Whose birthday it is Emmerson Mnangagwa, Zimbabwe’s president, who turned 84 on Tuesday.

— Where the name comes from The Mutapa empire, whose rulers held the title Munhumutapa from the fifteenth century.

— Who started it The youth wing of the governing party, which began marking the date in 2024.

— The wider change Zimbabwe abolished direct election of its president in July, and extended terms to seven years.

Zimbabwe closed on Tuesday for a holiday that did not legally exist last week. It carries the title of a pre-colonial empire and the date of the sitting president’s birth.

Harare. Government offices, schools and Zimbabwean consulates abroad closed for the new holiday. (Photo: “Harare – Harare3492” by lumoplank, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Zimbabwe observed Munhumutapa Day for the first time as a statutory public holiday on Tuesday. The instrument creating it was gazetted six days earlier.

A Holiday Six Days Old

Statutory Instrument 148 of 2026 declares that the fifteenth of September, every year henceforth, shall be a public holiday. It was published in an extraordinary government gazette on 9 September.

The legal basis is the Public Holidays and Prohibition of Business Act. Offices, schools and Zimbabwean consulates abroad closed, including the mission in Johannesburg.

The date is not incidental. Emmerson Mnangagwa was born on 15 September 1942 in Zvishavane, and turned 84 on Tuesday.

The main commemoration was held at Mvurwi in Mashonaland Central. Organisers laid on 260 buses and expected 30,000 young people, with attendance projected above 100,000.

Last year’s event was at Zvishavane in the Midlands. The commemoration rotates through Zimbabwe’s ten provinces.

Where the Name Comes From

Munhumutapa, also rendered Mwenemutapa, was the title borne by the rulers of the Mutapa empire. That state dominated the plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo from roughly the fifteenth century.

The empire is a genuine anchor of Zimbabwean national identity, predating Portuguese contact and British settlement. Using it for a birthday is what the argument is about.

The observance began with the youth wing of the governing party in 2024. It marked what the wing called the president’s leadership towards a 2030 development target.

Tuesday was the third commemoration. It was the first with legal force behind it.

Zimbabwe now has one more public holiday than it did a week ago, and its commemoration moves between provinces each year. (Photo: “Doon Estates, Harare, Zimbabwe – 557240027” by Tips For Travellers, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

The Constitutional Change Behind It

A new holiday would be a minor story on its own. It arrives two months after a change to how Zimbabwe chooses its president.

The third amendment to the constitution was signed into law on 7 July 2026. It passed the National Assembly by 216 votes to 42 and the Senate by 75 to four.

The amendment abolishes direct popular election of the president. The office is now filled by a joint sitting of parliament, requiring more than half of valid votes.

It also extends presidential, parliamentary and local terms from five years to seven. A transitional provision applies that longer term to the sitting president.

The practical effect is that the election due in 2028 now falls in 2030. The amendment also enlarges the Senate by ten appointed seats and alters how judges are chosen.

What Critics Say

Nelson Chamisa, the main opposition figure, called the pattern totally unacceptable in remarks on 12 September. He compared the trajectory to Robert Mugabe’s and to Ian Smith’s before that.

He also dismissed talk of Mnangagwa staying to 2035 as a fantasy with very short legs. That horizon has been floated within the governing party.

Others put it more bluntly on Tuesday. One Harare resident quoted by a regional agency said the president wanted to crown himself king.

Supporters make a different case. The Mutapa reference, on that reading, reclaims a pre-colonial history that colonial rule wrote out.

What It Adds Up To

Zimbabwe now has a holiday that honours a living head of state by date and a vanished empire by name. Neither element is unusual on its own.

What is unusual is the sequence. A constitutional amendment in July removed direct presidential elections.

A national holiday on the president’s birthday followed in September. The two read as one movement rather than as separate decisions.

The next scheduled national vote is in 2030, and parliament will decide who holds the office. Munhumutapa Day will be observed four more times before then.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Munhumutapa Day?

It is a Zimbabwean public holiday observed on 15 September, created by Statutory Instrument 148 of 2026 and gazetted on 9 September 2026. Tuesday 15 September 2026 was its first observance as a statutory holiday, although the governing party’s youth wing has marked the date since 2024.

Why 15 September?

It is the birthday of President Emmerson Mnangagwa, born in Zvishavane on 15 September 1942. He turned 84 on the day of the first official observance.

What was the Mutapa empire?

It was a southern African state that dominated the plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers from around the fifteenth century, whose rulers held the title Munhumutapa or Mwenemutapa. It predates both Portuguese contact and British settlement, and is a central reference point in Zimbabwean national history.

Has Zimbabwe changed how it elects a president?

Yes. A constitutional amendment signed on 7 July 2026 ended direct popular election of the president, transferring the choice to a joint sitting of parliament, and extended terms from five years to seven. A transitional provision applies the longer term to the sitting president, moving the next presidential vote from 2028 to 2030.

World.title: Sudan Aid Supplies Run Out at the End of This Month, the UN Migration Agency Says
World.content:
Sudan · Humanitarian

Key Facts — What the warning is The UN migration agency says its emergency shelter and sanitation stocks in Sudan run out on 30 September.

— Who is affected Sudan has 8.6 million people displaced inside its own borders after three and a half years of war.

— Who is fighting The national army and the Rapid Support Forces, a former state militia that turned on it in April 2023.

— How hungry the country is Nearly 19.5 million people, about two in five Sudanese, were in crisis or worse earlier this year.

— What it would take The agency is asking for US$15 million to hold its current capacity, and US$42 million to expand.

— Why the road matters A journey between two Darfur cities that used to take six hours now takes three days by car.

Two United Nations agencies said within hours of each other that the relief operation in Sudan is close to running dry. One gave a date. The other gave a number, and both were asking for money when they said it.

A displaced woman in Darfur. Sudan has 8.6 million people displaced inside the country, on the UN migration agency’s count. (Photo: “صورة لامرأة نازحة من الفاشر الي طويلة حيث ليس لها ماوى تاركن اولادها” by Ahmed 222222, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Sudan aid supplies held by the United Nations migration agency will be exhausted at the end of this month. The agency said so on Monday, and put a figure on what it would take to avoid that.

What the Agencies Actually Said

Amy Pope runs the International Organization for Migration. She said shelter, sanitation and emergency household items are expected to be depleted by the end of September.

She also said the humanitarian system could collapse within weeks without new funding. That is the sharpest language the agency has used this year.

That is a strong phrase, and it came attached to a request. The agency wants US$15 million to hold its present capacity, which reaches 305,000 people.

US$27 million would restore last year’s level of 570,000 people. US$42 million would stretch to a million.

The warehousing that supplies the whole relief network can be maintained only to December on present money. Since July 2023 it has reached 2.84 million people.

Carl Skau, acting head of the World Food Programme, spoke the same day. His agency is about one-third funded in Sudan, and he warned of significant cuts within weeks.

The food agency has received US$206 million this year against US$645 million last year. Its stated requirement to October is US$579 million.

The Scale of the Problem

Sudan has 8.6 million people displaced inside its borders and 4.9 million who have returned. Counting those who have left the country, the total displaced approaches 14 million.

Sudan aid supplies are stretched across a population in which food itself is short. The most recent full national assessment put nearly 19.5 million people in crisis or worse, about 41 percent of the country.

Within that number, more than five million were classed as being in emergency and around 135,000 in the most severe category. No area has been declared to be in famine.

The assessment did identify a risk of famine in 14 areas. Those lie across North Darfur, South Darfur and South Kordofan.

That assessment covered February to May and has not been replaced nationally. Later projections cover only 56 localities, because the data to do more did not exist.

Shelter material is one of the categories the migration agency says will be exhausted at the end of September. (Photo: “نازحه لا تملك سوى بعض الأقمشة لتأوي نفسها و اسرتها” by Ahmed 222222, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Why the Numbers Keep Moving

The war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces. It has settled into a rough partition rather than a victory for either side.

The army retook Khartoum state in May 2025. The Rapid Support Forces hold Darfur and run a parallel government from Nyala.

They took El Fasher in October 2025, after an eighteen-month siege. It was the last city in Darfur the army still held.

Kordofan is the front line, and that is where people are moving. More than 200,000 were newly displaced there in August, concentrated around El Obeid.

Another 78,000 were displaced in Blue Nile state and 18,000 in West Darfur over the same period. No September count has been published.

Getting Aid In Is the Other Half

The main crossing from Chad into West Darfur is at Adre. Sudanese authorities extended its authorisation only to 30 September, the same date the agency has put on its stocks.

Inside the country, roads have deteriorated to the point of changing the arithmetic. Skau’s own drive from El Obeid to El Fasher took three days, on a route that used to take six hours.

A convoy carrying 50 tonnes of flour was attacked near El Rahad in June, killing a driver. The government commission that reported it blamed the Rapid Support Forces.

That is one party to the war describing the conduct of the other. No independent account of the attack has been published.

The food agency has moved more of its work into the air as a result. Flying costs more and carries less.

What to Make of the Appeals

Both statements about Sudan aid supplies were funding appeals, and both sets of figures are the agencies’ own. They are reportable because the underlying displacement and hunger numbers come from separate assessments.

The wider picture is harder to pin down than either agency implies. The UN said in August that Sudan’s three-billion-dollar appeal was 40 percent funded.

Its own financial tracking service showed coverage far below that. The two figures have not been reconciled.

What is not in dispute is the direction. Money has fallen by roughly half year on year while the number of people needing help has not.

Sudan aid supplies and a border authorisation now expire in the same week. One is a warehouse problem and the other is a political one.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is running out in Sudan?

The International Organization for Migration says its emergency stocks of shelter material, sanitation supplies and basic household relief items in Sudan are expected to be exhausted by the end of September 2026. It is asking for US$15 million to maintain its current reach of 305,000 people and US$42 million to reach a million.

Is there a famine in Sudan?

No area has been formally classified as being in famine. The most recent national assessment placed nearly 19.5 million people in crisis or worse, including about 135,000 in the most severe category, and identified a risk of famine in 14 areas of North Darfur, South Darfur and South Kordofan under a worst-case scenario.

Who controls Sudan now?

The country is roughly partitioned. The Sudanese army holds the north, centre and east, including Port Sudan and Khartoum, which it retook in May 2025. The Rapid Support Forces hold Darfur, including El Fasher since October 2025, and run a parallel administration from Nyala. Kordofan is contested.

Why is delivering aid so difficult?

Roads have become impassable or dangerous, relief convoys have been attacked, and the main cross-border corridor from Chad at Adre operates under a Sudanese authorisation that runs only to 30 September. One senior UN official recently took three days to make a Darfur journey that used to take six hours.

Sources: UN News on the warnings from the International Organization for Migration and the World Food Programme, Radio Tamazuj on the IOM statement, IPC analysis of acute food insecurity in Sudan, Al Jazeera on displacement in Kordofan, UN News on the extension of the Adre border crossing, World Food Programme, Sudan emergency page

World.title: Nairobi 2029 Will Be the First World Athletics Championships Held in Africa
World.content:
Kenya · Sport

Key Facts — What was decided World Athletics awarded its 2029 championships to Nairobi at a council meeting in Budapest.

— Why it is a first The senior championships have never been held in Africa in their 42-year history.

— Who else wanted it London, Rome and Munich all bid. Munich was given the 2031 edition instead.

— Where it will be held Kasarani stadium in Nairobi, capacity 48,000, currently mid-renovation for football’s 2027 Africa Cup.

— Why Kenya is the natural host Kenyan athletes have dominated middle and long-distance running for half a century.

— What is not yet known No visitor, hotel or revenue projection has been published by anyone in Kenya.

The senior World Athletics Championships have been held nineteen times since 1983 and never once in Africa. That ends in September 2029, in a Nairobi stadium that is currently being rebuilt for a football tournament.

Kasarani stadium in Nairobi, which will host the 2029 World Athletics Championships. It seats 48,000. (Photo: “Inside the Kasarani Stadium” by Endesia94, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Nairobi 2029 will be the first senior World Athletics Championships staged on the African continent. The decision was taken at a council meeting in Budapest and announced on Tuesday.

The Decision

Four cities bid for the two available editions. Nairobi, London, Rome and Munich went to the council, which gave 2029 to Nairobi and 2031 to Munich.

Lord Coe, the World Athletics president, called the Kenyan bid compelling and emotional. Taking the championships to Africa for the first time, he said, will be historic.

No vote breakdown has been published. The council has 26 members and its evaluation process was not made public.

The event is the 22nd edition and falls in September 2029. The championships have been held every two years since 1983 and never in Africa.

That phrasing needs care. Africa has hosted World Athletics events before.

Kenya staged the world cross-country championships in Mombasa in 2007. It also held world age-group championships in Nairobi in 2017 and 2021.

What has never happened is the senior outdoor championships, the sport’s flagship. That is the gap Nairobi 2029 closes.

The Stadium Is Not Finished

The venue is the Moi International Sports Centre at Kasarani, which seats 48,000. It is currently a building site.

Kenya is rebuilding it for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which it co-hosts. The work runs in two phases at a combined cost of about 6.7 billion Kenyan shillings, roughly US$52 million.

The first phase cost 3.6 billion shillings, about US$28 million, and was finished in 2025 for an earlier tournament. A senior official later said that phase had been carried out in haste, which is why a second was needed.

The second phase covers a hybrid grass pitch, drainage, a spectator canopy, full seat replacement, floodlighting and video-assistant-referee infrastructure. It is due for completion before the 2027 tournament.

Kenyan media have called Kasarani the country’s longest construction site. No completion date has been published.

Kasarani is being rebuilt in two phases at a combined cost of about 6.7 billion Kenyan shillings, for football’s 2027 Africa Cup of Nations. (Photo: “Dn sports kpl 2701 ows” by Sila Kiplagat, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

How Kenya Is Paying for Stadiums

The financing model is unusual and worth understanding. Kenya’s sports fund draws revenue from taxes and levies on betting and gaming.

The government pledges that future revenue as security for bonds. A first issue of about 44.7 billion shillings, near US$346 million, was listed in July 2025.

That issue funds a new 60,000-seat stadium in Nairobi. The model turns gambling revenue into building sites.

A second issue of 38.74 billion shillings, about US$300 million, was announced at the start of September to complete 33 stadium projects. It is repayable over fifteen years.

The International Monetary Fund has urged Kenya to classify roughly 335 billion shillings of securitised money, near US$2.6 billion, as public debt. Members of parliament have separately raised concerns about unpaid bills on stadium work.

President William Ruto has described a large stadium-building programme in various figures. Published sources give 22 completed, 28 pledged and 33 under the current financing, and the numbers do not reconcile.

The Doping Question, Answered Before It Was Asked

Kenya’s anti-doping agency spent part of last year on the world body’s compliance watchlist after an audit found deficiencies. Being on a watchlist is not the same as being declared non-compliant.

The agency was removed from that list on 28 February 2026 after corrective work. Had it failed, Kenya could have lost the right to host international events.

That timing was not an accident. Clearing the list came before the bid, not after it.

Kenyan athletics remains in the highest risk category for doping and the national agency faces budget pressure. Those are real issues and they are separate from compliance status.

What Nobody Has Costed

There is no published Kenyan projection for visitors, hotel rooms, tourism revenue or economic impact from Nairobi 2029. Not from the tourism ministry, not from the tourism board, not in the bid material released publicly.

The only official comment so far is general. A cabinet secretary said Kenya must position its entrepreneurs to benefit, without attaching a figure.

World Athletics says 68 percent of Kenyans surveyed rated their interest in athletics as high, against a global average of 39 percent. That research is its own, and its method and sample were not disclosed.

For anyone in Nairobi hospitality, the useful number before Nairobi 2029 is the calendar. There are three years to the Africa Cup of Nations and six to the championships, on the same site.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this really the first time in Africa?

For the senior World Athletics Championships, yes. They have been held every two years since 1983 and never on the African continent. Africa has hosted other World Athletics events, including the world cross-country championships in Mombasa in 2007 and world age-group championships in Nairobi in 2017 and 2021.

Where will it be held?

At the Moi International Sports Centre at Kasarani in Nairobi, which seats 48,000. The stadium is currently being rebuilt in two phases for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, at a combined cost of about 6.7 billion Kenyan shillings, roughly US$52 million.

Which cities lost?

London and Rome bid for 2029 and did not get it. Munich also bid and was awarded the 2031 edition instead. World Athletics has not published a vote breakdown.

Is Kenya’s doping record a problem for hosting?

Kenya’s anti-doping agency was placed on the world body’s compliance watchlist in late 2025 after an audit found deficiencies, and was removed on 28 February 2026 after corrective work. It was never formally declared non-compliant. Kenyan athletics does remain in the highest risk category for doping under the sport’s integrity unit.

Sources: World Athletics on the award of the 2029 and 2031 championships, Capital FM on the Nairobi bid, K24 on the Kasarani renovation, Business Daily on the stadium financing, SJAK on Kenya’s removal from the anti-doping watchlist, Sacco Review on the government response to the award

World.title: Durban Refugees Moved to Gauteng After Four Months on a Pavement
World.content:
South Africa · Society

Key Facts — What happened South Africa moved 278 people from a pavement camp in Durban to a facility in Gauteng province.

— Who they are Mostly people from Congo, Burundi and Rwanda who had been living and working in Durban.

— Why they were on the street They were driven from homes and businesses in May by threats tied to anti-immigrant protests.

— What the papers showed Of 457 people checked by the city, all but three held valid documentation.

— Where they have gone Lindela in Krugersdorp, which is normally South Africa’s deportation holding centre.

— What comes next A protest movement has set 30 September as its own deadline for undocumented migrants to leave.

Two hundred and seventy-eight people boarded five buses in Durban on Tuesday, four months after being driven from their homes. Of 457 people verified at the camp they were leaving, three lacked valid papers.

Durban. The camp stood on the pavement outside the Home Affairs refugee reception office on Che Guevara Road. (Photo: “Durban City Centre (201291238)” by Chris Bloom from Durban, South Africa, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)
