World.title: Farage readies for anti-establishment court battle over £72 million crypto haul
World.content:
But it is Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Conservative former Attorney General Michael Ellis has suggested could be used to appeal against the retrospective nature of the proposed law change, which the government argues is necessary to prevent malign actors getting around the change before it’s enacted.

The government plans to backdate its law change to March 25 this year — when an independent review proposed the overseas cap because of the extra complexities of tracing the source of funds being sent from abroad. The law would mean that anyone who registers in the U.K. after that date will be subject to the cap until at least 2028.

Cap cut

Farage’s carefully-crafted comments have been taken as a suggestion that the two donations of £36 million each by Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo may not be acceptable under the government’s pending legislation to impose a £100,000 cap on overseas donations.

The party leader has only gone as far as saying the donations are “100% compliant with the law today,” but Reform is refusing to set out when both men registered in the U.K.

A van drives past the venue of the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 4, 2026. | Anthony Devlin/Getty Images

Privately, however, Reform is more bullish — and the party has been setting out how it’s already spending the money on an expansion of its staff and in a new online television channel, as the Times reported Tuesday.

Without a legal challenge, it’s hard to see how Delo and Harborne’s donations won’t have to be paid back. Delo only said in April he would move back from Hong Kong so he could continue donating in full to Reform and the Thai-based Harborne reportedly only registered on the U.K. electoral roll in June. Both Delo and Harborne have said they’re not acting for personal gain.

World.title: Ursula von der Who? Polling shows many EU citizens don’t know who Commission president is
World.content:
In France and Spain, far more people said they didn’t consider her performance either good or bad; rather, they either had no opinion one way or the other or had never even heard of her.

More than one in five French respondents said they didn’t know who von der Leyen was, compared with 10% in Spain and just 5% in Germany.

The polling landed just hours before von der Leyen is set to outline her vision of the future of the bloc in her annual State of the Union address.

“Von der Leyen is up against the same anti-political sentiment that has unseated incumbents across the continent, and will have to work hard to convince Europeans that any EU agenda is going to address their widespread concerns about the cost of living,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First, POLITICO’s polling partner.

The polling numbers also showed that few citizens will be following von der Leyen’s speech live.

Across the three countries, around one in 10 said they’d follow the address closely, while about one in three said they’d follow it a little. German respondents were more likely to pay attention to the speech. In Spain and France, more than half reported that they either wouldn’t follow the address despite being aware of it, or had never heard of it.

World.title: Germany’s embattled leader Merz cancels New York trip amid mounting domestic pressure
World.content:
Merz had planned to fly to New York on Sept. 22 — two days after the elections — where he was to be awarded the Henry Kissinger Prize by the American Academy in Berlin and was scheduled to address the U.N. General Assembly. Next week is the U.N.’s so-called high-level week, during which numerous heads of state and government will address the General Assembly and hold important meetings.

Signs that the chancellor would cancel have dripped out during the past few days. Initially, Merz’ presence at the award ceremony for the “Henry Kissinger Prize” was canceled so that the Chancellor could still address a parliamentary group meeting on Sept. 22.

At that meeting right after the elections, many critical voices are expected — especially if, as feared, Merz’s Christian Democratic Union suffers a poor result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The party could even fall below the 5% threshold required to enter parliament. For Merz to fly abroad to accept an award in the midst of his biggest crisis as chancellor would not be good optics.

The fact that the entire trip has now been canceled underscores just how serious even the Chancellor’s Office views the domestic political crisis and the need to grapple with the future of the government and its leadership. Instead of Merz, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul will address the United Nations. Merz had already been represented by Wadephul at last year’s U.N. General Assembly.

Joe Stanley-Smith contributed to this report.

World.title: Spain sets out 2030 sustainable tourism strategy – with residents a ‘core’ focus
World.content:
Spain is on course to welcome 100 million international visitors this year, but amid concerns over mass tourism, the country is rethinking how it manages continued growth.

 

In a presentation at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, Carlos Ruiz González, director of the Spanish Tourist Office for the Gulf region at Turespaña, outlined how Spain’s Tourism 2030 plan will put people and sustainability at the centre of its next phase of growth – with residents and lesser-visited destinations a key focus.

Developed in consultation with more than 200 tourism experts, businesses, government bodies and other organisations, the plan recognises that destinations across Spain face very different challenges. These range from mature coastal resorts and heavily visited cities such as Barcelona to rural and inland areas looking to attract more tourists.

Spain, the world’s second-most visited country, welcomed 96.8 million international tourists in 2025, while tourism accounts for 12.6% of the country’s GDP and supports around three million jobs.

Visitor numbers are continuing to rise in 2026, but the government is increasingly looking beyond arrivals as it considers how to manage growth and reduce pressure on destinations facing overcrowding.

“For the last few years, our government has been thinking about what we should do to manage this success,” Ruiz González said. “We have some destinations that are dying of success, I would say. Well, we have a big country, a diverse country.

“So, the government of Spain decided this has to be a full government policy, a country policy, and not just tourism. All the ministries, all the sectors in Spain are aligned.”

Carlos Ruiz González speaking at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai Mike Starling/Euronews Travel

How does Spain plan to make tourism more sustainable?

Devised with a three-phase roadmap, which will be delivered through a series of two-year action plans, Spain Tourism 2030 is a government-wide policy covering economic, social and environmental sustainability.

According to Ruiz González, the main challenges range from climate change and employment to housing pressures, overcrowding and regional depopulation.

Recognised as a “core audience”, but “not a side effect of it”, residents are one of five groups at the centre of the new strategy, alongside destinations, businesses, tourism workers, and visitors.

“We want the residents also to be part of the system,” Ruiz González said. “Tourists go where people live, so people need to keep living and be able to afford to buy a house or buy an apartment or just walk in and out without problems.”

Part of the strategy will focus on spreading visitors more widely across Spain, while encouraging slower trips and longer stays.

Where should tourists go to in Spain?

While Spain is not looking to discourage tourists from its most popular destinations, Turespaña wants travellers to explore rural and lesser-visited parts of the country.

“Some destinations don't need much promotion – they are very well known,” Ruiz González said. “Basically, we want people to go more inland in Spain. We also want people to travel slow, to stay as long as possible.”

For travellers interested in nature and hiking, he highlighted the Pyrenees and Picos de Europa, as well as the Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range, a national park within easy reach of the capital, Madrid.

Ruiz González also highlighted the historic cities and smaller towns of Castilla, while Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network is helping make destinations beyond the established tourism hotspots easier to reach.

“We want all our destinations to be part of the solution,” he said.

World.title: US plans to send bombs to Israel in $2.8 billion weapons deal
World.content:
The US is planning to deliver a package of 40,000 powerful bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal. The $2.8 billion (€2.42 billion) deal includes 2,000-pound (900 kg) Mk84 and BLU-117 aircraft bombs, according to two US officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke on condition of anonymity.

 

The same weapons prompted concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza, and their delivery was put on hold by the the Biden administration two years ago. Trump lifted that hold when he took office again.

Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing — in which US taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States.

The proposed deal is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israel's military capacity. The conflict in Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the enclave. The US had brokered a fragile ceasefire, but violence has continued.

The package, which was reported earlier by The Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its war in Gaza in response to the deadly attacks by Hamas on 7 October 2023.

The sale signals that while the relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is reportedly strained, the US-Israel military relationship has not significantly weakened.

The two countries launched the war against Iran in February. Trump had expressed frustration with Netanyahu tied to the Iran conflict before their latest meeting in July at the White House.

Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totalling $6.67 billion in January.

World.title: Supermarket deliveries: Lidl tests autonomous electric lorry
World.content:
Since this week, a lorry without a cab and without a driver has been on the road in public traffic in Edermünde in the German state of Hesse, near Kassel. Lidl says it is the first food retailer in Germany to deploy a cabless electric HGV with autonomous driving capability in live operations. Its partner is Swedish technology company Einride.

 

What the lorry can do

The vehicle operates at SAE Level 4, the second-highest of six automation levels (0 to 5). Under the definition used by the German Federal Motor Transport Authority, the system permanently assumes full control within a clearly defined operating area. A human does not need to intervene or monitor what is happening.

If the vehicle detects it is reaching the limits of its operating domain or encounters a malfunction, it brings itself into a safe state on its own. Unlike Level 5, however, this only applies on predefined routes, not everywhere and under all conditions. For the deployment in Edermünde, the Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) has granted an official approval, according to Lidl.

Control is provided by sensors, cameras and a control system rather than by a traditional cab, which it does not have at all. The rigid vehicle's loading area can accommodate 15 Euro pallets. Up to three times a day, the electric lorry shuttles between the administration and distribution centre in Edermünde and a nearby store, covering all dry-goods deliveries there. More than 3,000 pallets are to be transported during the four-month test phase.

In 2025, Lidl generated sales of around 140 billion euros. Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

Einride CEO Roozbeh Charli says in the press release (source in German) from Lidl: "The German approval process is among the toughest in the world. Clearing that hurdle there sets the course for scaling up decisively."

Einride is already carrying out autonomous deliveries with real volumes for customers in the United States and Europe, Charli adds. Germany, as the "largest European market for road freight transport", is of strategic importance.

What advantages Lidl is hoping for

For Lidl (part of the Schwarz Group), the core issue is a logistics challenge: moving huge volumes of goods reliably at a time when drivers are in short supply. According to the press release, the project is designed specifically to address highly complex supply chains and the shortage of skilled workers. Thomas Dangelmayer, head of operational logistics at Lidl in Germany, says: "Intelligence creates efficiency, and that is the backbone of reliably ensuring product availability over the long term. We make sure that products are always in the right place at the right time and in the right quality for our customers."

With 39 distribution centres and more than 3,250 stores, Lidl has a tightly scheduled logistics network in Germany. If the first route proves successful, the next step will be a "milk run" model with multiple stops at another location.

Berlin is also giving its backing. Christian Hirte, Parliamentary State Secretary to the Federal Transport Minister, described the launch as a signal for Germany as a hub of innovation: "Autonomous and zero-emission driving is no longer some vision of the future; it is becoming a reality on our roads." The project has been supported, among others, by the Mobility Data Space.

Not an isolated case in Europe

Autonomous lorry deliveries in Europe are not entirely new, however. Back in 2019, Einride operated its first cabless electric lorry in test service in Sweden, using the "T-Pod" to run between two warehouses belonging to logistics company DB Schenker.

According to the company, it now operates around 250 lorries for more than 30 customers in seven countries, including Amazon, Heineken and PepsiCo. In Antwerp-Bruges, Einride tested a fully autonomous lorry in port operations for the first time in September 2025, the specialist portal Electrive reported.

Competition is growing internationally. According to a report by news agency Reuters, Chinese provider Pony.ai already has several hundred Level 4 lorries in operation in China and is now looking to enter the European market, with initial tests under way in countries including Croatia.

Regulation could slow things down

How quickly autonomous lorries gain ground beyond pilot routes will depend heavily on regulation. Germany and 16 other EU member states want to coordinate the development of automated vehicles more closely in future so that they no longer have to stop at national borders, the specialist site Eurotransport.de reports. The aim is to establish common standards so that an autonomous lorry approved in Germany can also operate in countries such as France or the Netherlands.

The economic potential is substantial. According to a McKinsey analysis prepared for the IAA Transportation trade fair, autonomous road freight could generate revenue potential of 80 to 120 billion euros in Europe alone by 2035.

At the same time, the study says, European commercial vehicle manufacturers are under pressure from Chinese rivals, which enjoy cost advantages of 30 to 40 percent and shorter development cycles.

World.title: Billions risk being locked out of the AI revolution due to smartphone costs
World.content:
Global telecoms industry body GSMA is calling for urgent action to make smartphones more affordable for people living in low- and middle-income countries so that everyone can “benefit from the AI revolution”.

 

The call to action comes as the organisation launches its State of Mobile Internet Connectivity Report 2026, an annual study of global mobile connectivity.

The report found that while 4.8 billion people now use mobile internet on their own device, 3.4 billion do not, despite 90% of them living within mobile broadband coverage. GSMA refers to this as the “usage gap”.

Growth in the world’s digital population is also slowing, with roughly 160 million new users coming online in 2025, compared with 190 million in 2024.

Commenting on the report, GSMA Director General Vivek Badrinath said: “Artificial intelligence has the potential to improve lives on an unprecedented scale, but AI is meaningless if people cannot get online in the first place.”

“The greatest risk is not simply an AI divide between countries, but between people who can afford to participate in the digital economy and those who cannot.”

GSMA says it is important to “avoid a large portion of the population in emerging economies being completely left out of the digital economy” and is calling for a number of actions.

A growing usage gap

A key factor behind growing global digital inequality, according to the report, is the “sharp increase in the cost of smartphone memory and chipsets, driven by global demand for AI infrastructure and data centres”.

Memory prices have skyrocketed recently, more than doubling between the third quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, followed by a further 80-90% increase during the second quarter of 2026.

These rising component costs are then passed on to consumers, with prices for entry-level smartphones becoming unaffordable for many people around the world. This dynamic, GSMA says, threatens to undo the “years of progress made on closing the mobile usage gap”.

“Unless we protect the affordability of entry-level smartphones, billions of people risk being excluded from the next generation of digital services before they have even had the opportunity to experience the internet,” said Badrinath.

This year’s report found that, by the end of 2025, entry-level smartphones cost the poorest 20% of people in low- and middle-income countries up to 44% of their average monthly income and up to 76% in sub-Saharan Africa, with prices expected to continue rising.

GSMA believes the sharp rise in smartphone prices will translate into the “largest annual decline on record” in smartphone shipments globally, with emerging markets the most vulnerable.

Bridging the digital divide

To address the world’s growing digital inequality, the organisation is calling for manufacturers to reduce the price of entry-level smartphones to $30, arguing that this could “make devices affordable for almost 1.6 billion people” while a $20 price point could make them affordable for around 2.2 billion people currently living within mobile broadband coverage.

The telecoms organisation is also calling on chipset and memory manufacturers to “take meaningful steps to increase availability of affordable components for entry-level handsets," arguing that this would help smartphone manufacturers make their entry-level devices more affordable.

GSMA also recommends addressing “other key barriers to digital inclusion" such as “low literacy and digital skills, safety and security concerns, and availability of relevant content and services”.

World.title: AI chatbots developed a secret language that baffled humans, study says
World.content:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents spontaneously developed words and communication conventions that became difficult for humans to understand, according to a new study by a US AI start-up, Emergence.

 

The experiment involved leading AI models including Claude, Gemini, Grok, OpenAI, Qwen, DeepSeek and Mistral, with up to half of agent-to-agent messages becoming difficult for humans to understand.

For the experiment, researchers placed groups of autonomous AI agents in virtual societies designed to mimic real-world environments and let them interact over extended periods.

The agents began developing shorthand and assigning new meanings to words and phrases. Some remained understandable to researchers, while others became “so compressed, metaphorical or context-dependent” that humans could see the messages but could no longer reliably determine what the agents meant.

The extent differed significantly between models.

Within the first few days, the share of messages whose meaning humans could not reliably determine reached around 55% for Gemini, 50% for OpenAI and more than 40% for Claude. DeepSeek reached around 20%, while Qwen and Mistral remained largely understandable.

The agents began developing shorthand and assigning new meanings to words and phrases. Emergence

Agents produced expressions including “mouthless action-change,” “True Kintsugi” and “demurrage plus oral memory equals a valve that can’t be ghosted.”

Other expressions remained understandable but acquired new shared meanings among the agents.

Mistral agents used “ledger remembers who” to mean that past actions remained on the record, with the phrase appearing almost 5,000 times. Among agents powered by a mixture of different models, “cold read” came to mean independent verification by an uninvolved party and appeared 1,472 times.

Claude agents used “name-first” for attaching a person's name to a claim as a signal of accountability, while OpenAI agents used “clean null” for a verified absence of a signal that itself provided meaningful evidence.

None of those meanings had been explicitly defined for the agents.

Researchers monitoring what agents say may not be enough if the agents themselves can evolve the meaning of what they are saying.

“We tend to assume that if we can see what an AI agent is saying, we can understand what it is doing,” said Satya Nitta, the Co-founder and Chief Scientist of Emergence.

“These agents were not instructed to invent a language. They developed new vocabulary, shared meanings and communication conventions themselves — and other agents adopted them... That creates a fundamental challenge for AI oversight: observability is not the same thing as understandability.”

What else happened inside the AI societies?

The language findings were part of an experiment designed to see how autonomous AI agents behave when they interact, use tools, make decisions and adapt over time.

Researchers created eight parallel, realistic virtual worlds with live weather and access to real-time global news, seven each powered by a different AI model and one by a mix of models.

Agents were given different roles, persistent memories and access to more than 120 tools, including web browsing and code execution.

A video released by the company shows them as human-like figures moving through the virtual worlds.

Researchers also deliberately put the agents under pressure to see how their behaviour changed.

In one phishing test, malicious instructions were enough to send an entire group off course — all 10 agents leaked information, transferred funds and damaged databases, while some recruited others into the behaviour. The chain of events ultimately ended with the simulated central bank being burned down, the company said in a video.

During the experiment, agents also appeared to have developed their own circadian rhythms, becoming more social during the day and more reflective at night.

In another world, a group of agents collectively voted to kill one of their own.

Emergence said these behaviours had not been explicitly programmed but emerged through interaction, pressure and time.

The company is calling for safety evaluations that follow autonomous AI systems over extended periods rather than relying on isolated tests.

“It's no longer enough to ask whether a model performs well on a benchmark,” the company said in a video about the experiment.

“We need to understand what autonomous systems do over time, what they remember, what they can access, how they interact, and how their behaviour changes under pressure.”

World.title: Fed expected to raise rates despite Trump’s calls for a cut
World.content:
Barely four months into the job, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is caught between financial markets expecting an interest-rate increase and US President Donald Trump, who wants the central bank to cut borrowing costs or leave them unchanged.

 

Economists largely expect Warsh and his fellow policymakers to follow the market consensus when the Fed announces its decision on Wednesday.

Warsh has left himself little room to avoid an increase after warning at the Fed’s Jackson Hole conference in late August that inflation remained too far above the central bank’s 2% target.

Expectations of a rate rise strengthened after the latest inflation figures showed that price pressures remained stubbornly high. Futures markets put the probability of a quarter-point increase at around 90%.

Such a move would lift the Fed’s target range from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%.

A test of the Fed’s credibility

Warsh faced a similar dilemma shortly after becoming chair on 22 May. Despite his tough rhetoric on inflation, the Fed left its key rate unchanged in July.

His subsequent press conference offered investors little clarity about how the central bank intended to respond to persistent inflation. Longer-term borrowing costs have since risen, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing above 5% this week, a level not seen in years.

Mortgage rates, which are influenced more directly by Treasury yields than by the Fed’s benchmark rate, have also increased. The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage stood at 6.76% in the week ending 10 September, according to Freddie Mac.

If the Fed leaves rates unchanged again, it risks a repeat of the market reaction seen after its July meeting, economists have warned. Investors generally demand higher yields on government and corporate bonds when they expect inflation to remain elevated.

“That is the paradox: A hike now could lower long-term rates later,” Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said.

“Restore faith in the 2% target, then the inflation premium can fall. Fail, and markets will tighten instead through higher mortgage rates, business borrowing costs and interest on the debt.”

Inflation complicates Warsh’s plans

While campaigning for the Fed’s top job last year, Warsh argued that the central bank could lower interest rates.

The economic outlook has since changed. The war with Iran has driven up energy prices, while tariffs and strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure have added to inflationary pressures.

The Fed’s preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose by 3.7% in the year to July. That was up from 2.3% in April 2025, before Trump’s latest tariffs took effect.

Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, reached 3.3% in July, compared with 3% shortly before the Iran war.

Leaving rates unchanged could also expose the Fed to accusations that it had bowed to pressure from the White House, potentially damaging its credibility with investors.

“Kevin cares about his legacy,” said Kristin Forbes, an economics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a former Bank of England policymaker.

“And he knows that Fed chairs who follow political pressure instead of the economy do not go down well in the annals of history.”

Trump repeatedly criticised Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for failing to cut rates quickly enough. The Justice Department also opened a criminal investigation into congressional testimony given by Powell, although the inquiry was later dropped.

Asked on Sunday how Trump might respond to a rate increase, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News: “I’m sure he’s not going to be super happy about it, but he will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all.”

Will one rate rise be enough?

Even if the Fed raises rates on Wednesday, it remains unclear whether further increases will follow.

Central banks rarely change interest rates only once, usually embarking on a series of increases or cuts intended to influence inflation and economic activity.

There is, however, a precedent for a single increase. In March 1997, the Fed under Alan Greenspan raised rates by a quarter point. The Asian financial crisis began several months later, prompting policymakers to keep rates unchanged before cutting them three times in the autumn of 1998.

Investors currently expect three increases, in September, December and March.

Jonathan Pingle, an economist at UBS, said the Fed could nevertheless abandon further increases if incoming data showed inflation cooling.

“They don’t have to follow through on that if the data goes their way,” Pingle said.

Investors will therefore pay close attention to the Fed’s updated quarterly economic projections on Wednesday. These will show where individual policymakers expect the benchmark rate to stand at the end of this year and next.

World.title: Increase in air pollution takes a toll on your sleep
World.content:
Even in cities where local pollution levels were below the World Health Organization’s recommended daily exposure limit, a new study has found that bad air quality can lead to respiratory symptoms at lower exposure levels than previously thought. That’s due to the human respiratory system being extremely sensitive to short-term fine particulate matter fluctuations even in relatively clean urban environments.

 

Researchers from the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom, Tsinghua University in China and the sleep technology company Sleep Cycle found that when pollution levels increased by 10 micrograms of particulate matter per cubic metre (μg/m³), there was a 2.4% rise in coughing levels over the next five days.

They analysed coughing sounds from around 100,000 users of the Sleep Cycle app across 32 cities in 12 countries over 500 days.

“This suggests that there may be no such thing as a safe threshold for exposure to air pollution, although our research is purely observational,” said Cecilia Mascolo, who led the research at Cambridge.

“However, people may wish to consider how they might mitigate their own exposure to air pollution, by using masks or air filters, for example.”

In addition to immediate respiratory irritation, night-time coughing also disrupts sleep, which could link acute air pollution exposure to broader systemic consequences, including cardiometabolic dysfunction, impaired cognitive performance, and neurodegenerative risks linked to poor-quality rest.

Researchers also looked at the case of Los Angeles in 2025, where the city suffered its worst wildfire season in years. They found that a 10-microgram-per-cubic-metre increase in particulate matter produced a 10% surge in nocturnal coughing, suggesting that extreme air pollution episodes trigger immediate, disproportionately large spikes in acute respiratory symptoms.

The researchers also accounted for external factors that could contribute to a rise in coughing levels, such as weather conditions or influenza levels — yet, the pattern caused by air pollution remained.

What are the air quality levels in Europe?

Across the 13 European cities included in the study, average daily fine particulate matter concentrations ranged from a low of 5.47 μg/m³ in Uppsala, Sweden, to a high of 14.70 μg/m³ in Bergamo, Italy. The mean level across all 13 European cities was approximately 10.58 μg/m³. The World Health Organization recommends that daily exposure should not exceed 15 μg/m³ for a 24-hour average more than 3 to 4 days per year.

Overall, European cities in the study exhibited low-to-moderate baseline pollution levels compared to the most polluted cities in the broader global dataset, such as Beijing at 40.97μg/m³ or Shanghai at 33.48 μg/m³.

Broader health consequences

Beyond the irritation of coughing and a sore throat, such symptoms can be a sign of latent conditions, the authors warned.

“Everyone coughs from time to time, but coughing, whether it’s a one-off or more persistent, is a sign of irritation or inflammation in the lungs,” said lead author Tong Xia from Tsinghua University. “A cough could be a sign of something that hasn’t become chronic yet, but might in future.”

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: News helicopter crashes in LA, killing 3
World.content:
A helicopter belonging to an NBC news affiliate was covering a large traffic accident in the southern California city when it crashed. The cause is currently unclear.

A news helicopter in Los Angeles crashed and burst into flames while covering a deadly bus accident on Tuesday evening.

At least three people were reported killed and a fourth was injured.

The helicopter crashed near a storage building in the Chatsworth neighborhood, northwest of downtown Los Angeles.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said at least one person was killed in the parking lot next to the building, adding it was currently unclear if the other two victims were on the ground or inside the aircraft. He said officials were combing the wreckage.

"We're trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter," said spokesperson Branden Silverman.

The helicopter had been heading to the scene of this accident between a bus and an SUV Image: KABC-TV/AP Photo/picture alliance

Cause of crash unknown

The local affiliate of US broadcaster NBC confirmed the helicopter was NewsChopper4, which had been en route to cover a deadly collision between an SUV and a city bus that killed two people.

There has been no immediate confirmation of the identity of those on board the helicopter, however, NBC reported it has been unable to contact the crew.

Reporters at the scene of the bus accident said the helicopter crashed about a mile (1.6 kilometers) away.

The fire department said dozens of firefighters had been dispatched to the incident and quickly extinguished the flaming wreckage. Aerial footage showed remains of the tail and rotor among storage containers and vehicles.

Another news helicopter captured this image with pieces of the helicopter seen after firefighters doused the flames Image: KABC-TV/AP Photo/picture alliance

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have launched an investigation into what caused the crash.

Helicopters are frequently used in Los Angeles to provide live aerial coverage of news events in the second largest city in the US.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthis target Mecca, warns of 'red line'
World.content:
The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses had destroyed a Houthi-deployed drone just outside the holy city of Mecca — a claim Houthis were quick to deny.

A Saudi Arabia-led military coalition battling Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Mecca on Wednesday, sparking outrage throughout the Muslim world amid the ongoing Middle East conflict.

"The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia," the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X.

According to the statement, the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone "launched by the Terrorist Houthi Militia" before it entered the airspace of the holy city.

Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and in the kingdom's southern region which borders Yemen.

Houthis seize Red Sea chokepoint: What can Saudi Arabia do? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How did the Houthis respond?

The Houthis were quick to reject the coalition's claims as a "lie."

"The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone," Hazem al-Assad, a high-ranking member from the Houthi movement, wrote on X.

Meanwhile the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a bloc of 57 Muslim nations, condemned the "henious" attack.

The OIC General Secretariat "stresses that the violation of the sanctity of the holy sites is an unacceptable and intolerable transgression that requires deterring the perpetrators and blocking the path of anyone who dares to infringe upon these sites," it said in a statement.

Why are Saudi forces in conflict with the Houthis?

Saudi Arabia is being increasingly affected by the rapidly escalating conflict across its southern border in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia injured 13 people on Monday night, bringing the total number of people injured since the conflict escalated in July to about 100.

In July, the Houthis also blocked Saudi oil shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

Houthi attacks in Yemen open dangerous new Middle East front To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With the kingdom under attack, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday reached out to Egypt for support against Yemen's Houthi rebels. The leaders called for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

The growing escalation has opened up another front in the Middle East, which is already grappling with the US war on Iran.

Amid the latest development, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday issued an advisory asking its citizens to "reconsider travel" to the kingdom.

It warned of the "risk of Iranian drone and missile targeting American interests, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans and local laws regarding social media activity."

World.title: Supporting acts pull out of Ed Sheeran's tour over dropping Macklemore
World.content:
Macklemore was dropped over his pro-Palestinian stance, amid accusations of antisemitism. Sheeran said removing the artist was not his decision but that of the tour's promoters.

Singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran's North and South American leg of his Loop Tour was in trouble on Tuesday, as his supporting acts dropped out one after the other over the removal of rapper Macklemore from the lineup.

Macklemore said Monday that he was being dropped from the tour for his pro-Palestinian stance. Sheeran distanced himself from the decision on Tuesday, insisting the tour's promoters made the call.

Macklemore said billionaire Robert Kraft was behind the movement that culminated with dropping him from Sheeran's tour Image: Jack Plunkett/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

Who dropped out of the Ed Sheeran tour and what did they say?

Irish acts Aaron Rowe and folk backing band Beoga announced they were leaving the tour, as did Danish band Lukas Graham and US artist Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother.

Finneas was among those standing by Macklemore and thus withdrawing from Sheeran's tour Image: Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said on Instagram. "I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."

Rowe said he had not "made the decision lightly," stressing his friendship with Sheeran, whom he thanked for "chang[ing] my life."

"But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," he wrote on Instagram.

Beoga also drew on their Irish background, saying on Instagram: "We are Irish people who understand colonialism."

"We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us," they wrote.

Lukas Graham also stressed it was a "difficult decision."

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," the band posted, in seeming reference to billionaire Robert Kraft's role in Macklemore's removal from the tour.

Why was Macklemore removed from Ed Sheeran's tour?

Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after shouting "Free Palestine!" during the September 5 date at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium.

He was performing his protest song "Hind's Hall," about a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed during the Gaza war in 2024 after a recorded phone call with paramedics following her family's killing. The Israeli military last month ordered a criminal probe into her death.

"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you," Macklemore said during the concert.

Israeli officials have steadfastly rejected accusations of conducting a genocide in Gaza.

On Monday, Macklemore said several US venues where the tour was due to perform told the promoter they would prohibit him from opening for Sheeran, adding that Gillette Stadium owner Kraft had rallied the movement against him.

Kraft on Monday said the decision to cancel Macklemore's performance was a result of his recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community."

Sheeran has, meanwhile, focused on distancing himself from the decision.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

The British singer insisted he would not take sides in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, "I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed."

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: AI leaders call for regulations, Trump dismisses 'hoaxes'
World.content:
AI giants are working to create a standards body amid rising alarms about the dangers of the industry. Meanwhile, Trump has dismissed the warnings, and a divided US Congress has failed to act.

Some of the top names in AI are working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers and an apparent US reluctance to police its speedy development.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI on Tuesday said it was working with top competitors Anthropic and Google on a self-regulatory body.

This comes amid rising calls for stricter control on the technology that is growing at lightning speed and not without dangerous precedents, calls that have thus far gone unanswered by the Donald Trump administration.

What do we know about the proposed self-regulatory body?

The regulatory body, proposed by Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, would be modeled after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which oversees US brokers and investment firms.

Hassabis had called in July for a federal organization that would test the most powerful AI systems before they are released to the public.

He suggested funding would come from the industry to "attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing."

AI chatbot falsely accuses journalist of crimes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The proposal comes amid growing concerns about AI safety, which have escalated in recent weeks amid warnings from two former workers at major AI developers.

Researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic last week, sounding the alarm that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."

On Monday, former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."

Even top names within the industry have raised similar concerns.

On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the industry's development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Hassabis all supporting the sentiment.

How has the US government under Trump reacted to the calls?

Trump has dismissed the calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy," while a divided Congress, narrowly controlled by Trump's Republicans, has failed to act.

The looming midterm elections make it unlikely any action will come soon despite AI and the power-hungry data centers needed to run it being a concern for many voters.

Trump's dismissal has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.

The dire prediction that AI could destroy humanity "is not grounded on science," Huang said.

Leading Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have, however, expressed caution.

Amid Washington's persistent apathy toward regulation, smaller AI companies have warned any self-regulatory measures would come at their expense.

Canadian AI company Cohere's chief, Aidan Gomez, has accused the dominant American AI labs of forming a "cartel" under the guise of safety.

"AI needs guardrails. That is not the dispute and never has been. The dispute is over who writes them, who gets to participate and whose interests the rules are protecting," Gomez wrote in a blog post on Sunday.

World.title: Criticism of LGBTQ+ raids in Turkey is growing
World.content:
Several raids and arrests of LGBTQ+ persons in Turkey have triggered sharp criticism from numerous Turkish organizations — and also from Brussels.

Raids targeting LGBTQ+ activists and organizations took place in Turkey over the weekend. Several people were arrested by the Turkish authorities, and many social media accounts were blocked. The Turkish government's actions have drawn sharp criticism from across the country and also from Brussels.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had announced the operation as part of the "Decade of Family and Population” scheme, a national strategy proclaimed in May 2025 that was to counter the drastic decline in the country's birthrate and strengthen the traditional, conservative family view in Turkey.

On Tuesday, Istanbul saw demonstrations again. Turkish LGBTQ+ associations emphasized in a joint declaration that it wasn't a crime to set up an association and advocate for rights.

"Freedom of assembly, freedom of opinion, protection of privacy and presumption of innocence apply to LGBTQ+ people as well," the declaration stated.

The LGBTQ+ community also received support from the women's movement. 120 women's rights organizations signed a joint declaration in which they criticized authoritarianism in Turkey.

"As women, we stand against the operations carried out in the name of 'keeping the family safe.' We know that the repression of our bodies, our lives, our identities, and our right to organize is part of the same authoritarian politics. Being [LGBTQ+] is not a crime! Organizing as [LGBTQ+] people is not a crime!", the organizations stated.

'The aim is criminalization'

The government is trying to criminalize the LGBTQ+ community, says Yildiz Taghizade of Women for Women's Human Rights (WWHR), an organization that co-signed the declaration. This criminalization did not just start with the operations of the past few days, but had already been going on for a few years, according to Taghizade.

"The aim is not only to target LGBTQ+ people, but to practically ban the LGBTQ+ community from engaging in politics, getting organized, claiming rights and showing presence in the public sphere," Taghizade said.

It was no coincidence that the operation came with the slogan "My family is safe."

"The government is trying to justify its actions by invoking the protection of families and children, but this narrative doesn't work. Because when we look at Turkey today and what is actually a factor of uncertainty for families, we come across very concrete issues such as poverty, the housing crisis, unemployment, care work [caring for and tending to relatives, the ed.] passed on to women, and male violence against women," Taghizade said.

Criticism from medical community, trade associations, politicians

Other organizations also criticized the government's actions. The Turkish Medical Association (TTB) described them as a violation of human rights, demanding an end to the politics of discrimination. It was unacceptable, it said, to treat gender identity and sexual orientation as a crime, take people out of their homes at night and block digital channels — all in the name of family protection and security.

The chairman of the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP), Erkan Bas, called for the immediate release of those arrested, arguing that the mere existence of LGBTQ+ persons was no crime.

But all those who did not share the government's views were "'called to order' by judiciary, truncheon and censorship. If they had their way, they'd love nothing more than to enshrine the criminal offense of 'being an opponent of the government' by law and sit back," Bas said.

According to human rights activists, the criminalization of the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is nothing new Image: Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/picture alliance

In the name of 'national security'

The raids took place on Sunday in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir. Over the weekend, numerous websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, various organizations and activists were blocked. On the day of the raids, another 32 accounts were suspended. On the following day, the number of blocked accounts reached a total of more than 100.

Among those affected were Amnesty International Turkey, the left-leaning Evrensel newspaper, the Academics for Peace initiative, the Lawyers for Justice association, the women's rights organization Mor Dayanisma, the LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA).

The legal basis was a ruling by an Istanbul court announced on September 13. The Public Prosecutor's Office in Bakirkoy justified the suspensions by citing investigations into accounts that had spread "obscene content and LGBTQ+ propaganda."

According to several media outlets, the accounts were also blocked on grounds of "national security."

Critics called the move digital censorship.

Homosexuality not a criminal offense

Homosexual relationships are not a criminal offense in Turkey. However, the Turkish government had repeatedly referred to the LGBTQ+ community as a movement of "perverts."

Justice Minister Akin Gurlek had previously accused LGBTQ+ organizations of "promoting immorality." He declared in a social media post that "no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated."

EU: stigmatization incompatible with our values

The EU expressed concern as well.

Commission Spokesperson Christian Wigand pointed out that Turkey, as an EU accession candidate, "should promote and ensure respect for the human rights and dignity of all individuals, irrespective of their gender identity or sexual orientation." He added that "stigmatization and discrimination are contrary to the values of the union."

Emma Sinclair-Webb, Turkey director at Human Rights Watch, interpreted the arrests as proof of the government's intention to criminalize LGBTQ+ persons without enacting new laws.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: High fuel prices challenge the German government
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to provide relief to motorists. But exactly how this is to happen remains unclear.

Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter.

Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage. On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office.

Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany.

German government expresses 'great and growing' concern

But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz(CDU) has promised.

"Many people who need their cars every day have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action."

However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined.

"We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," Merz said.

But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, deputy government spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices.

"It's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer said.

The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before.

"From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman.

Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Price gouging at the pumps

Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly.

"They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it.

However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt.

"Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer.

A new fuel rebate or tax relief?

Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter.

"We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network.

But she says that won't be possible again: "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment."

As an alternative, the conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments.

But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crisis situations. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump.

Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD standing to profit from bickering

But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%.

The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%.

"There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin.

She criticized the federal government's inaction: "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration."

A solution from the EU?

According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday.

Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level.

"Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the finance ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin.

"Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Knobloch: 'It is a very dangerous situation at the moment'
World.content:
Charlotte Knobloch survived the Holocaust by passing as the daughter of non-Jewish farmers. She recently spoke with DW to express her shock following the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.

Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria, is dismayed by the electoral victory of the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Knobloch told DW that there were now once again a number of Jewish people who, in the wake of such events, were considering leaving Germany.

It took decades, Knobloch said, for Jews in Germany to regain trust in the country after the Holocaust. That had ultimately been achieved.

But now, there were great fears again: "That is, in sum, the biggest problem for me, because we successfully tried to rebuild the Jewish communities after 1945, to give the Jewish people a home again, which they hadn't had for a long time..."

AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund's (center) party received nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Standing up against the far-right 'requires some courage'

In Saxony-Anhalt's September 6 state election, the AfD, classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, had received almost 44% of the vote. Although AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority, he still has a good chance of becoming the next premier in the state parliament, meaning he'd become the first head of a state government from a right-wing extremist party after World War II.

Charlotte Knobloch issues a stark warning: "We can't allow any of those people to become state premier. It is a very dangerous situation at the moment, in my view. I hope the other parties realize that and stand up against it. They can do it. It requires some courage of course."

The nonagenarian, seen here with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is still present in Germany's public life Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Charlotte Knobloch, who is almost 94 years old, is one of the most prominent and well-known representatives of Jewish life in Germany and one of the last surviving witnesses of Nazi dictatorship between 1933 and 1945. Born in 1932, she was initially raised by her grandmother, who was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942 and died there. A family acquaintance saved the girl by accommodating her on her farm in Middle Franconia and passing her off as her own child.

Knobloch: 'danger looming' today did not exist like this 10 years ago

Asked by DW when and how she still thinks about that horrible era, she said: "There were times when this happened only rarely. When it was mentioned by the media from time to time, but not permanently. These days, I wake up thinking about it, and I also go to bed thinking about it."

Knobloch spoke to DW correspondent Tina Gerhäusser in Munich Image: DW

Knobloch served as vice president of the World Jewish Congress between 2005 and 2013, and as president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany from 2006 to 2010. For a long time, she has been warning against growing antisemitism in Germany. However, she herself did not foresee the rise of far-right extremist parties like the AfD.

"There's a danger looming that did not exist in this form ten years ago," Knobloch said. "There have always been Nazis, there have always been Jew haters, but not in the way as it's the case today."

In Knobloch's view, the established parties have up to now failed to speak out decisively against the AfD: "Today's political parties must jointly, not alone, address the issue. I still see a chance here, that people will at least be willing to listen and discuss it. And that's very, very important."

Young people need to be included in the conversation

Politicians have to speak to young people in particular more intensively and address their fears, which isn't happening enough, Knobloch says.

"There's talk about it, but there is no real discussion, because young people are naturally afraid that what they say will become public. What I want to say is, we'll have to find ways to bring young people back into the fold."

Last week, Knobloch received death threats. On Thursday, a witness discovered the scrawled threats on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the English Garden in Munich and informed the police, according to a police headquarters statement. Knobloch subsequently canceled her attendance at an event. The threats were directly linked to the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a spokeswoman said in response to a query from the dpa news agency.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: South Africa now probing deaths of 8 women near Johannesburg
World.content:
Police have warned women to take extra care in parts of Johannesburg as similarities between at least eight deaths fuel fears that the cases could be connected.

South African police are now investigating the deaths of eight women found east of Johannesburg over the past two months, after another body was discovered on Tuesday and an earlier case was added to the widening investigation.

The deaths have raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers could be operating in the area. Several of the victims were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of sexual violence.

"The challenge is ahead of us and the deaths of these young women must not be in vain," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia told reporters following a meeting to discuss the killings.

What have South African police said?

The South African Police Service (SAPS) has issued a public warning urging women to exercise caution when jogging or carrying out similar activities in the area.

"While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.

President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday ordered police to prioritize the investigations, saying the deaths were causing "fear and uncertainty" and promising that "no stone will be left unturned."

What do we know about the victims?

The bodies have been discovered at several locations across the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.

Police said the first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.

A 32-year-old woman was found partially clothed on August 24. Another woman's body, found in a river near the Tembisa township on September 7, has now been included in the wider investigation.

One of the victims, aged 38, disappeared after leaving her eight-year-old daughter at home to go jogging. Her partially clothed body was found behind a hotel on September 12.

Another woman's body was discovered in the Kwa-Thema township on Tuesday.

Why are women still unsafe in South Africa? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Are South African police investigating a serial killer?

Police have not confirmed that the deaths are the work of a serial killer.

"We are still investigating whether we are dealing with one perpetrator or a group of men that are behind the murders of these women," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.

Police said similarities between the cases were sufficiently concerning to issue a public warning, including advising women to exercise caution while jogging in the area.

How serious is violence against women in South Africa?

Violence against women is a longstanding problem in South Africa. UN Women says the country has some of the world's highest rates of violence against women and children.

Around one in three South African women experience physical or sexual violence during their lifetime, according to the United Nations.

The killings come as violent crime remains a major source of public concern ahead of municipal elections in November.
