Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new Financial Times report on how Polish state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million (856 million zloty) trying to buy Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, unsecured payments and cryptocurrency transfers. Tusk called the case a further example of “dirty deals” conducted under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was in power at the time. Orlen was then led by Daniel Obajtek, who is now a member of the European Parliament representing PiS. Obajtek himself today said that he wants the issue to be clarified in court and suggested that the current authorities are using the case to distract from current soaring fuel prices. How Poland lost $230mn trying to buy Venezuelan oil with crypto https://t.co/Xo07JkYy1t — Financial Times (@FT) September 15, 2026 In a report today, the FT provided new details on a case that has already drawn public attention in Poland. In April 2024, Orlen revealed that its Swiss oil trading subsidiary had lost around $400 million in prepayments for Venezuelan oil and petroleum products that were never delivered. Orlen, which was under new management after Obajtek had been fired earlier that year following the arrival of Tusk’s government, said that the losses included around $240 million paid to a Dubai-based intermediary run by a 25-year-old from Hong Kong. A week later, Polish prosecutors announced that they had launched an investigation into the case, focusing on Orlen Trading Switzerland (OTS), the subsidiary that oversaw the Venezuela deal. Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into OTS, @GrupaORLEN's Swiss subsidiary which had lost $400 million on prepayments for oil that was never delivered. It also announced that the homes of Orlen's former senior management had been searchedhttps://t.co/QQ5QJMsHg4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 1, 2024 The FT detailed how the then head of OTS, a Lebanese-born Polish citizen of Palestinian descent, who can be named only as Samer A. under Polish privacy law, had sought in 2023 to commission the import of Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, who were given a $230 million advance without any security or guarantees. Although the United States, under then-President Joe Biden, had temporarily suspended sanctions on Venezuelan oil, allowing companies such as Orlen to buy it, Venezuela’s state oil company, PDVSA, remained largely cut off from the global financial system. The FT detailed how the intermediaries therefore sought to use cryptocurrency to facilitate the deal. However, although oil tankers leased by Orlen to collect the oil sat waiting (accruing further large costs), the promised oil was not delivered, and Orlen’s advance payments were lost. The issue is now the subject of a criminal investigation in Poland and an ongoing arbitration case with the intermediary in Dubai, Hannon International. Speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said that the FT story is a “disgrace in front of the entire world”. He called the Venezuelan oil incident “the biggest scandal, or one of the biggest scandals, in our country’s history”. Turning his aim on the opposition, he said that the case includes “everything that has recently been associated with PiS”, including “dirty deals” and cryptocurrencies. That was a reference to an ongoing investigation into alleged links between a collapsed crypto firm, Zondacrypto, and figures associated with the opposition. Tusk also noted that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has recently blocked government bills intended to better regulate crypto markets and to levy a windfall tax on fuel firms. “We may be dealing with a network of dirty and highly dangerous dealings,” said the prime minister. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk: Cała Polska dzisiaj to komentuje. Wstyd na cały świat. Financial Times pisze o jednym z największych skandali w historii naszego kraju i cały świat dzisiaj o tym czyta. pic.twitter.com/Ej17Csi4DL — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 15, 2026 Later on Tuesday, the regional prosecutor’s office in Warsaw also responded to the FT article by issuing a statement providing an update on the investigation into the Venezuelan oil deal. They noted that the Polish authorities are continuing to seek the extradition of Samer A. from the United Arab Emirates, which last year rejected a request from Poland for him to be extradited. The prosecutors also reported today that, last month, they issued indictments against three former senior Orlen and OTS executives for failing to fulfil their duties to oversee the companies’ assets, resulting in losses of $378 million. Prosecutors have charged the former head of the charitable foundation of Polish state energy giant Orlen for allowing its funds to be used to support a political campaign of the former ruling PiS party in violation of the foundation's statute https://t.co/w1Xtmivn0I — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 6, 2026 Obajtek himself responded to the FT’s story, writing on social media that the newspaper “describes an important part of the OTS case”. He then suggested that the new management of OTS had terminated the Venezuelan oil contract too quickly, saying that the oil could in fact have been delivered. “I hope this matter will be fully clarified, including before a Polish court!” wrote Obajtek. In a further post, he suggested that Orlen and the authorities are “trying to cover up current issues again, such as the most expensive fuel in history”. In response, Orlen’s press office wrote under one of Obajtek’s posts that they would “help [him] with English”. “The article is about how your team transferred hundreds of millions of dollars to a company owned by a 25-year-old from Dubai. He converted them into cryptocurrencies, which he copied onto USB drives. And then he handed them out in restaurants to people posing as oil traders…In this story, only Orlen’s money, which they lost, was real.” Panie Pośle, pomożemy z angielskim. Artykuł jest o tym, jak pana ekipa przelała setki milionów dolarów do firmy 25-latka z Dubaju. On zamienił je na kryptowaluty, które zgrał na pendrivy. A później rozdawał w restauracjach ludziom, podającym się za handlarzy ropą. To jak „kupić”… — Biuro Prasowe ORLEN (@b_prasoweORLEN) September 15, 2026 Obajtek rose rapidly under the former PiS government, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. He went from being the mayor of Pcim, a rural commune of 11,000 people in southern Poland, to the CEO of Orlen, Poland’s biggest company, in the space of three years. Under Obajtek’s leadership, Orlen expanded rapidly, swallowing up other state energy firms and expanding into new areas of activity. By 2023, it was ranked among Europe’s 50 biggest companies. However, Obajtek was also accused of using the company’s considerable resources to support PiS politically, including through Orlen’s purchases of hundreds of local media outlets – many of whose editors were replaced with PiS-friendly figures – and lowering fuel prices ahead of the 2023 elections. Last year, at Poland’s request, the European Parliament stripped Obajtek of legal immunity to face charges for allegedly using Orlen’s funds to serve his own private interests. Polish prosecutors are also pursuing him for allegedly violating Poland’s press law and falsely reporting his income in a tax return. A Polish ice cream chain has launched a campaign to stamp out sexual harassment of staff by customers, including empowering employees to refuse to serve such clients. The campaign is based around the fact that the Polish word for ice cream, “lody”, also has an informal vulgar meaning, referring to oral sex. The company, Good Lood, which runs 37 outlets, says that its female staff regularly suffer lewd comments from male customers incorporating this double entendre. In response, in late August it launched a campaign titled “Nie bądź oblechem”, meaning “Don’t be a creep”, with information displayed prominently at its ice cream stands and on its social media platforms. The firm said it condemned “crude remarks, inappropriate jokes and verbal harassment directed at service workers” and promised to support its staff in dealing with them. “Everyone deserves respect, without exception!” Good Lood advised employees to respond to inappropriate comments with a short, firm retort such as “Great, that’s the 20th time I’ve heard that” or “Perhaps you could repeat that more loudly, so the rest of the queue can hear?” It also called on other customers to react if they witnessed such behaviour. In a follow-up social media post last week, the company confirmed that staff had its backing if they decided not to serve a customer. “If someone is a creep and makes inappropriate comments and verbally harasses them, our team have the right to refuse them service.” That post alone has so far garnered more than 50,000 likes or other positive responses on Facebook. Good Lood says that its messages posted as part of the campaign have already received over 10 million organic views on social media. Comments on the company’s posts show overwhelming support, with many commenters sharing their own experiences. “At last someone has spoken out about this!” wrote one, who said she worked in an ice cream parlour as a teenager. “I remember how outraged I felt when I heard comments like that from men who could have been my fathers, or even my grandfathers. I wonder what would happen if someone spoke to their daughters or granddaughters like that.” Good Lood says it want to start a broader conversation on the “global issue” of harassment and disrespect towards front-line staff in retail and hospitality. “Working in service or hospitality does not mean consenting to disrespect. The safety and wellbeing of our team will always come before profit. We are not afraid to lose a customer who cannot show basic human respect,” the company said in a press release. Founded 10 years ago in Kraków, Good Lood now has 37 outlets there as well as in the Warsaw area. It also sells its products throughout Poland at Biedronka, the country’s largest supermarket chain. The ministry says the content is based on its official security handbook, which it sent to all 17 million Polish households earlier this year, and is intended to help people prepare for emergencies before they occur. “We only find out whether we’re prepared for difficult situations when they actually arise,” said Mateusz Jarecki, who is presenting the segments. “That’s why, in collaboration with specialists, we’ve produced a series of short, easy-to-follow videos that will help you prepare for various life scenarios.” The government is sending copies of a booklet advising how to prepare for and act in emergencies to all 17 million households in Poland. A moose wandered onto the tracks at Warsaw Central Station on Sunday evening, disrupting rail services in the Polish capital for more than 80 minutes before it was safely removed. The animal first appeared on a platform before moving onto the tracks, forcing Polish Railway Lines (PLK), the company responsible for Poland’s rail infrastructure, to suspend, cancel and divert several train services. View this post on Instagram A post shared by TVP3 Warszawa (@tvp3warszawa) Videos and photographs shared online showed the moose lying on the tracks and running along the railway line at Warsaw Central, the capital’s busiest station, which is mainly underground and therefore not easy for such a large animal to access. Police do not know how the moose ended up at the station, reports broadcaster TVN24. Officers were first alerted at 7:10 pm on Sunday and cordoned off the platform where the animal was located. When emergency services arrived, the moose was tranquilised. It was then placed on a large sheet and carried out of the station by police officers and emergency workers before being loaded onto a specialist vehicle to be returned to a forested area. PLK, which named the moose Emil, later confirmed that the animal had been safely removed and that normal train services were being restored. The company added that the disruptions lasted just over 80 minutes, using a pun combining the Polish words for moose (łoś) and 80 (osiemdziesiąt) to produce the word “łosiemdziesiąt”. ❗Aktualizacja❗Zwierze zostało bezpiecznie zabrane z torów. Przywracana jest rozkładowa organizacja ruchu pociągów. Utrudnienia trwały przeszło łosiemdziesiąt minut. https://t.co/Xui2B6SxyU — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) September 13, 2026 The Eurasian moose (also known as the Eurasian elk) has long been native to Poland, but by the mid-20th century hunting and habitat loss had brought the species close to extinction in the country. Its population subsequently recovered, reaching an estimated 6,000 animals by the 1980s and around 30,000 by 2019, helped by a moratorium on moose hunting introduced in 2001. Several hundred live in the Kampinos national park on the northwestern outskirts of Warsaw. They are therefore relatively frequent visitors to the capital, according to the Interia news website, although venturing onto train lines in the centre is unusual. The growth in the moose population, combined with urban expansion and changes to its habitat, has led to other high-profile encounters in areas inhabited by humans. In 2022, a moose was spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in the northern Polish city of Elbląg. A moose was this morning spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in Poland. World.title: Poland issued EU’s third most residence permits to immigrants in 2025
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland issued first residence permits to almost half a million immigrants in 2025, which was the third-highest figure in the European Union, behind Spain and Germany but ahead of Italy and France. However, the number of permits issued by Poland fell for the fourth year running, as the country continued to tighten its migration rules. Previously, between 2017 and 2022, Poland had led the EU figures for six years running, reaching a peak of almost one million permits in 2021. The new data, released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU’s statistical agency, show that Poland issued 467,314 first residence permits to immigrants from outside the EU in 2025. As was the case last year, Spain (635,438) issued the most, followed by Germany (605,292). Poland was then followed by Italy (433,099) and France (377,462). However, whereas in those four other countries the number of permits rose in 2025 (by 13.1% in Spain, 11.1% in Germany, 25.0% in Italy and 9.2% in France), in Poland the figure fell by 4.4%. That decline has come amid a tougher new migration strategy by the current government, a coalition that ranges from left to centre right, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ahead of elections in 2023, Tusk, then in opposition, accused the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which had ruled Poland since 2015, of allowing “uncontrolled” migration, including through widespread abuses of the visa system. Shortly after coming to power in those elections, Tusk, a former president of the European Council, declared that the “survival of Western civilisation” depends upon preventing mass migration. His government has since introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students, suspended asylum rights for migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus, and stepped up deportations of immigrants who have committed crimes or entered the country unlawfully. Poland has introduced tougher new rules regulating the entry of foreign students and immigrant workers. “This is another step towards regaining control over migration and increasing the safety of Poles," says the government https://t.co/gYdikpc6pL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2025 The new 2025 data show that, in relative terms (the number of permits issued in relation to countries’ populations), Poland was only ninth in the EU (12.8 permits per 1,000 people), behind Malta (56.9), Cyprus (46.7), Portugal (27.3), Lithuania (18.5), Ireland (13.4), Croatia (13.2), Luxembourg (13.1) and Spain (12.9). That marks a significant decline since 2021, when Poland issued 967,345 permits, which was the highest in the EU in absolute terms but also second-highest in relation to population. In 2025, as in previous years, Poland issued the most first residence permits to Ukrainians (241,126, 51.6% of the total), who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. They were followed by Belarusians (128,468, 27.5%), Georgians (10,249, 2.2%), Indians (9,230, 2%) and Turks (7,533, 1.6%) – the same top five nationalities as in 2024. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Following a decade of unprecedented mass migration, the number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland this year passed two million for the first time, making up just over 5% of the country’s population. Around 1.5 million of those are Ukrainians. In June, the number of foreigners working in Poland reached 1.14 million, making up almost 7% of the workforce. While Ukrainians constitute two thirds of the total, the fastest-growing nationalities are Colombians and Indians, who are now the third- and fourth-largest groups of foreign workers. The rise in migration has come as Poland’s economy has boomed but the country has also faced a demographic crisis, with a shrinking, ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in the world. In 2023, the state Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) calculated that, in order to maintain its ratio of working-age population to retirees, Poland would need to attract almost two million immigrant workers over the following decade. However, it admitted that that target was “unrealistic”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. World.title: Prague Run Day to Bring Six Races to Riegrovy Sady on September 19
World.content:
On September 19, runners of all levels can take part in a new running event combining track and park races in one of Prague’s best-known green spaces.

There are six different races to choose from, so whether you’re looking for a serious challenge or just want to get out and run, there’s an option for you.



Six races to choose from

The programme includes six races, ranging from a short family run to a one-hour challenge.

The day will begin with the 800m Family Run, designed for young runners and their accompanying adults. There will also be an 800m race on the athletic track, offering participants the opportunity to compete over a short distance in a traditional track setting.

For those looking for a longer challenge, the 1 Mile race will take place on the athletic oval. The organisers describe it as a special opportunity to race over the classic distance, with participation limited to a maximum of 30 runners.

The 5km Solo Run will offer a more familiar challenge for runners of different experience levels. It is followed by the 4x3km Relay, a team race in which four runners each complete two 1.5km laps.

The final event of the day will be the Golden Hour Race, a one-hour running challenge taking place during the golden hour.

The event will be based at the Sokol Vinohrady athletic oval, which will serve as the main hub for the day.

Find all race distances, times and registration details at praguerunday.cz

📍 Riegrovy Sady Athletic Oval

📅 Saturday, September 19

🏃 6 races for different levels

🏅 Medal for every participant

World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Riegrovy Sady to Host Goodbye Summer Party With Three Live Acts
World.content:
Summer may be drawing to a close, but the music season at Riegrovy Sady is not over yet.

On Thursday, 17 September, Energy Pub will host the Goodbye Summer Party, organised by Ploom in cooperation with Energy Pub.



The evening will feature a DJ set by Forgen, a performance by Jirka Drtil and a live concert by Renne Dang, following his sold-out show at Forum Karlín.

Tickets cost CZK 100 and the event is open exclusively to guests aged 18 and over.

The last long days and warm evenings of summer will get a musical send-off at Riegrovy Sady. The Goodbye Summer Party is designed for everyone who is not quite ready to say a final goodbye to summer and wants to enjoy one of the last outdoor evenings of the season.

The evening will kick off with a set by DJ Forgen, followed by a performance by musician Jirka Drtil. The main highlight of the evening will be a concert by Renne Dang, Ploom brand ambassador, whose current music blends elements of rap, pop and pop-punk.

His distinctive personal lyrics and energetic guitar-driven sound have already taken him to some of the country’s biggest stages. His recent achievements include a sold-out concert at Forum Karlín.

The Last Party of the Summer

Music will not be the only reason to head to Riegrovy Sady in September. The evening will also feature a dedicated Ploom zone, where adult guests can take a break during the programme and enjoy the atmosphere of one last summer party.

Every ticket holder will also receive a complimentary welcome drink. A food pop-up by Pavel Berky will be part of the event as well.

When: Thursday, 17 September 2026, doors open at 6:00 PM

Where: Energy Pub, Riegrovy Sady 28, Prague 2

Line-up: DJ Forgen, Jirka Drtil, Renne Dang

Tickets: CZK 100, including a welcome drink

Entry: 18+ only

Capacity: Limited

World.title: Fresh from France: Meet Benjamin, the Founder of The French in Prague
World.content:
For the past 12 years, Benjamin has been building a life in Prague – and helping bring a taste of France to the Czech capital.

What began as a business supplying wine to hotels, restaurants and wine bars 10 years ago has gradually grown into The French, a food business focused on bringing French products directly to Prague.

The company started with an e-shop selling mainly wine, pâté, jam, honey and foie gras. But Benjamin soon realized there was something missing: fresh French produce.

“The idea, step by step, was that we were missing fresh products to be able to open a physical shop. That’s how, two years ago, we started importing fresh products.”

Today, The French operates two shops in Prague and imports a wide range of products directly from France, with a focus on freshness and quality while keeping prices accessible.

“It cannot be fresher than what we import.”

From Breakfast to Dinner

Fresh fruit and vegetables have become one of the shop’s main attractions. The products are imported weekly, with a truck leaving France every Tuesday carrying oysters, mussels, cheeses, fish, meat, fruits and vegetables.

“Two days ago it was in the sea and today it’s already in Prague, sitting in our fridge.”

The shop aims to cover the entire day, from breakfast to dinner. Customers can pick up croissants and pain au chocolat in the morning, fresh coffee, and a selection of French products for lunch and dinner.

Among the more distinctive products are French crème fraîche and salted butter. Benjamin points out that the natural colour of the dairy products can change during the year depending on what the cows eat. “If you have the same colour of butter or cream throughout the whole year, it’s because they are not eating grass.”

A New Home in Vinohrady

The company recently expanded with a larger shop in Vinohrady, giving customers access to a wider range of ultra-fresh products imported directly from France, as well as cosmetics from Provence.

The French also supplies restaurants and hotels across Prague with products including butter, cream, cheese, ham, sausages and olives. Much of the range comes directly from the Rungis International Market near Paris, one of the largest food markets in Europe.

The company also works with direct farmers, with some products clearly marked as coming from individual producers. “In Prague, you don’t have any shop that is grouping all of these categories of products.”

Customers can also order through The French’s e-shop at francouzske-speciality.cz and either have their purchases delivered or collect them from a shop.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The French.cz (@the_french_cz)

But Benjamin says the experience is intended to be more personal than a standard supermarket. “We are not a shop where people are just behind the cash desk. We have people going into the shop to explain what we have, recommend what to cook and what to pair.”

The shops also have a weekly tasting calendar, giving customers the chance to try different products and discover new flavours.

French Food for Everyone

Although many customers are French, The French is not specifically aimed at the French community.

The Vinohrady shop attracts a large number of expats, while the company’s Prague 4 location has a much higher proportion of Czech customers. Benjamin says the goal is to serve people living in the neighborhood regardless of nationality. “We are not targeting especially expats or especially French. We are trying to target everyone living in the area who like gastronomy.”

There are, however, some differences in what Czech and French customers look for. Stronger French cheeses, for example, can take some getting used to, while certain French cuts of meat differ from traditional Czech ones.

Some types of fish are also relatively unfamiliar. Red mullet, or rouget, is widely used in French cuisine and high-end restaurants but is less common in Czech kitchens.

Growing Across Prague

The French has ambitious plans for the coming years. After opening its Vinohrady location and another shop in Prague 4, the company is preparing to open another location in Prague 9 in January.

The long-term goal is to operate five or six shops across Prague, with Holešovice, Karlín and Dejvice among the areas being considered.

World.title: Prague Has the Most Unaffordable Rents for Minimum-Wage Earners in the EU
World.content:
Prague has the highest rent-to-minimum-wage ratio among EU capitals, with the average two-bedroom apartment costing 185% of the gross minimum wage.

Prague has become the European Union’s least affordable capital for minimum-wage earners looking to rent a home, according to a new analysis by the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC).



The average monthly rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the Czech capital reaches €1,710, compared with a gross monthly minimum wage of €924. This means rent alone amounts to 185% of the minimum wage.

Lisbon follows in second place, with rent accounting for 168% of the gross minimum wage. Budapest ranks third at 159%, followed by Bratislava at 158%.

Other capitals where average rent exceeds the gross minimum wage include Sofia (154%), Athens (153%), and Riga (151%).

The figures highlight the pressure facing minimum-wage earners in cities where housing costs have risen significantly faster than incomes.

How Prague Compares with Western Europe

Prague’s position is particularly striking when compared with several Western European capitals.

In Paris, average rent accounts for 138% of the gross minimum wage, while the figure stands at 125% in Madrid and 113% in Dublin.

At the other end of the ranking, Brussels is the most affordable capital for minimum-wage earners in the comparison. Average rent there represents 70% of the gross minimum wage. Berlin follows at 76%, while the figure is 85% in Nicosia and 87% in Luxembourg.

Housing Costs Across the EU

According to Eurostat’s latest figures cited in the analysis, housing and utility bills account for 23.6% of household spending across the European Union.

The ETUC has called for stronger collective bargaining, greater consideration of housing costs when setting minimum wages, and increased investment in social housing.

The organisation also noted that rents can be more affordable when measured against national minimum wages rather than those in capital cities. Among the 16 EU countries analysed, the share of the gross minimum wage required for rent ranged from 33% in Poland to 61% in Malta.

World.title: Prague 8 Pirates to Host English-Language Guide to Czech Local Elections
World.content:
EU citizens living in Prague 8 can learn how to vote in the upcoming municipal elections at an event on 17 September.

The Prague 8 branch of the Czech Pirate Party is inviting international residents to an English-language evening explaining how EU citizens can take part in Czech local elections.

The event, titled “Hey, You Can Vote Too!”, will take place on Thursday, 17 September, at 6 PM at Pauza Palmovka in Prague 8.



The evening will offer a practical introduction to the Czech voting system, an overview of the Prague 8 Pirates’ local programme, and an opportunity for international residents to share their views on life in the district.

Organisers say the event is intended to help EU citizens understand their voting rights and discuss what they would like to see improved in Prague 8.

Who Can Vote in Czech Local Elections?

Citizens of other EU Member States can vote in Czech municipal elections if they meet certain conditions.

Voters must:

Be at least 18 years old by the second day of the election.

Have permanent or registered temporary residence in the municipality.

Be entered in the supplement to the permanent electoral register.

EU citizens who are not already registered must apply by 7 October 2026 at 4 PM.

“Many people from other EU countries live in Prague 8, work here, raise their families here and use the same schools, parks, streets and public services as everyone else. Yet many still do not know that they can vote in local elections,” said Martin Štěrba, the Czech Pirate Party’s candidate for mayor of Prague 8.

“We want to explain how it works and hear directly from them what Prague 8 could do better.”

The Czech municipal elections will take place on 9 and 10 October 2026.

Voters in Prague 8 will elect representatives to both the Prague 8 Municipal District Council and the Prague City Assembly.

World.title: Nearly 40 Percent of Young Czechs Experience Financial Stress Every Month
World.content:
Money worries affect almost one in three Czech adults, but younger people are facing a greater burden.

A new survey found that 39 percent of people aged 18 to 26 experience financial anxiety at least once a month, with household income playing a major role in how people feel about their finances.



Financial concerns are common across the Czech Republic. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos for Home Credit, 28 percent of adults experience worries about money at least once a month. Another 35 percent report financial stress several times a year.

Young adults face the greatest pressure

People aged 18 to 26 are the most likely to experience regular financial stress. Nearly four in ten respondents in this age group said they worry about money at least once a month.

Home Credit attributed the pressure partly to the cost of housing and everyday expenses. For young adults trying to establish themselves financially, rising prices in recent years have made it harder to absorb unexpected costs.

An unplanned bill or other expense can therefore create a serious problem, particularly for those who have limited savings.

Household income makes a significant difference

The survey found a clear relationship between household income and financial anxiety.

Among households earning up to CZK 40,000 per month, 41 percent of respondents reported experiencing financial stress. The proportion decreases as household income rises.

People living in households with monthly incomes above CZK 70,000 reported the lowest levels of financial concern.

Age and education also appear to influence how people view their finances. Respondents aged 54 to 65 and university students reported lower levels of stress than some other groups. In both categories, 43 percent said they did not experience financial stress at all.

Financial stress may also affect physical health

The consequences of financial difficulties can extend beyond anxiety and everyday worries.

The material also refers to research published by the American Mayo Clinic in 2025. According to the research cited, long-term financial distress and food insecurity may be associated with poorer cardiovascular health and a higher risk of death.

The findings underline the potential connection between financial security and overall well-being. However, the Czech survey does not establish whether financial stress directly causes health problems.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos in June 2026 among 1,026 people.

World.title: A Prague Institution: Indian Jewel Celebrates 30 Years of North Indian Flavours
World.content:
The family-run restaurant has been bringing authentic North Indian flavours and warm hospitality to Prague since 1996.

For 30 years, Indian Jewel has been serving authentic Indian cuisine in the heart of Prague. Established in 1996 by Sanjeev Wadehra, the family-owned restaurant is celebrating three decades in the Czech capital in 2026 — a milestone that makes it one of the longest-standing Indian restaurants in the country.



The restaurant’s story began with Sanjeev Wadehra, who brought recipes, cooking traditions and spice blends directly from India to Prague. Today, the kitchen continues to focus on authentic North Indian cuisine, with dishes prepared according to traditional recipes rather than adapted to passing culinary trends.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Indian Jewel Prague (@indianjewelprague)

To celebrate its 30th anniversary, Indian Jewel is offering Prague Morning readers a complimentary welcome drink or dessert. Simply mention Prague Morning when you visit.

Among the highlights are tandoor specialities, prepared in the traditional clay oven, alongside lamb, chicken and shrimp curries. The menu also offers a wide selection of vegetarian dishes, as well as biryanis, freshly baked naan and other Indian classics.

Popular choices include Butter Chicken, Chicken Tikka Masala and Lamb Rogan Josh, while the tandoor menu offers another way to explore the flavours of North India.

But food is only part of the restaurant’s story. Indian Jewel has built its reputation on consistent quality and warm, personal hospitality. Many members of the team have been with the restaurant for years, creating the family atmosphere that Sanjeev and his wife, Mohini, consider an important part of its success.

The restaurant moved to its current location at Rybná 9 in 2021, after many years at its previous home in the historic Týn Courtyard. Despite the change, the philosophy has remained the same: authentic food, attentive service and a welcoming atmosphere.

World.title: Hungary-based energy group secures 25-year deal for massive 500 MW solar project in Africa
World.content:
Hungary-based EnerSynk Group today announced the signing of a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with ZESCO Limited for the development of a 500 MW utility-scale solar power project in Zambia’s Copperbelt Province.

The agreement marks a major milestone in the development of the project and reflects EnerSynk Group’s long-term commitment to supporting Zambia’s energy security, economic growth and diversification of its power-generation mix.

The project is planned for development in phases and is expected to supply electricity into Zambia’s national power system.

Jason Temasfieldt, Founder and Executive Chairman of EnerSynk Group, said: “Today represents an important milestone not only for EnerSynk, but for the long-term partnership we want to build with Zambia.

“We have tremendous respect for Zambia, its people and its potential. Our ambition goes beyond developing a single solar project. We want to become a trusted long-term partner — bringing together international capital, technology, expertise and partnerships to help develop the energy infrastructure Zambia needs for its next chapter of economic growth.”

The signing comes as Zambia continues efforts to increase electricity generation, strengthen energy security and attract greater private-sector investment into the power sector.

Zambia Development Agency Director General Albert Halwampa said: “Projects of this nature are important to Zambia’s efforts to expand electricity generation and strengthen energy security. Private-sector investment will be critical to achieving our national energy ambitions, and we welcome investors who are prepared to develop projects that contribute to reliable power supply, economic growth and the diversification of our energy sector.”

If you missed it: Hungarian government announces one of the country’s largest renewable energy investment programmes in decades

Bishop Joshua Banda, EnerSynk Group’s Strategic Advisor in Zambia, said: “This is more than an energy project. It is an investment in Zambia’s future. Reliable electricity supports industry, businesses, families and communities, and we look forward to seeing this project contribute meaningfully to the country’s development.”

The Power Purchase Agreement establishes the commercial framework for the sale of electricity generated by the project to ZESCO over a 25-year period.

EnerSynk Group will now advance the project through its next stages of development, including technical studies, environmental and regulatory processes, project financing and implementation in collaboration with relevant government institutions, stakeholders, investors and technical partners.

“There is still important work ahead,” Temasfieldt added. “But today is an opportunity to recognise how far we have come and to thank ZESCO, the Government of Zambia, the Zambia Development Agency, the Energy Regulation Board, our local partners and everyone who has helped bring the project to this milestone.”

Upon completion, the project is expected to rank among Zambia’s largest utility-scale solar installations and contribute significant new generation capacity to the national electricity system.

The project forms part of EnerSynk Group’s wider strategy to develop reliable, sustainable and scalable energy infrastructure across Africa.

World.title: Another side of Poland: factories, startups and city-building in Lower Silesia
World.content:
In two cities in south-western Poland, we looked at how local leaders are trying to attract multinational companies, strengthen home-grown businesses and create an environment where people want not only to work, but also to live. As part of an eight-member international group of journalists, we visited Wałbrzych and Wrocław on a study tour organised by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute. From a Mercedes plant and a Polish SME to a technology company that started life in a garage, a surprisingly consistent strategy emerged. Hungarian cities and their leaders might also find ideas worth considering here.

The multi-day programme was supported on behalf of the Warsaw Enterprise Institute by Marta Roels and Łukasz Wojdyga. Both work in strongly international fields: Roels is a WEI project coordinator and analyst, while Wojdyga specialises in international academic and research cooperation.

Our first major economic stop was Wałbrzych. One phrase kept returning during the opening presentations: building an ecosystem. In other words, bringing in a factory is not enough. Everything that enables it to operate successfully over the long term has to be built around it. And the right environment can benefit SMEs just as much as the industrial giants next door.

Poland’s industrial zone is no longer only about gigafactories

The presentation of the Wałbrzych Special Economic Zone – WSEZ “Invest-Park” was opened by Marcin Lerner, president of the company’s management board. Katarzyna Prociak, director responsible for investment acquisition and sales, then gave us a closer look at how the zone operates.

According to the figures presented, nearly 450 investors are active in the zone, with total investment worth around PLN 48 billion. Companies operating there are credited with creating approximately 90,000 jobs.

Some of the best-known names include Toyota, Mercedes-Benz and Electrolux, while Mercedes also operates a plant in nearby Jawor. Yet one message was repeatedly stressed during the presentations: the strategy is no longer focused solely on gigafactories. Polish and foreign small and medium-sized companies are also actively targeted.

Investors can also receive tax incentives. What makes the scheme interesting is that the support is not paid out as one large grant. Instead, an eligible company can gradually use the approved amount when paying tax. The level of support depends, among other things, on the size of the company and the investment itself, with a benefit of up to 25 per cent available in the most favourable cases.

Invest-Park also runs a training centre supporting companies already operating in the region, while InvestUp connects startups with established businesses. The thinking behind both programmes is the same: a factory needs suppliers, skilled workers, research capacity and a new generation of companies around it.

Roman Szełemej talks about an entire city, not isolated projects

At Invest-Park, Roman Szełemej, Mayor of Wałbrzych, introduced us to the city. A cardiologist by profession, he has led Wałbrzych since 2011 and was re-elected in 2024 with 71 per cent of the vote. The impression from his presentation was that residents have largely embraced the direction he has set for the city and that development is being treated as a broader community project.

Roman Szełemej, Mayor of Wałbrzych

Perhaps the most striking part of Szełemej’s presentation was that he did not try to sell us one spectacular flagship development. He spoke about housing, transport, healthcare, education and energy supply with the same emphasis as industrial investment.

Wałbrzych, which is celebrating its 600th anniversary, has a population of roughly 100,000. According to the presentation, 66 per cent of its territory is covered by green space and around 750,000 tourists visit annually. One of the city’s priorities is keeping young families there, partly through the construction of new municipal housing.

Szełemej also spoke with particular pride about the expanding role of biomass-based energy. At the same time, Wałbrzych is trying to turn its geography into a competitive advantage: the Czech border is just over 20 kilometres away, while Berlin, Prague and Vienna are all close enough that it makes little sense to view the city’s economic position only in relation to Warsaw.

The city’s concrete investment opportunities were presented by Arkadiusz Grudzień, head of InWałbrzych. The role of the municipal company is essentially to turn broader urban strategy into tangible investment offers.

A large company and an SME: John Cotton and WLV

The afternoon factory visits demonstrated what supporting both large and smaller companies means in practice.

Our first stop was the John Cotton Europe plant. According to Michael Harrington, the group’s managing director, the more than century-old family business now operates in seven countries across three continents and employs around 1,600 people.

Tesco played an important role in bringing the company to Poland, inviting it into Central Europe as a partner. Its next major step will be automation: the company is preparing a new logistics centre where, once a lorry arrives, the movement of goods could eventually be handled entirely by automated systems.

One of the more memorable side topics during the factory visit was pillow replacement. Harrington surprised the group by saying that, from a hygiene perspective, pillows should ideally be replaced every six months. Polish consumers, he said, reportedly keep theirs for around eight and a half years on average. Hungarian households may not necessarily perform much better.

From there, we travelled to the plant of WLV W. Kocoń M. Joński. The Polish SME works with industrial plastics technology, air and gas purification systems, tanks and other specialised industrial solutions.

WLV may be a less recognisable name than Mercedes, but that is precisely why its inclusion in the programme mattered. Poland’s huge number of SMEs collectively provides a major base for employment, production and tax revenues. What is more, some of today’s medium-sized local businesses could become the large Polish manufacturers and brands of the next 10 or 20 years.

After a packed day in Wałbrzych, the programme became somewhat more relaxed: the evening ended with a George Dyer Blues concert at the Vertigo Jazz Club in Wrocław.

Vertigo Jazz Club, Wroclaw, Poland. Photo: Daily News Hungary

The day in Wrocław began with State Secretary Michał Jaros

The following morning, Michał Jaros, state secretary at Poland’s Ministry of Development and Technology, joined us for an informal breakfast. Jaros himself has strong ties to Lower Silesia and, as both a politician and economist, was able to discuss the region from a national economic policy perspective after we had spent the previous day looking at it from factory level.

He currently serves as a state secretary in the Polish government, and our closed-door discussion touched on some of the most important investment issues facing the country.

Wrocław immediately feels like a different world from Wałbrzych. The architectural legacy of the former German city of Breslau remains highly visible, while the modern city around it feels young, energetic and conspicuously international.

Radosław Michalski, director responsible for Wrocław’s city brand, explained this side of the city in more detail. His role is essentially to combine Wrocław’s economic, tourism and cultural strengths into a single, recognisable image.

Alongside him, Magdalena Okulowska, president of the Wrocław Agglomeration Development Agency, or ARAW, presented the investment potential of the wider metropolitan area. ARAW works, among other things, on attracting investors and supporting development projects across the agglomeration.

According to the presentation, one in five Wrocław residents is a foreigner, while around 60,000 foreign students and employees representing more than 120 nationalities live in the city. Wrocław also has 30 international schools and kindergartens.

More than 126,000 students attend 30 higher education institutions, while several hundred research and development units operate across the region. The presence of LG is also worth highlighting, as it has helped create particularly strong business links with South Korea.

Don’t miss it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ

Wrocław wants to persuade more than investors

Quality of life features surprisingly prominently in Wrocław’s economic strategy. Culture, life along the Oder River and, increasingly, gastronomy all form part of the city’s pitch.

In 2026, 28 Wrocław restaurants were included in the Michelin Guide, six more than the previous year. BABA and MOST each received a Michelin star, three restaurants were awarded Bib Gourmand status, while the others were included among Michelin’s recommended establishments.

We had the opportunity to experience this side of the city ourselves. One evening took us to Przystań & Marina, which is among the Wrocław restaurants recommended by the Michelin Guide. Located on an island directly beside the Oder, the restaurant is highlighted by the guide for its Mediterranean-inspired cooking, use of local ingredients and waterside setting.

Our group worked its way through a multi-course tasting menu, which proved unanimously popular among the eight international journalists. After days of presentations and factory visits, it also offered a chance to understand Wrocław’s much-advertised quality of life through something other than investment statistics.

That matters because Wrocław is clearly not simply trying to sell jobs. The city also wants to convince engineers, researchers, managers and their families arriving with new investors that there are reasons to stay for the long term. International schools, cultural institutions, parks and riverside areas, together with an increasingly Michelin-recognised food scene, all form part of the same strategy.

From laboratory to market

At Wrocław Technology Park, or WPT, we saw the idea of a business ecosystem in physical form.

According to the presentation, more than 200 companies operate on the campus and employ over 2,000 people. The eight-building complex provides around 66,000 square metres of offices, laboratories, research infrastructure, production facilities and warehouse space.

We were also shown a pilot production area where companies can test a process on a small scale before potentially building an entire factory around it. This is particularly important for smaller businesses: a startup does not have to invest millions of euros in its own laboratory before it can begin experimenting with a real product.

A garage startup and the future of digital identity

Our final business stop was Identt, which began as a classic garage startup and now develops digital identity solutions for banks, financial companies and other regulated sectors.

One of the system’s jobs is to verify whether the person on the other side of a camera really is who they claim to be. The same technology can also be used in access-control systems: stealing or borrowing somebody else’s entry card is of limited use if the system also identifies the person holding it.

The next major change could come with the European Digital Identity Wallet. Under the concept, users themselves will be able to control exactly which pieces of information they share from their identity documents, driving licence, diploma or other digital credentials, and with whom.

Poland no longer simply wants to be cheaper

After visiting the two cities, we ended up back where Marcin Lerner and Katarzyna Prociak began in Wałbrzych: with the idea of an ecosystem.

Roman Szełemej and Arkadiusz Grudzień are trying to transform a former industrial city into a place where domestic companies such as WLV have a future alongside Mercedes. In Wrocław, Radosław Michalski and Magdalena Okulowska are working with the tools available to an international city: universities, foreign talent, technology infrastructure, culture, multinational companies and startups.

And that may have been the most interesting lesson of the trip. This part of Poland is no longer trying to compete with Western Europe simply by being cheaper. The aim is to build an environment in which the investment of a foreign industrial giant matters just as much as the local small business that may one day grow into Poland’s next major international brand.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar to meet Pope Leo XIV in private Vatican audience
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is set to travel to the Vatican on 24 September, where he will be received by Pope Leo XIV in a private audience.

Péter Magyar is about to visit the Vatican very soon

Magyar announced the visit on Facebook, adding that he will subsequently hold talks with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s Secretary of State and a key figure in its diplomatic and governmental affairs. The meeting will give Magyar an opportunity to discuss issues of interest with the head of the Catholic Church before his talks with one of the Vatican’s most senior officials.

The Pope had a meeting not so long ago with Viktor Orbán

Pope Leo XIV has previously received former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán at the Vatican. Orbán met the pontiff in October last year and was accompanied by his wife, Anikó Lévai, and several members of his family, writes VG.hu.

During that meeting, the two sides discussed bilateral relations and the role of the Catholic Church in Hungarian society. Family policy, the education and future of young people, and the protection of Christian communities living in war zones were also among the topics addressed. Orbán said afterwards that he had asked the Pope to continue supporting Hungary’s efforts to promote peace.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Tisza delegation previously met the Pope

The upcoming meeting will also follow an earlier Vatican encounter involving Magyar’s political movement. In April, Pope Leo XIV received representatives of the European People’s Party at the Vatican, including members of the Tisza Party. Magyar’s private audience therefore means the continuation of the relations between the Vatican and the Tisza politicians.

Read also: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges

World.title: Talented Hungarian footballer Patrik Farkas joins Liverpool FC
World.content:
Liverpool have signed another Hungarian player, with 19-year-old midfielder Farkas Patrik securing a professional contract with the Premier League club. Farkas returns to Merseyside as a free agent from Blackburn Rovers, having previously spent time in Liverpool’s academy between 2021 and 2022.

From Szeged to Liverpool

Farkas began playing football in Szeged before moving to Kecskemét and subsequently continuing his development in England. After his first spell at the club, he joined Blackburn’s academy and became a free agent this summer, as per Liverpool FC.

The midfielder has now returned to the Reds and was already included in the U21 squad for a Premier League 2 match on Monday. Although his professional contract does not make him a member of Liverpool’s senior first team, the U21 side represents an important pathway towards the club’s senior squad.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

‘A dream come true’

Farkas described his return as a dream come true. “I’m very happy and can’t wait to get started,” he said, according to the club’s official website. “I’m happy to be back in Liverpool. There are some new faces, but it’s good to see old friends again and get to know everyone else.” The 19-year-old describes himself as a box-to-box midfielder capable of playing in several positions.

His brother as also at the club

Farkas is not the only member of his family at the club. His younger brother, Erik Farkas, plays for the U18 side. The 17-year-old has made an impressive start to the season, scoring twice and providing an assist in his first two matches. Patrik said the brothers have played together since Erik was four and continue to push each other to improve.

Another Hungarian at Merseyside

Farkas Patrik joins Dominik Szoboszlai, Milos Kerkez and Ármin Pécsi among the Hungarian players currently linked with Liverpool. Pécsi is on loan at Austrian club Hartberg. With Patrik now beginning his professional journey at the club, Liverpool’s connection with Hungarian football continues to strengthen.

World.title: One more warm day until cold front splits Hungary in two
World.content:
Hungary is set for a dramatic weather divide this week as a wavy cold front crosses the country, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures to the west while summer-like warmth lingers in the east.

Wednesday will bring us one more warm day

According to a forecast video from the meteorologists at HungaroMet, the contrast will be particularly noticeable on Thursday, before another, even stronger cold front arrives early next week.

Wednesday will begin with a southerly airflow, bringing temporary warming to the Carpathian Basin. After patches of morning fog clear, mostly sunny conditions are expected, with afternoon temperatures reaching 23–28°C. Winds will strengthen in several areas, with particularly strong gusts possible around the Kisalföld region and Lake Fertő.

Cold front will divide the country

The weather will change considerably on Thursday as a cold front reaches Hungary and becomes temporarily stalled over the country. This will create a striking contrast between the western and eastern parts of the country.

Temperatures in western and north-western Hungary are expected to reach only 19–20°C, while the eastern Great Plain could still see highs of 28–30°C. Despite the unusually large regional difference, HungaroMet says the national average temperature will remain broadly in line with the seasonal norm.

The temperature divide will persist into Friday, while conditions become increasingly favourable for precipitation across a larger part of the country. Rain, showers and thunderstorms may develop in several areas, making Friday a more unsettled day.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Weekend offers temporary respite, but cold reclaims Hungary on Monday

By Saturday, the frontal system is expected to move eastwards away from Hungary. Some light rain may still occur across southern and eastern areas, but sunshine will dominate elsewhere. The temperature contrast will remain, with noticeably cooler conditions in Transdanubia while temperatures fall less sharply across the Great Plain.

Western areas may begin to warm gradually again during the weekend, but the improvement is unlikely to last. A new, fast-moving and more pronounced cold front is forecast to reach the region on Monday, bringing another 3–4°C drop in temperatures nationwide. The next front is not expected to produce particularly heavy precipitation, however, with only moderate rainfall effects currently anticipated.

World.title: Hungarian minority in Ukraine: Our reader writes from the scene – agreement signed, but where are the results?
World.content:
Hungary and Ukraine have recently reached an agreement in order to restore the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine. The agreement defines basic rights in language, education, social and political, and cultural spheres. The Ukrainian side undertook to expand the range of rights of the Hungarian minority in settlements where ethnic Hungarians make up more than 10% of the population.

This article was written by our reader, P. M.

These are key known points from the agreement:

Names of streets, squares, and plates on buildings of local administrations must be translated into Hungarian

People may address local authorities using the Hungarian language, and local officials must speak it

Agitation for elections, voting rules, and ballot papers at local elections must be translated into Hungarian

Public events may be held in Hungarian. People are allowed to use Hungarian national symbols, but they can’t dominate Ukrainian ones

Educational facilities with Hungarian-speaking groups get the “school of national minority” status. Such schools must have a Hungarian-speaking principal and a vice principal. Students and teachers have a right to speak Hungarian in schools off-hours

Educational diplomas and certificates must be translated into Hungarian. Tasks of national exams (except Ukrainian language and History) must be translated too

The agreement was signed in June this year; however, Kyiv’s been slow to meet Budapest’s requirements, and, unfortunately, things are staying the same for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine now.

Who has the right to represent the Hungarian minority in Ukraine?

A bilateral group working on ensuring the rights of ethnic Hungarians was established after signing for rapid response to possible violations. From the Ukrainian side, we have non-governmental organisations and influencers. However, there is a nuance. There is a rising concern that Kyiv doesn’t fulfil the agreements responsibly.

Rumour has it that the group doesn’t consist of the largest organisations representing the Hungarian diaspora in Ukraine or organisations which are trusted not only by the local minority but also by Budapest, but consists of little-known regional organisations, which don’t even have any political representation in local authorities. For example, one of the participants of the group is Boris Vashkeba, a chairman of a small and rather young organisation called “Transcarpathian Society of Hungarians”.

It’s legitimate to ask about such organisations’ right to fully represent the interests of the community and about the appropriateness of their presence in important groups like this one.

Are the rights of the Hungarian minority a loophole for Ukraine’s EU accession?

There is also a certain point of view that Kyiv has agreed to this deal only in order to make Hungary stop interfering with negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession. However, it didn’t work out. Only two (Fundamentals and External Relations) of the six negotiation clusters were opened. Budapest refused to approve screening results for the Internal Market and Competitiveness clusters on 1 September, for the third time since July.

The situation is pissing Ukrainian officials off, so they continue to blame Budapest for halting Ukraine’s EU integration. Despite this, Magyar states that Ukraine, like any other country, should have no privileges for EU accession and promises to open the other clusters only when all agreements are implemented, including the ones concerning ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine.

Fate of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine remains uncertain

After signing the agreement this summer, Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Orban claims that Ukraine’s accession process will automatically be halted if Ukraine fails to comply with the minority agreement. It’s reported that Ukraine undertook to implement education measures by the end of 2026, and social and political measures in 2027. It’s also reported that there would be an audit soon, which would determine if there was any work being done in this field.

Meanwhile, Magyar has recently said that Hungary doesn’t see enough progress made by Ukraine in complying with the agreement and once again has confirmed that the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine are a very important problem for Hungary. That’s why Budapest voted against the EU’s initiative to stop granting temporary protection to military-age Ukrainian men.

Magyar explained that many people escaping from Ukraine to Hungary belong to Ukraine’s Hungarian minority, which his government tries to protect. Nevertheless, Kyiv keeps repeating that it’s illegal to cross the border for military-age men in Ukraine now.
