Tokayev said Kazakhstan was investing heavily in railways, roads, ports, terminals and other infrastructure to increase the capacity, speed and reliability of the country’s transport links between Asia and Europe.

“We believe the time has come to expand Korea’s participation in the development of the Middle Corridor,” he said.

The President highlighted the activities of Korean logistics companies, including CJ Logistics and LX Pantos, which are developing logistics centers, multimodal terminals, warehouse facilities and digital supply-chain solutions in Kazakhstan.

Tokayev also welcomed cooperation between Kazakhstan’s Shin-Line and Lotte Global Logistics to develop new logistics opportunities.

AI cooperation targets regional technology leadership

Artificial intelligence and new technologies were identified as another major area for future cooperation. Tokayev stressed that human capital would be central to Kazakhstan’s AI strategy and highlighted cooperation with Seoul National University of Science and Technology on establishing Kazakhstan’s first Institute of Artificial Intelligence.

“Our goal is to position Kazakhstan as the main computing center of Central Asia and a bridge between Europe and Asia,” Tokayev said.

He said Kazakhstan was ready to deepen cooperation with global technology companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, including supplying materials and components for microelectronics and semiconductor production.

Human capital remains central to partnership

Tokayev emphasized that technological and economic cooperation would depend on developing human capital. Universities in Kazakhstan and South Korea currently maintain academic cooperation through more than 230 agreements, laying the groundwork for expanding research and educational partnerships.

He also said Kazakhstan’s next stage of economic modernization would focus on new industries, technologies, research capabilities and human capital. South Korea’s own transformation into a global economic and technological power, he noted, provides valuable experience for Kazakhstan as it pursues its modernization agenda.

“I am confident that today’s event and the agreements being signed will give a powerful impetus to a more ambitious partnership,” Tokayev said, calling on Korean businesses to increase investment in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Astana AI Film Festival Attracts More Than 8,000 Entries From 125 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana AI Film Festival (AAIFF 2026) will take place from Oct. 1 to 3, bringing together AI-generated films from 125 countries and offering a combined prize and investment pool of US$2.75 million, organizers said at a briefing in Astana.

More than 8,000 films were submitted to the international competition, highlighting the rapid growth of AI-assisted filmmaking and the expanding global community around the emerging field. The festival received 8,067 submissions from 4,756 unique creators. The total running time of the submitted works exceeded 100,000 minutes.

The competition is divided into two sections. A total of 3,138 films were submitted under the festival’s main theme, The Future Worth Living In, while another 4,929 entries were submitted to the open competition without thematic restrictions.

The United States led in submissions with 1,395 films, followed by Kazakhstan with 829, India with 702, China with 550 and South Korea with 349. The United Kingdom, Indonesia, Japan, Brazil and France also ranked among the countries with the highest number of entries.

AI filmmakers experiment with new forms

The submitted works span 19 genres, with participants using artificial intelligence not only to generate visual content but also to experiment with storytelling, genres and the creation of cinematic worlds. The longest film submitted runs for four hours and three minutes, while one project combines five separate fictional universes.

“Just a few months ago, we were launching an international competition, and today we have received more than 8,000 works from 125 countries,” said Almas Zhali, co-founder of the festival and chairman of the AAIFF board.

“These are no longer isolated AI experiments – we are seeing full-fledged films, complex stories, characters and entire universes. This scale shows how quickly AI cinema is developing,” he said.

The participants include emerging directors and independent teams alongside established figures in the international AI creative industry. Among them are AI production studio The DOR Brothers, which has more than 370,000 followers, director Zack London’s Gossip Goblin project and Robert Gaudette, whose works have previously been presented and recognized at international film festivals.

Organizers estimate that participants spent more than $4 million using more than 80 generative AI models. Among the most widely used tools were Suno AI, Seedance 2.5, Kling, Wan 2.6, GPT Image 2 and ElevenLabs.

All submitted films undergo mandatory plagiarism checks.

Festival offers $1.75 million in prizes

The main thematic competition will distribute $1.75 million in prize money, while another $250,000 will be distributed among five categories in the open competition. A separate $1 million investment fund has also been established for promising AI teams. Entrepreneur and investor Balaji Srinivasan, former chief technology officer of Coinbase, former general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, and founder of The Network School, provided the capital.

“We want strong projects to continue after the festival. That is why, in addition to the prize fund, there is a separate investment capital,” said Aizatulla Hussein, co-founder of AAIFF.

The investment is intended to help selected creators continue production, scale their projects and develop them from Kazakhstan. Selected teams will have an opportunity to join Astana Hub, he said.

AI cinema still searching for its identity

Despite the rapid growth of AI-generated filmmaking, the field has yet to develop a distinct and consistent form, according to Hussein.

After reviewing thousands of submissions from different countries, organizers found no single established model for AI cinema. Some filmmakers use AI to reproduce traditional cinematic forms, while others create experimental works that are difficult to classify within conventional filmmaking.

“The trend and the form itself are only taking shape and being explored. Previously, trends could remain for months, but now everything changes practically every day,” Hussein said.

He noted differences in the approaches taken by creators from different countries. South Korean submissions, for example, frequently featured noir and horror aesthetics, as well as stories set in office environments. Chinese creators more often turned to animation and demonstrated distinctive visual approaches, he said.

Kazakh filmmakers also showed recurring themes, with national motifs and visions of the future appearing in many submissions. Yurts, the steppe and robots feature in some of the country’s science-fiction-inspired works. Hussein said it remains difficult to draw a clear line between entertainment content generated with AI and what can be considered full-fledged AI cinema.

“Some try simply to reproduce traditional cinema, while others experiment in ways that do not look like cinema at all, but are very interesting,” he said.

He expressed hope that the festival could contribute to defining a new form and potentially even a new name for this emerging type of entertainment and filmmaking.

AAIFF 2026 will take place from Oct. 1 to 3 as part of AI Month, a series of events dedicated to artificial intelligence. For the first time, finalists will have an opportunity to present their AI-generated films to audiences on a large cinema screen in Astana.

The festival program will also include business sessions, panel discussions and master classes for filmmakers and industry representatives. The awards ceremony and announcement of winners will take place on Oct. 3.

World.title: Kazakhstan, South Korea Advance Investment Cooperation Ahead of Central Asia–Korea Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and South Korea are advancing a growing portfolio of investment and industrial projects, including 67 initiatives worth a combined $6.9 billion in Alatau City and 51 joint industrial projects, as the two countries prepare for the first South Korea–Central Asia Summit in Seoul on Sept. 16.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev held a series of meetings with the leaders of major Korean companies, while senior Kazakh officials engaged with Korean businesses and government representatives on projects spanning automotive manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, hospitality, artificial intelligence and space technologies.

Alatau City emerges as major platform for Korean investment

During a meeting with Lotte Group Chairman Shin Dong-bin, President Tokayev highlighted the company’s longstanding contribution to Kazakhstan’s economy, including its activities in the food industry and the modernization of production facilities in Almaty and Shymkent.

Lotte also plans to expand its presence in logistics and hospitality. Tokayev welcomed the signing of an agreement to build the first Lotte-branded hotel in Almaty and noted the potential for further expansion. Shin confirmed Lotte’s plans to invest in food production, logistics and hospitality and said the company intends to participate in Alatau City development projects, including the Iconic Complex.

The development of Alatau City was also central to Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev’s meetings in South Korea with representatives of Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO), Lotte Hotels & Resorts, Doosan Enerbility and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI).

With KEPCO, the sides discussed the development of Alatau City’s power infrastructure, including electricity transmission and distribution systems, substations, integration with the national grid and local power networks. Doosan Enerbility and GGGI discussed the development of the city’s own generation capacity. One option under consideration is a 2×250-megawatt gas-fired power plant, with the potential for a subsequent transition to hydrogen. Doosan Enerbility could serve as the project’s technology and EPC partner, with a public-private partnership mechanism being considered.

Lotte Hotels & Resorts also discussed a multifunctional complex in Alatau City featuring an L7 by Lotte hotel. The project, valued at more than $200 million, is expected to include a 180-room hotel, office space and residential apartments.

Kazakhstan and South Korea explore new digital and space projects

At a meeting with Hanwha Group Vice Chairman Kim Dong-won, Tokayev outlined Kazakhstan’s efforts to build a national artificial intelligence ecosystem and develop digital infrastructure. He invited Hanwha Group to implement joint projects in Kazakhstan and use the country as a technological platform for entering Central Asian markets.

Separately, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev visited CONTEC Space Group’s assembly and testing complex in Seoul. The sides discussed CONTEC’s potential investment in the Galam project, joint satellite and component production, and development of a network of ground stations.

One proposal is to establish a manufacturing hub in Kazakhstan for satellite components, with subsequent supplies to markets in Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. The sides are also considering localizing the production of large ground-based antenna systems.

Another area of cooperation is using artificial intelligence to process satellite imagery, potentially expanding the use of Earth observation data for practical applications. A Kazakh subsidiary of CONTEC is expected to be established in the near future, with further details of the partnership expected to be presented during Tokayev’s state visit to South Korea.

Hyundai seeks deeper automotive localization

During a meeting with Hyundai Motor Group President and Head of Strategy and Planning Sung Kim, Tokayev discussed expanding investment and industrial and technological cooperation.

Representatives of Hyundai Engineering and Kia also took part in the meeting. Tokayev identified a longer-term goal of turning Kazakhstan into a major regional center for automobile production and exports, with an emphasis on developing full-cycle manufacturing.

Electric mobility was also identified as a promising area of cooperation, including electric vehicle and component production and the development of charging infrastructure.

Hyundai Motor Group confirmed its intention to expand its presence and deepen production localization in Kazakhstan. Hyundai Engineering said it is ready to develop cooperation in the oil and gas sector, industry and infrastructure, while Kia representatives said they intend to cooperate on developing a national Kazakh automotive brand.

Several agreements were exchanged following the meeting, including between QazaqGaz, Hyundai Engineering and SICIM Kazakhstan on constructing a gas processing plant in western Kazakhstan, and between Hyundai Motor Company and Astana Motors on producing a new Hyundai Tucson model.

KIND to support Alatau City and transport infrastructure

Tokayev also met with Kim Bok-hwan, president and CEO of the Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corporation (KIND). The meeting focused on KIND’s potential involvement in the development of Alatau City. Tokayev emphasized the project’s potential and called for greater Korean participation in infrastructure and investment initiatives in the new city.

He also invited KIND to participate in Kazakhstan’s large-scale plans to modernize social and transport infrastructure. The sides also discussed establishing a Kazakh-Korean joint investment fund to attract Korean capital and technology to infrastructure and energy projects in Kazakhstan.

The sides also discussed potential KIND participation in modernizing the country’s transport and logistics system, including the development of the ports of Aktau and Kuryk and projects involving the construction and renovation of regional airports.

The meeting was followed by an exchange of documents, including a memorandum of understanding between Caspian Group and KIND, an agreement between Alatau City Authority and KIND on developing a master plan for Alatau Smart City, and a strategic agreement between Qazaqstan Investment Corporation and KIND.

The series of meetings comes ahead of the first Korea–Central Asia Summit, which will bring together South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and the leaders of all five Central Asian states in Seoul on Sept. 16.

The summit is expected to provide a high-level platform to strengthen cooperation between South Korea and Central Asia, while business meetings involving Kazakhstan and major Korean corporations underscore the growing focus on investment, technology transfer, infrastructure and industrial cooperation.

World.title: Building Capabilities for Future of Agriculture
World.content:
How Eurasia Group is developing people and advancing technology adoption to support the future of agriculture in Kazakhstan

In 2026, Eurasia Group received a HUMANRISE Award for Digital AgroLeaders — an educational initiative that has been introducing students to modern agriculture and preparing a new generation of professionals for an increasingly technology-driven industry for more than 15 years.

HUMANRISE recognizes achievements in human capital development and employer branding. For Eurasia Group, however, the value of Digital AgroLeaders extends far beyond HR. As a long-standing John Deere dealer and partner, Eurasia Group sees its role not only in bringing advanced agricultural technologies to Kazakhstan, but also in developing the people and capabilities needed to put those technologies to work. Advanced equipment, precision ag solutions, connectivity, and data can only deliver their full value when the industry has people who understand these technologies and know how to use them effectively.

Digital AgroLeaders helps build this technology readiness before young professionals even enter the workforce.

Technology adoption starts with people

Agriculture in Kazakhstan is undergoing a significant technological transformation. Precision ag, automation, connected machines, and data are creating new opportunities to improve productivity, operational efficiency, resource use, and decision-making.

At the same time, the skills required across the industry are changing. Technical professionals need to understand increasingly sophisticated equipment and digital systems. Agronomists need to know how to turn data into actionable insights. Farm managers need to understand the value of precision technologies and make informed, data-driven decisions. And the industry increasingly needs professionals who can bring equipment, agronomy, connectivity, and digital solutions together across the production system.

Developing this next generation is also part of a broader sustainability challenge. Agriculture in Kazakhstan must become more productive and efficient while responding to climate pressures, water scarcity, rising input costs, and workforce shortages — challenges that are increasing the importance of both advanced technology and new professional capabilities.

For a John Deere dealer, market development includes customer engagement, service support, equipment demonstrations, and helping customers adopt and get more value from technology. Digital AgroLeaders adds another dimension to this work: building the capabilities of future market participants before they even begin their professional careers.

Digital AgroLeaders: building technology readiness since 2010

In 2010, Eurasia Group launched its first student competition focused on John Deere equipment and technologies. Over the past 15 years, the initiative has evolved into an educational ecosystem that brings together students, universities, faculty, agricultural businesses, and industry experts.

Participants work on real-world business challenges, attend master classes, explore modern agricultural technologies, and gain access to mentorship, internships, and career development opportunities.

For students, this provides practical experience that complements their university education. For the agricultural industry, it helps create a generation of professionals entering the workforce with a deeper understanding of precision ag, connected machines, digital agriculture, and the role data can play in improving farm performance.

For Eurasia Group, the ambition goes beyond developing future employees. Digital AgroLeaders is designed to help young people see agriculture as a modern, innovative, and attractive industry in which they can build meaningful careers and contribute to the future of Kazakhstan.

2026: reaching a new scale

In 2026, Digital AgroLeaders reached the largest scale in the project’s history. More than 2,500 students from Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan participated in the initiative — more than twice as many as the previous year — while the program also expanded its geographic reach.

As a result, thousands of future agronomists, engineers, technical specialists, IT professionals, and agricultural leaders have had the opportunity to experience modern, technology-enabled agriculture beyond the university classroom.

The long-term value of this reach goes beyond the number of students involved. By introducing future agricultural professionals to precision ag, connected machines, and data-driven farming early in their careers, Digital AgroLeaders helps build a broader base of knowledge and technology readiness across the industry. Over time, these capabilities can support faster technology adoption, more effective use of advanced solutions, and stronger decision-making across Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector.

“We believe that technology alone does not transform an industry — people do. Bringing advanced equipment and digital solutions to the market is only part of the equation. We also need to develop the knowledge and capabilities required to unlock their full potential. Digital AgroLeaders reflects our long-term commitment to developing people, supporting innovation, and contributing to a more productive and sustainable future for agriculture in Kazakhstan,” said Sergey Glokke, COO of Eurasia Group.

External recognition of a long-term strategy

In 2026, this approach received external recognition through the HUMANRISE Award.

For Eurasia Group, the award recognizes more than 15 years of investment in the next generation of agricultural professionals. It also reflects a broader approach to market development — one in which technology, knowledge, and people advance together.

The long-term partnership between Eurasia Group and John Deere is an important part of this approach, combining technology expertise with knowledge transfer, capability development, service support, and customer adoption.

The HUMANRISE Award recognizes the success of Digital AgroLeaders, but the initiative’s greater value lies in its long-term impact: helping build the skills and technology readiness that will support a more productive, innovative, and sustainable future for agriculture in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Trump Tower project unveiled in Tbilisi
World.content:
Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi

The Trump Tower project was presented at Mtatsminda Park in Tbilisi on the evening of 15 September. The 62-storey skyscraper will be part of the Downtown Tbilisi development planned on the site of the former hippodrome.

The event was attended by representatives of the Georgian government and ruling party, the president of the National Bank, the chairman of the Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission, the prosecutor general, business representatives and other invited guests.

Hundreds of people attended the presentation, leaving some guests standing throughout the event.

The event also featured a video address by Eric Trump, executive vice president of The Trump Organization and son of US President Donald Trump.

“When we undertake projects, the overall climate is very important to us. We build the best buildings in countries where there is a welcoming environment. We want to have outstanding buildings in different countries around the world. My father supports this,” Eric Trump said.

Eric Trump addresses Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi remotely

The presentation featured speeches by executives of the companies involved in the construction of Trump Tower, as well as government representatives.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the project would receive $2 billion in investment. The complex will have a total area of approximately 600,000 square metres.

Kobakhidze said Trump Tower will have 62 floors and stand 282 metres tall. Construction is scheduled to be completed in 2031, with the entire complex due for completion in 2033.

“This is a bold project that will give Tbilisi a new appeal, putting it on a par with the world’s leading urban centres,” Kobakhidze said.

Georgian government and business representatives at the Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi

Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili said the project “will create new jobs from day one”, facilitate the exchange of knowledge and expertise, introduce modern international standards, and “take cooperation between Georgian and international companies to a new level”.

During the presentation, government representatives and executives of companies involved in the project symbolically pressed a red button.

A drone show was held at the site, with the words “Trump Tower Tbilisi” appearing in the sky. The evening ended with a fireworks display.

During the Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi, government representatives and executives of companies involved in the project symbolically pressed a red button

Project announced in April

Information about plans to build a Trump Tower in Tbilisi was released in April 2026. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report on the project.

According to the newspaper, a 70-storey skyscraper is planned for Tbilisi, with the design being developed by US architecture firm Gensler.

The Trump Organization’s partners are named as Georgian companies Archi Group, Biograpi Living, Bloxi Group and Finvest Georgia, as well as US-based The Sapir Organization.

According to The Trump Organization, once completed, the building will be the tallest in Tbilisi. The complex is planned to include luxury residential apartments, retail space and restaurants.

The organisation described the project as the first official use of the Trump brand in the region.

The exact location was not initially disclosed. The Trump Organization only said the skyscraper would be built in a “prestigious location” overlooking Tbilisi’s Central Park.

Local media immediately linked the project to a planned mixed-use development on the site of the former hippodrome. A development plan for the area has already been approved, providing for seven high-rise buildings. The tallest will be 79 storeys.

Central Park Avenue, the company developing the area, is linked to Wissol Group and Biograpi Living, which are involved in the Trump Tower project.

What The Wall Street Journal writes

On 13 September, The Wall Street Journal published an extensive article about the Trump Tower project in Tbilisi.

The headline was: “The Latest Spot for a Trump Tower: An Ex-Soviet Republic Moving Closer to Russia” In the subheadline, the newspaper highlighted the fact that the land designated for the skyscraper in Tbilisi was acquired from a fund linked to billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, who is under US sanctions.

The WSJ examines the project not only as a real estate development, but also in the context of deteriorating Georgia-US relations and Georgia’s domestic political situation.

The newspaper writes that despite a significant deterioration in relations between Tbilisi and Washington in recent years, one of the largest new projects involving a brand associated with the current US president is being developed in Georgia.

A significant part of the WSJ article focuses on the deal for the land designated for the project. According to the publication, the Trump Tower project provided a financial benefit to the family of Bidzina Ivanishvili, who was placed under US sanctions in late 2024.

According to the WSJ, in 2023 the developers agreed to purchase the land from a fund controlled by the Ivanishvili family, with the deal valued at up to $85 million.

News in Georgia

World.title: EU to urge Syria to withdraw recognition of Georgia’s occupied regions
World.content:
Syria to withdraw recognition of Abkhazia

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that during talks with the Syrian leadership, the EU intends to raise the issue of Syria withdrawing its recognition of the independence of Georgia’s Russian-occupied territories — Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

This is stated in a letter in which von der Leyen responded to an appeal from Georgia’s Coalition for Change, an informal political group bringing together pro-Western liberal parties. The coalition currently includes Akhali, Girchi-More Freedom, Droa, the Republican Party and the Activists for the Future movement.

Syria recognised the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia on 29 May 2018, under Bashar al-Assad. At the same time, Syria announced that it was establishing diplomatic relations with both regions. Georgia responded by severing diplomatic relations with Syria.

Coalition leader Nika Gvaramia said at a briefing that the coalition had asked the European Commission president to make the withdrawal of recognition of Georgia’s and Ukraine’s occupied and annexed territories one of the key issues in talks with Syria.

According to Gvaramia, von der Leyen’s letter states that the EU remains committed to Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Gvaramia said this position is particularly important for Georgia because Syria needs European assistance. “Therefore, such pressure could play an important role in the decision to withdraw the recognition,” he said.

He also recalled that on 30 July, the government of Nauru officially withdrew its recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

Four UN member states currently recognise the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia: Russia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and Syria.

What the Coalition for Change said in its letter to Ursula von der Leyen

“For more than three decades, Abkhazia and so-called South Ossetia have been under Russia’s illegal occupation, while the decisions to recognise them adopted by the Assad regime directly undermine Georgia’s sovereignty,” the letter says.

The coalition believes that EU cooperation with Syria’s new government creates an opportunity to reverse these decisions and restore respect for Georgia’s internationally recognised borders.

The coalition said it is ready to assist the European Union in this process by providing information and helping establish contacts.

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Poland is ready to support Armenia’s ambitious goal of joining EU’ — Marcin Bosacki
World.content:
Polish official on Armenia’s EU integration

“Being an influential member of the European Union, Poland can support Armenia in pursuing its ambitious goals, whatever they may be,” Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said in an interview with the Armenpress news agency.

He noted that if Yerevan’s goal is to expand trade with the European Union and conclude a free trade agreement, Warsaw can support the process. The deputy minister also stressed that Poland can support the ambitious goal of joining the EU.

“It will not happen overnight, but it is entirely possible,” he said.

Marcin Bosacki discussed Poland’s experience of European integration, military-technical cooperation with Armenia, and efforts to establish peace in the South Caucasus.

EU membership would open new doors for Armenia

“European Union is a huge market for you. 460 million people, rich people, relatively speaking in terms of the world. And Armenia has some advantages from IT business and gaming even to agriculture, which fit quite nicely into European market. So, this is the big opportunity, and probably you need to diversify your economic ties and directions of export. So, European Union countries like Poland is a natural choice, but yes, there are two challenges, obstacles.

One is institutional, you know, European Union in its core is a free trade zone, which means we really trade freely, without any barriers between ourselves between twenty-seven members of the European Union, but we do have barriers for others.

So, to remove, or at least ease those areas is very important for Armenia, and we are in talks of that. Some of that already happened, like Poland imported one thousand tons of Armenian fruits this year, and temporarily this market was open for you in the scope of European Union. But we need to have trade deals, maybe pre-accession deals.

When you become a candidate for EU, if you become, then it will be much easier to open those doors for you, with the benefit of your producers, not only agricultural producers, but also industrial producers.”

“It is worth becoming a member of this club”: Poland’s experience of European integration

“Poland joined EU twenty-two years ago. So, twenty-three years ago, twenty-five years ago, twenty-seven years ago, we were a candidate country, and we know how to prepare for cooperation and possibly membership with European Union, and then how to negotiate with European Union. And I’m so proud that today with Deputy Minister Vahan Kostanyan, we opened the training of your diplomatic corps by Polish diplomats and experts who were active in those talks and negotiations with European Union when Poland wanted to join, 23, 25 years ag

There is one lesson. It is worth to be in this club. Thirty-five years ago, just after Poland, as one of the first actually as the very first country got rid of communism in 1989, Polish economic situation and Polish economic development was on par with Ukraine’s.

Now we are at least three times richer than Ukraine in terms of GDP per capita, purchasing power and we grew into the sixth biggest economy in the EU, twentieth economy in the world. And we are almost fifty percent richer than we would have been, if we were not members of EU. Polish economic success is magnificent. We didn’t have a year of recession since 1991.

The only year of recession was the year of COVID, 2020, but that was global. And Poles really are five to six times richer than they were a generation ago. It is not always easy. The first years are not easy of economic reforms and the preparations for joining EU, but the benefits for a hardworking, energetic, full of entrepreneurs country like Poland is, those benefits are enormous, and I firmly believe that Armenia will follow Polish path, because you are also a very energetic, very ambitious. And full of entrepreneurs, nation and country.”

Armenia–Poland military-technical cooperation

“In many areas. Yes, in many dimensions of this, yes, really recently opened an area, because just last May, our respective Ministers of Defense signed this agreement on cooperation in this sphere between Poland and Armenia. You know, Polish defense industry is an expert in transitioning of Soviet or post-Soviet armory into NATO standards, into Western standards.

So, we can help you with that if you wish so. Another one is that those two wars, Russian war in Ukraine, and between U.S. And Iran, really emptied the magazines for ammunition, from very simple one to the very developed anti-air and anti-ballistic missiles. We can help produce more of it in cooperation between Armenian and Polish industries, and those talks are already between our two countries.”

Supporting peace and stability in the South Caucasus

“Poland has been and is supporting peace and stabilization of South Caucasus region. We do support TRIPP project, we do support the reconciliation agenda between Armenia and Azerbaijan, and we strongly encourage our Turkish friends to normalize relations with your great country of Armenia, because we really believe that the world, based on peace and democratic values, and the protection of sovereignty of each particular country, is the world in which economy is booming, people are safer and more happy, and the world is more stable.

And therefore, we do wish Armenia all the best on your decisions to diversify, both economically and politically, your future. And we not only wish, but we will help how much you want us to help.”

Polish official on Armenia’s EU integration

World.title: ‘Suleyman’s community case’: Baku dormitories and courses become subject of legal proceedings
World.content:
Suleyman community case in Azerbaijan

Unregistered religious instruction allegedly took place at preparatory courses and student dormitories in Baku linked to the “Suleyman community”.

Witnesses in the case say they were provided with accommodation and three meals a day for 150 manats (approximately $88) a month. They also attended lessons on the Quran and Islamic prayer. The trial of Said Mikailov is ongoing.

What is the “Suleyman community”, what does Azerbaijan’s legislation say about religious education, and what questions about the case remain unanswered?

What happened?

Following an operation carried out by the State Security Service, Said Mehman oglu Mikailov was charged with a criminal offence. He reportedly presented himself as the “head of the Baku branch of the Suleyman community”. Authorities also took administrative measures against several other people.

The case is being heard by the Binagadi District Court in Baku. According to a court report by the pro-government APA news agency, investigators believe that religious rituals took place at premises operating in Baku as preparatory courses, a student dormitory and a kindergarten. The activities allegedly took place without approval from the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations, and some involved minors.

Media reports do not specify which article of the Criminal Code Mikailov faces charges under, whether he is in custody or what position his defence has taken.

The next court hearing is reportedly scheduled for 30 September.

What do the witnesses say?

The testimony of three witnesses questioned in court suggests that similar arrangements operated at different addresses. They offered low-cost accommodation and meals, general education classes, and parallel lessons on the Quran, the Arabic alphabet and the rules of Islamic prayer.

Ibrahim Teymurov, a former head of the Nasimi student dormitory, said he returned to Azerbaijan after receiving religious education at courses run by the “Suleyman community” in Turkey. He said he initially worked at the dormitory as a supervisor and security guard. He later taught Quran classes two or three times a week and was eventually appointed head of the dormitory, replacing Said Mikailov.

According to Teymurov, each student paid 150 manats a month in cash in exchange for accommodation and three meals a day. He said the services were used mainly by children from low-income families who had come from the regions. The witness stated that the religious books in use were commercially available, but acknowledged that no government body had registered the religious instruction.

Another witness, Ismayil Serverli, said he managed an educational centre in the Bakikhanov settlement. According to him, five students lived at the centre, where they also studied literature, mathematics and English. Most teachers worked without employment contracts. Serverli attributed this to their unwillingness to pay taxes. He also said that income was insufficient to cover expenses, so the centre placed a donation box at the entrance.

Elton Abdullayev, a former head of another dormitory in Binagadi, said around 17–18 students lived there, each paying 150 manats a month. According to him, teachers with religious training who lacked permission to teach religion instructed students in the Arabic alphabet and the Quran. They also performed Islamic prayers together with the dormitory residents. The report says that this dormitory also installed a donation box to help cover expenses.

What is the “Suleyman community”?

The “Suleymanists”, or the “Suleyman community”, is the name of a religious community that brings together students and followers of Turkish religious figure Suleyman Hilmi Tunahan. Tunahan received religious education during the final years of the Ottoman Empire. In the first decades of the Turkish Republic, he taught the Quran and religious subjects.

According to a biography published in the Turkish Religious Foundation’s “Encyclopaedia of Islam”, as well as a 2024 academic study, the movement’s main activities included Quran courses and student education. After Tunahan died in 1959, his students continued this work by organising courses and dormitories, and later various educational and social institutions.

The model described during the trial in Baku — combining education with accommodation in dormitories — therefore resembles the organisational structure the movement has historically used in Turkey. However, this similarity alone does not prove that individuals in Azerbaijan received direct instructions or funding from the movement’s leadership in Turkey. The published trial materials contain no documents or information about financial transactions confirming such a connection.

What does Azerbaijani law say?

Article 48 of the Constitution of Azerbaijan guarantees everyone freedom of conscience, the right to determine their own attitude towards religion, and the right to perform religious rites individually or jointly with others. However, exercising this right must not violate public order or conflict with public morality. Article 18 of the Constitution separates religion from the state and establishes the secular nature of the state education system.

Article 6 of the Law on Freedom of Religious Belief allows citizens to study religion and receive religious education individually or jointly with others. However, establishing a religious educational institution or organising courses on sacred texts through religious organisations is subject to a separate procedure. A religious educational institution may be established by a religious centre with the approval of the relevant state body. Courses on sacred texts must follow the religious organisation’s charter, receive approval from the religious centre to which it is subordinate, and be reported to the authorised state body.

Under Article 6-1 of the law, mass religious rites generally take place in houses of worship and pilgrimage sites. Holding them outside such locations requires the consent of a state body. At the same time, Article 21 allows religious rites to take place in dormitories at the request of their residents.

The key legal question in this case, therefore, is not simply whether people read the Quran together. The court will have to establish whether the activity constituted individual and voluntary religious practice or systematic religious instruction organised without the required authorisation. The assessment may also take into account the participation of minors, the official designation of the premises, and the mechanisms used to manage and finance the activities.

Parents have the right to raise their children in accordance with their religious beliefs. However, the law prohibits forcing a child to practise a religion and requires religious upbringing not to harm their physical or mental health. Open sources do not specify how many minors are involved in the case, how old they are, whether their parents gave consent, or which religious rites they took part in.

Receiving religious education abroad is not, in itself, a violation of the law. In 2024, the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations reported that Azerbaijani citizens who had received religious education abroad could attend an interview and receive official appointments as religious figures. At the time, the committee said that 19 people with foreign religious education had received such appointments.

Parallel investigation in Turkey

Several months after the trial began in Azerbaijan, Turkey also launched a major investigation into the community’s leadership. Ankara’s Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office describes the case as an investigation into the activities of a “criminal organisation led by Alihan Kuriş and established for the purpose of financial gain”. Authorities detained 38 suspects. On 16 August 2026, a court remanded 32 of them, including Alihan Kuriş, in custody. It placed the other six under house arrest as a judicial-control measure.

Turkish media report that the investigation concerns alleged fraud, tax evasion and the laundering of criminal proceeds. According to Anadolu Agency, investigators also found 200 kilograms of gold bars during one of the searches. Their origin remains unknown.

At present, open sources contain no information about a direct procedural link or evidence connecting the Baku case with the investigation in Ankara. The two proceedings can be viewed as parallel investigations into the activities of the same religious network. However, there is currently no basis for treating them as part of a single case.

Suleyman community case in Azerbaijan

World.title: Ruling Georgian Dream adds another party to lawsuit seeking opposition ban
World.content:
Gakharia’s party ban

Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party is asking the Constitutional Court to declare the parliamentary opposition Gakharia – For Georgia party unconstitutional and ban it, parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia said.

The party’s leader, exiled former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia, responded: “Even with a parliamentary majority, the Ivanishvili regime could not tolerate the presence of even one opposition party in parliament because it has no answer to criticism.”

Georgian Dream previously asked the Constitutional Court to declare four opposition groups unconstitutional and ban them: the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia – Lelo and the Federalists.

Georgian Dream alleged that the parties had “been involved in unconstitutional activities, including sabotage against the Georgian state, and had adopted essentially identical positions for many years”.

The Gakharia – For Georgia party will now be added to the revised submission.

Kirtskhalia said the party had not initially been included because Georgian Dream wanted to give it an opportunity to participate in parliamentary work, “despite its past ties and direct coalition with the ‘collective National Movement’” (the ruling party’s term for the country’s entire opposition – JAMnews).

He said the revised application seeking to ban the opposition parties would be submitted to the Constitutional Court this week.

Kirtskhalia said the decision to include the party in the case was prompted by its conduct in parliament and its public statements.

“The case is based on numerous indisputable facts,” he said. “Look at how openly, crudely and brazenly they refuse to recognise the country’s constitutional order, and at their numerous destructive actions in parliament and public comments.”

He again accused Gakharia – For Georgia of links to the “collective National Movement network” and said that, in his view, the party “serves the same insidious cause”.

Kirtskhalia added that the case did not seek to strip Gakharia – For Georgia representatives of their seats in either parliament or local councils.

Former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia and his party

Gakharia’s party joined three other opposition groups in boycotting parliament after the 26 October 2024 parliamentary elections, alleging that the vote had been rigged.

However, in November 2025, the party decided to take up its seats in parliament and municipal councils.

According to the Central Election Commission, Gakharia – For Georgia holds 12 seats in parliament and 26 seats on municipal councils across the country.

Giorgi Gakharia is living in forced exile after two criminal cases were brought against him.

1. “Gavrilov’s Night”, or the “20 June case”. On the night of 20-21 June 2019, security forces violently dispersed a large protest in Tbilisi. Investigators allege that Gakharia, then interior minister, ordered riot police to use crowd-control weapons without warning or giving peaceful protesters an opportunity to leave the area. Dozens of people were injured by rubber bullets, including two who each lost an eye, while five others suffered serious injuries.

2. The “Chorchana episode”. Investigators allege that in August 2019, Gakharia, then interior minister, unilaterally ordered the installation of an additional police checkpoint near the village of Chorchana in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone, without coordinating the move with the prime minister or the State Security Service and without informing the EU Monitoring Mission. The move sharply escalated tensions in the conflict zone.

Giorgi Gakharia’s statement

Following the ruling party representative’s announcement, Giorgi Gakharia, who now lives in Germany, posted his response in English on X.

Giorgi Gakharia: “Despite severe restrictions, we have consistently contested every election, regarding elections as the only peaceful and democratic path to political change.

Our party remains the only opposition force represented in parliament.

“By targeting us, Ivanishvili is seeking to ban the country’s only genuinely functioning parliamentary opposition.

“Even with a parliamentary majority, the Ivanishvili regime could not tolerate the presence of even one opposition party in parliament because it has no answer to criticism.

“This is another step by the Ivanishvili regime towards formally establishing authoritarian rule in Georgia and suppressing the political opposition.

“Whether we are banned or not, we will not abandon our goal of restoring democracy in Georgia and defending its European and Euro-Atlantic course,” Gakharia wrote.

News in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan factory workers complain of ‘up to 16-hour shifts’
World.content:
Workers at the Nati biscuit and chocolate factory in Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan exclave have complained of poor working conditions, saying their shifts often significantly exceed eight hours.

Employees told Gündəlik Naxçıvan they worked long hours for a monthly salary of 400 manats (about $235), which had not increased for three years. They also complained of low overtime pay and alleged that workers who raised concerns about conditions were dismissed.

The employees said they also worked on Saturdays.

One worker, identified as N.B., said:

“We are made to work 12 to 14 hours a day, and sometimes as many as 16.”

He said the long hours left workers physically exhausted and struggling to get home.

‘Those who complain are fired’

Workers said it was also unsafe to speak openly about conditions at the factory, alleging that those who complained were identified and then dismissed. Most therefore did not want to reveal their names.

Another employee called on the State Labour Inspection Service to investigate the factory.

“Why doesn’t the Labour Inspectorate come and inspect this factory?” the worker asked.

Employees alleged that after previous complaints, factory management learned the identities of those behind them and the workers subsequently lost their jobs. If confirmed, the allegations would raise concerns not only about working hours and pay, but also about possible retaliation against employees seeking to assert their labour rights.

What does the law say?

Under Azerbaijan’s labour legislation, the normal working day may not exceed eight hours, while the working week may not exceed 40 hours. A six-day working week is permitted; however, with a 40-hour working week, the working day may not exceed seven hours, and on the day before a day off, it may not exceed six hours. Therefore, working on Saturdays is not in itself a violation of the law. What matters is the total number of hours worked per week and the length of rest periods.

Even at enterprises where cumulative working-time accounting is used, a single shift may not exceed 12 hours. These limits are also set out in the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection’s 2026 work calendar. The workers’ claims that they work 14- and 16-hour shifts may therefore indicate violations of labour law.

According to guidance from the State Labour Inspection Service, overtime is permitted only in exceptional circumstances. Article 165 of the Labour Code stipulates that, for employees paid on a time basis, each hour of overtime must be paid at no less than twice the normal hourly rate.

The 400 manats mentioned by the workers corresponds to the minimum monthly wage in force since January 2025. However, the minimum wage is the minimum amount payable to an employee who has worked the full monthly quota of working hours and does not include payment for overtime.

Factory is part of Ləzzət Group

According to the company’s official information, the factory began operating in 2010 as Ləzzət Biskvit və Şokolad Fabriki LLC. It produces wafers, biscuits, cookies and other confectionery products under the Nati brand and other trademarks.

The Ləzzət Group website says the factory has a daily production capacity of 30 tonnes and exports its products to a number of countries. The company also says that in 2019 the factory received an honorary diploma for creating healthy and safe working conditions. The workers’ current complaints stand in stark contrast to this information.

At the time of writing, no comments from the Nati factory, Ləzzət Group or the State Labour Inspection Service regarding the workers’ specific allegations could be found in publicly available sources.

The employees are calling on the relevant state authorities to investigate working hours at the factory, overtime pay, wage levels and working conditions in general.

World.title: Wall Street Journal: New Trump Tower to be built in Georgia as country draws closer to Russia
World.content:
Trump Tower in Georgia

A 70-storey Trump Tower, set to become the tallest building in Tbilisi, is the latest business project planned in Georgia, a country that has distanced itself from Washington and drawn closer to Moscow in recent years, the influential US newspaper Wall Street Journal reports.

The newspaper said the skyscraper is set to be built on land in Tbilisi bought from a fund linked to US-sanctioned billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili.

According to the Wall Street Journal, Georgian developers are launching a marketing campaign for the project this week, promoting the skyscraper as one of Georgia’s most significant new developments.

In May 2026, the developers signed a branding agreement with the Trump Organization, allowing them to use the Trump name and brand. As with other international projects, the Trump Organization is not directly involved in construction but licenses its brand to developers.

However, the Tbilisi project differs from a typical property deal because it comes amid a sharp deterioration in Georgia’s relations with the United States.

Georgia moves away from US while embracing Trump brand

The Wall Street Journal noted that the project comes amid a sharp deterioration in US-Georgian relations.

Georgia was once regarded as one of Washington’s closest partners in the former Soviet Union, with President George W Bush calling it a “beacon of liberty” during a 2005 visit to Tbilisi. The newspaper said relations with the West had deteriorated under the ruling Georgian Dream party, which has faced criticism over democratic backsliding, while Tbilisi has moved closer to Moscow and its EU accession process has effectively stalled.

Against this backdrop, Georgian developers are pressing ahead with a skyscraper bearing the name of the US president, the WSJ said.

The deal comes as the Georgian government faces growing criticism from Washington and the country moves closer to Russia, the paper reiterated.

Land plot, Bidzina Ivanishvili and $85m

The Wall Street Journal reported that the developers bought the land for the project in 2023 from a fund controlled by the family of Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Georgian corporate records cited by the newspaper showed the deal was worth up to $85m and was completed in July 2026.

Ivanishvili, who made his fortune in Russia and served as prime minister in 2012-13, remains Georgia’s most influential political figure despite holding no government post.

His Georgian Dream party denies Western and opposition accusations of democratic backsliding and rigging the 2024 parliamentary election.

New era for Trump’s business

The Wall Street Journal said the Tbilisi project also reflected the expansion of the Trump Organization’s overseas business since Donald Trump began his second term.

Restrictions on new foreign deals imposed during his first presidency have been lifted, with Trump-branded projects also under development in Abu Dhabi, Vietnam and the Maldives.

Trump reported $59m in income from foreign property licensing deals in 2025, up from $45m in 2024, according to the newspaper.

The Trump Organization says its business is run independently of the administration and denies any conflict of interest, while Democrats and governance groups argue that overseas earnings could create conflicts with US foreign policy.

‘Positive rapprochement’

The Wall Street Journal said some Georgian analysts saw the Trump Tower project as more than a commercial deal.

Economist Giorgi Khishtovani said it could be aimed at establishing a connection with the Trump administration.

In May, Georgian investors including Wissol Group president Samson Pkhakadze and former Georgian Dream MP Ilia Tsulaia signed the agreement with Eric Trump at Mar-a-Lago.

Tsulaia had also joined a Georgian delegation to Washington in 2025 seeking to improve relations with the new US administration and discuss sanctions.

A former senior US official involved in the talks told the newspaper that the group was seeking a “positive rapprochement” with Washington.

Trump Tower in Russia’s shadow

The Wall Street Journal said the planned Trump Tower brought together the US president’s global business interests and Georgia’s changing foreign policy.

The newspaper noted the contrast between Georgia’s efforts to rebuild ties with Washington and its improving relations with Moscow, particularly given that parts of Georgian territory have remained under Russian occupation since the 2008 war.

The WSJ stresses that, if built, the skyscraper will become Tbilisi’s tallest building, but its real significance may have little to do with its height.

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhazia plans to welcome 5 million tourists a year by 2030. Why is this impossible?’
World.content:
Abkhazia plans to welcome 5 million tourists a year by 2030. The ambitious target forms part of the republic’s socio-economic development programme for 2026–2030.

However, blogger and business consultant Kirill Bazilevsky believes the target is unattainable, given the state of Abkhazia’s infrastructure.

In a blog post, he uses statistics to analyse the situation and explain his position.

Kirill Bazilevsky: “Let’s look at the figures available at the moment.

In 2025, Abkhazia welcomed a record 1.88 million tourists. This was the best result in the republic’s post-Soviet history.

The target for 2026 is to surpass the 2 million mark.

But it is already clear that growth has slowed.

According to tour operators, demand for holidays in Abkhazia fell by 19% in July and August 2026 compared with the previous year. The season was marked by stagnation rather than a boom.

The reasons include fewer flights from Russian regions, inflation, which has made holidays in Abkhazia significantly more expensive, as well as Russia’s overall economic situation and other factors that are holding back activity in the tourism market.

In addition, the republic’s current accommodation capacity is estimated at 2.1–2.2 million beds per season. To welcome 5 million tourists, Abkhazia would need at least 2.5 to three times more. The republic will not be able to build that much capacity in just a few years.”

Next comes infrastructure. Where are the weak points?

Energy. Abkhazia’s power grid is in a critical state. Every year from November to April, the republic faces an energy shortage as water levels in the Inguri Hydroelectric Power Station’s reservoir fall. Welcoming 5 million tourists would require new generating capacity and major investment in utilities. One power plant would not be enough.

Abkhazia’s power grid is in a critical state. Every year from November to April, the republic faces an energy shortage as water levels in the Inguri Hydroelectric Power Station’s reservoir fall. Welcoming 5 million tourists would require new generating capacity and major investment in utilities. One power plant would not be enough. Wastewater treatment. The situation is critical. Tourists complain that, in the resort town of Gagra, sewage is discharged directly into the sea in some places, while treatment facilities cannot cope with the influx of visitors. As a result, outbreaks of rotavirus are regularly reported. If tourist numbers doubled, this would become a permanent problem. Waste. This problem has remained unresolved for decades. The Institute of Ecology at the Academy of Sciences predicts a disaster in the near future. The Sukhum landfill covers around 60 hectares, and there is no new land available for additional landfill sites. Staffing. There is an acute shortage of qualified workers, including service personnel. Sukhum airport has already faced a staffing shortage and is looking for employees from Russia. Health tourism would also require doctors, nurses and other medical staff, whom Abkhazia is critically short of.

Lessons from past mistakes

Only recently, there were attempts to launch large-scale construction projects in Abkhazia. Draft laws on apartment hotels and the development of the republic’s eastern districts were put forward, along with an investment agreement with Russia. All of these initiatives ended in an acute political crisis. The reasons for their failure included the lack of clear figures, environmental risk assessments and a transparent roadmap.

Several months ago, plans to build a ski resort were announced. They prompted scepticism both among the public and experts. The reasons were the same: threats to the environment, weak energy infrastructure and the absence of a transparent business plan.

My conclusion

Abkhazia cannot reach a tourist flow of 5 million visitors a year by 2030 if we are talking about actual results rather than distorted statistics. Even during the Soviet period, when conditions were much more favourable, the republic never reached such a figure.

The statistics for the 2026 season — stagnation and a 19% drop in demand — provide no grounds for believing that the situation will change dramatically in 2027–2029. Geopolitical and economic realities do not support optimistic forecasts.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.
