World.title: ‘An attack on me’: Brisbane agent fights to keep licence
World.content:
A prominent Brisbane real estate agent convicted of an overseas assault is fighting in court to get his licence reinstated, claiming his business is suffering as others stand to gain financially from his downfall. Last year Tony O’Doherty, formerly the principal at McGrath Bulimba, pleaded guilty and received a two-year fully suspended sentence for a 2013 one-punch assault on a man outside a nightclub in Ireland. The victim suffered a fractured skull and a bleed to his brain. Tony O’Doherty speaking outside court. Cloe Read O’Doherty’s legal team are appealing against a decision by the Office of Fair Trading to cancel his licence.



Under the Property Occupations Act 2014, a person is considered unsuitable to hold a real estate licence if they were convicted within the previous five years, regardless of when the conduct occurred. Justice Soraya Ryan on Wednesday heard arguments from O’Doherty’s barrister, Rob Anderson KC, who said there was urgency in the case, given the agent’s livelihood had been curtailed by the automatic termination of his licence. Anderson put forward arguments around the interpretation of the law, including whether a foreign offence should be included under Queensland law. He told the court there was no option in the Irish criminal justice system to not record convictions, whereas under Queensland law, a judge would consider aspects of a defendant’s life, such as their occupation. He said the impact on O’Doherty’s real estate licence was not considered by the Irish judge.



Barrister Angus Scott KC, representing the Department of Justice, said the law was in place to protect the community and consumers. “The ultimate point we make throughout this legislation is it is concerned with the protection of the community,” he said, adding that the criteria under the law considered whether the offence involved violence. Speaking outside court, O’Doherty said the loss of his licence had had a detrimental impact on his business, and the McGrath team were hopeful it would be short term. “It is an incredible attack on the business, and I’m going to go against my legal advice and say that this is an attack on me,” he said. “It is an attack. Let’s just say other people stand to gain commercially and financially by my downfall, and they have not been silent.”



O’Doherty said he took full responsibility for what happened more than a decade ago, saying he made a poor decision. He said there had been an altercation, and he wished it never happened. “I think a lot of the media’s coverage hasn’t been in its entirety, and it never is,” he said. “The night in question was by no means a brutal attack, which is what the headlines have been. I’m not condoning my behaviour.” He questioned how many other people with criminal convictions were operating in the real estate industry after cases the media had not covered. The Limerick Post reported that O’Doherty was at the Club Mission nightclub in Newcastle West when the victim, James Fitzgerald, threw a glass over his shoulder, which smashed near O’Doherty and splashed a drink on him.



Fitzgerald, who was severely drunk at the time, was removed from the nightclub by security. O’Doherty ran after Fitzgerald and confronted him, hitting him in the jaw. He was sent backwards and banged his head into a door, according to the Limerick Post. Ryan reserved her decision for a later date. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: Outgoing National MP Andrew Bayly discusses his 'brutal' resignation in final speech to Parliament
World.content:
Outgoing National MP Andrew Bayly has used his final speech in Parliament to set the record straight about his resignation, calling it one of the "most brutal experiences" of his life.

The Port Waikato MP delivered his valedictory speech on Wednesday evening.

Bayly revealed he had resigned from his ministerial portfolios based on a false premise, wrongly believing a staff member had complained about his conduct.

That happened last year, and at the time the former commerce and consumer affairs minister recounted an "animated discussion" that ended with him putting a hand on a staff member.

At the time he apologised, saying he had been inappropriate and taken the discussion too far, but denied using any force.

In his valedictory speech, Bayly said at the end of a meeting with three of his advisers, he had placed his hand on the arm of a male adviser and said "we can do this".

"The next night, I was told a serious allegation had been made. I couldn't believe it," he said.

Bayly said when he told his wife Tina, she turned away and cried.

"That was when I understood this was no longer just about a ministerial job.

"It was hurting the person I loved most."

Bayly said the Department of Internal Affairs had told him all three people at the meeting had corroborated the allegation.

He might have contested the account of one person, or two people, he said.

Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Andrew Bayly speaks following his resignation from all ministerial positions on 24 February 2025. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

"But if all three corroborated a serious allegation, I could not remain a minister," he said.

"It was on that premise that I took the decision to resign."

Shortly before he announced that, Bayly said he met with the complainant.

"During that conversation, he told me that he had not made a complaint and would not have done so," he said.

"The next day, the second witness described the meeting as a storm in a teacup."

Three months later, Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche confirmed the ACC chief executive had initiated the investigation, and no formal complaint was ever made about his conduct, Bayly said.

He said ministers must be accountable for their behaviour, however that accountability must rest on facts and a fair process.

"Mine did not," he said.

Bayly said he was in a "very dark place" following his resignation.

Being a minister had been the greatest privilege of his life, he said, but his time in Parliament was tough on his family, referencing death threats made against his wife and children.

"You did not choose it. You did not deserve it. And I will always be sorry."

In his speech, Bayly discussed some of his wins, which included advancing open banking, completing major insurance law reform, beginning the first "serious" review of New Zealand's competition settings in decades, and commissioning two major reviews into ACC and managing its fund.

At the end of his speech, he called on MPs to raise the Superannuation age to 68, beginning gradually from 2029.

World.title: Tom Phillips case: 'Circuit breaker' moment was missed, says mayor
World.content:
The mayor of Waitomo asked the Children's Commissioner to intervene and bring the government agencies involved in the Tom Phillips case together in a "circuit breaker" moment, a year before Phillips was killed.

A public inquiry has found authorities minimised the potential for Phillips' three children to be harmed and did not collaborate well, resulting in missed opportunities to end the saga.

Waitomo mayor John Robertson feared there was something awry years ago.

"A year before the tragedy of the shooting of Tom Phillips and the finding of the children, I made a call to the commissioner for children, pondering whether there was another way through this.

"And someone of standing, a commissioner for children seemed to me to be appropriate to try to bring the parties, the government parties that were involved together and see if there was some way to, you know, create a circuit breaker in this."

Robertson said the report made interesting reading.

"The comments, the criticism that our government departments weren't being collaborative enough or working together enough on this. That's certainly something I wondered [about] a year before, after year three, really, of the Tom Phillips and the children being away."

He said he'd had cordial discussion with then-Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad.

"I called her on the phone to ask if she would intervene - by bringing the police and the Family Court / Oranga Tamariki together to see if there was an opportunity to 'negotiate' a way through the impasse. It was a good conversation, she said she would reflect [on it], but I heard no more."

Achmad remembered the call.

"Yes, I do, and I really appreciated Mayor Robertson contacting me with his suggestions for how things could be progressed.

"I remember that the mayor was understandably very concerned about the ongoing safety and wellbeing of the children, and he was, of course, advocating strongly throughout for their safe return."

Former Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

She took up the baton.

"Of course took those suggestions and concerns forward to Oranga Tamariki and to police at the highest level, at chief executive and commissioner level. And I made clear that I had concerns, of course, about seeing the safe return of the children.

"I also made an offer at that time, following the mayor's prompting, that if there was anything that I could do from my independent role as Children's Commissioner, then those agencies were welcome to call on me for that independent role to the extent that I could.

She got a lukewarm response.

"Those offers were not taken up, and I received assurances that everything was being done to ensure the safe return of those children, and that the agencies were working closely together on bringing those children home safely and locating them."

Achmad said in light of the assurances given to her, the inquiry's findings were deeply disappointing.

"What's absolutely clear to me, having read this inquiry report, is that the concerns that had been coming forward from the whanau and from the community had clearly been minimised by these agencies, and it's clear to me now that these agencies were not working together as closely as they should have been.

"And that's incredibly, incredibly disappointing and unacceptable in my view."

Achmad was puzzled that Robertson believed he had not heard back from her.

"I think that might be a bit of a miscommunication. My memory, my recollection, is that a call was put through to the council office and a message was left. I remember that I couldn't reach him there that day.

"My recollection is that I left a message at the council offices just letting him know that I had heard his concerns and suggestions and that I was taking those forward."

Achmad said she would follow up with the mayor.

Meanwhile, Robertson welcomed the "very frank" inquiry's findings, which had helped fill-in gaps in the information available to him and locals over the four years Phillips was on the run with his three children.

"I'm pleased to see a report come out that's not redacted. And having the commentary on Oranga Tamariki and the sorts of advice that was given at the time is helpful to understanding what was going on.

"I mean, at the beginning of the report it talks about two critical themes and one of them is that the harm caused by isolating the children from the family, friends and society was underplayed, minimised or overlooked by agencies.

"So, that sort of statement, I guess, sums things up. So, it's good now to find what the agencies were thinking, which, you know, the report is pretty critical of."

Robertson said it was easy to be critical in hindsight, "but I think there were lessons [to be learned], or certainly the inquiry pulls no punches in saying there were some things that weren't done terribly well".

Robertson said while the report was also critical of aspects of the police operation to find Phillips and his children, he had a good relationship with police through the ordeal.

"They were alerting me or advising me on incidents as they went on. They were usually public incidents. So I felt very well briefed by the police and I felt for them in terms of their frustration through that time in trying to find Tom Phillips.

He said the report gave more detail what police were doing with NZ Defence Force and SAS involvement.

"I guess we all understood what the police were doing or trying to do in their frustrations. What we didn't know was the Oranga Tamariki side of the story.

"Those were the gaps that the public, and certainly I, you know, found through the four years."

Robertson welcomed the formal apology to the maternal whānau and older siblings of the Phillips children.

"I'm really pleased to see an apology to the children from the Minister [Louise Upston] on behalf of the Crown, because this report does highlight some inadequacies and I think it's only proper that there is an apology."

Robertson said the local community was still digesting the findings.

"Look, I think it's too early to say [what the reaction is]. I've sat down and worked through the report.

"I think the conclusion is that, you know, the government departments needed to work better together."

Phillips first went missing with his three children for 18 days in September 2021 before disappearing again in December of the same year.

World.title: Splitting up Foodstuffs: Would it actually drive down grocery prices?
World.content:
National wants to split Foodstuffs in two in a bid to drive down grocery prices - but would it work?

It announced the proposal on Wednesday, which would require a Commerce Commission review to determine whether it would leave shoppers better off.

Foodstuffs - made up of two co-operatives - currently manages all New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square stores.

National's plan would split them up, leaving the country with three nationwide supermarket chains: Pak'nSave, New World/Four Square and Woolworths.

University of Auckland senior marketing lecturer Drew Franklin said it was a step in the right direction.

"Structural separation or intervention that's seeking to structurally reform the sector has been shown to work overseas because it lowers the concentration of the market so there are more players in the game."

National's modelling estimated 3.5 percent lower prices after a year and 5 percent lower after six years with Foodstuffs split in two.

Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Nicola Willis, speaking as the party's finance spokesperson, said it could eventually save households up to $1320 a year.

"The short answer is time will tell," Franklin said. "That sort of structural separation putting downward pressure on prices isn't going to happen in a hurry."

Jon Duffy, chief executive of Consumer, welcomed the idea.

"The debate has really moved forward from where we were even six weeks ago, where we were still debating whether some form of intervention was needed beyond the pretty lukewarm measures that have been implemented since the Commerce Commission's study - pretty much all the major parties with the exception of ACT have some form of structural reform or measure to address price gouging, that sort of thing, in their election manifestos. This is a step forward for New Zealand."

He said it was positive that National's plan was to require that the Commerce Commission first consider what it would mean for customers with what was effectively a reverse merger assessment.

"The commission is very skilled at doing this type of analysis. So it's saying instead of hypothesising what a market would look like if two entities merge, hypothesise what they will look like if they demerge, and work out whether there's a net benefit to consumers."

Foodstuffs manages all New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square stores. Supplied

He said National's plan seemed intended to treat the "disease", while Labour's announcement on anti-price gouging measures was addressing the symptoms of a lack of competition.

The savings being talked about showed how badly the market was treating consumers, he said.

"It's strange territory for the National Party but that's how bad the problem is."

BusinessNZ director of advocacy Catherine Beard said it was a concerning proposal that could undermine New Zealand's reputation for regulatory stability, respect for property rights and predictable policy settings.

"This is a very concerning move by the National Party and sends a chilling signal to businesses across New Zealand that the government can break up businesses. It also sends the wrong signal to foreign investors looking to invest in New Zealand."

She said the government needed to be clear on what the problem was that it wanted to fix.

"Because one of the important bits of information that Commerce Commission's not really gotten to the bottom of is how does our basket of groceries stack up in New Zealand versus international comparators when a lot of other countries don't put GST on their food and New Zealand does? And I think the Commerce Commission acknowledged in their last report that that is an area that needs further work."

She said there could be a scenario where prices rose when the business was split because it lost efficiencies of scale.

But Franklin said while it was strong intervention and BusinessNZ was right to demand strong evidence and safeguards, it would only be overreach in the absence of a demonstrated problem.

"We've done our own research here at the University of Auckland that has identified that the concentration problem is well documented.

"And so, that's the problem that the structural separation is seeking to fix effectively. It's not the government setting grocery prices or running supermarkets or co-opting supermarkets like some of the other policies that we've heard to date."

He said the Commerce Commission needed more teeth and a much more legitimate role in trying to respond most appropriately to entrenched market power.

BusinessNZ said the supermarket proposal could undermine New Zealand's reputation for regulatory stability. Unsplash / Getty Images

"I think it's a step in the right direction."

It would also be important to consider supply arrangements and what a split would mean in areas that were only served by one supermarket brand, he added.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said New Zealand's food price increases over the last 20 years had been in about the middle of OECD countries.

"The increase in food prices and cost of living pressures has been a global phenomenon and it's hard to point at New Zealand-specific factors to suggest our prices are dramatically different to what's happened with the global trend, which has been to higher prices."

He said splitting Foodstuffs was unlikely to be a silver bullet to fix the cost-of-living crisis.

Foodstuffs has been approached for comment.

World.title: Winston Peters mocks National as 'Great Pretender' over supermarket policy
World.content:
National's proposed supermarket shake-up has set the coalition partners against one another, with New Zealand First crying "copy cat" and ACT labelling it "desperate and visionless".

In a surprise policy announcement on Wednesday, National announced a plan to sever Pak'nSave from New World in a bid to drive down grocery prices, contingent on a six-month review by the Commerce Commission.

Heading into the debating chamber, NZ First leader Winston Peters paused to play reporters a snippet of the 1955 song "The Great Pretender" on his phone.

"Everybody's borrowing our policies, as you'll notice, and we're getting a bit sick of it," Peters said.

He told reporters National had simply "cut and pasted" NZ First's plan to break up the duopoly which it announced in April.

But Peters said the development had come "far too late" to make a difference this term.

"If they'd done it in April, we could have had it all through Parliament and fixed up already."

Asked about ACT's virulent opposition, Peters suggested National could have secured the necessary support from opposition parties.

Responding, National leader Christopher Luxon laughed off the Great Pretender jab: "Isn't he great with the singing? I mean, it's one of the great joys of working with him."

Luxon said he was pleased National had found "political consensus" with NZ First on "something serious and substantive".

The ACT Party, however, was certainly not joining that consensus, issuing a scathing media release deriding "desperate and visionless campaigning" driven by focus group.

ACT leader David Seymour warned such "heavy-handed intervention" would have a chilling impact on investment and dissuade new entrants from setting up here.

Speaking to reporters, Seymour suggested National was "not entirely committed" to the idea and had given itself an out by asking the Commerce Commission to look at it.

"The ACT party is starting to sound like what the National Party should be: standing up for the rights of people to save, invest, and sacrifice, and have a better life as a result."

Seymour said the policy was little different from "the Greens' roundly-mocked Government-owned supermarket".

That argument was somewhat bolstered by the Green Party itself, which celebrated National's announcement, jokingly referring to its MPs as "our comrades".

"We've finally got the National Party coming to the table on things that they accused us for being communist about just two weeks ago," co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins also ridiculed the disagreement between the coalition parties, saying they were panicking after failing to improve the cost of living.

"No one can believe Christopher Luxon. David Seymour doesn't believe him. Why should New Zealanders?"

Hipkins would not be drawn on whether he supported breaking up Foodstuffs, but said Labour would have more to say about supermarket competition before the election.

The EMA business association said National's proposal was "a step too far".

Head of advocacy Alan McDonald said the policy was "not quite nationalising a private business but it's too close for comfort" and would send a "terrible signal" to investors.

Following through would undermine previous attempts to tackle the problem of a lack of competition, he said.

"Seeing a right-of-centre, business-focused political party like National suggest this type of policy will sit uneasily with businesses in New Zealand. It might be a populist policy for a grumpy electorate but that doesn't make it a good policy."

Consumer chief executive Jon Duffy told Checkpoint that making Pak'nSave and New World compete against each other could be the answer to the country's high grocery prices.

"There wouldn't be the restrictions that are on them at the moment imposed by head office which basically separates out different geographical and demographic patches for each brand.

"They'd need to be watched but in theory they'd compete with each other.

"That would have the good results that strong competition has, which is lower prices, more innovation, better service - all the things we don't see at the moment in the market," he said.

Nothing had changed materially in the past few years regarding grocery prices, despite multiple "light touch" interventions, Duffy said.

"There needs to be bold action, and what we're seeing from National's policy, and also from the Greens, is propositions that are bold.

"We've now moved into a situation where all of the major political parties, bar ACT, recognise that there's a problem, recognise that the cost of food and groceries is the number one financial concern consumers are reporting, and they're offering up solutions.

World.title: Southern motorists warned to be careful as snow and flooding hit highways
World.content:
State highways in the lower South Island are being hit by flooding and snowfall as a cold front passes through the area.

Roading crews have been assessing snow and using grit trucks on State Highway 6 between Lowther and Parawa in Southland.

Surface flooding has been reported in places across State Highways 96 and 99, as well as on State Highway 1 in central Dunedin.

The NZ Transport Agency said no closures or restrictions were currently in place, but motorists should drive to the conditions.

MetService has road snowfall warnings in place for South Island alpine passes from today through to tomorrow.

A heavy snow watch is in force covering Central Otago, Queenstown Lakes District and the Mackenzie Basin until the early hours tomorrow.

World.title: Watercare to spend $95 million on Ōtara wastewater
World.content:
Auckland's water provider is spending $95 million to boost wastewater capacity in Ōtara.

Watercare plans to upgrade the suburb's wastewater network to reduce wet-weather overflow into the environment.

Ōtara's existing wastewater network was reaching capacity and could be overwhelmed in heavy rain, causing overflows, it said.

Watercare will build a new pump station on Hannah Road as well as install several underground storage tanks at the existing Ōtara Pump station.

Local councillor Alf Filipaina said it was important that infrastructure kept pace with community growth.

"These upgrades will help improve the resilience of the wastewater network, reduce the risk of wet-weather overflows, and support a cleaner environment for local residents, now and in the future," he said.

The investment was great news for Ōtara, Filipaina added.

Alf Filipaina RNZ / Felix Walton

Watercare's general manager of capital delivery, Mike Marsden, said the new infrastructure was a key part of the organisation's $15.2 billion, 10-year capital investment programme.

"This project is a great example of how we're delivering the infrastructure Auckland needs today while planning for future generations and helping to protect the environment," he said.

Watercare has set up its main construction site on Great South Road, with smaller construction sites at both pump stations.

It said a 2.5km section of the new wastewater pipeline will be made by relining a decommissioned section of the Hunua 1 watermain already in the ground, which will minimise disruption to the community.

World.title: Who hired the new nurses? Labour and National can't agree
World.content:
National deputy leader Nicola Willis says more than 2000 nurses being recruited by Health NZ will be working by the end of the year.

The government has faced repeated criticism for Health NZ's go-slow on hiring and for not having enough nurses in place in time for this winter.

But appearing on Morning Report's political panel with Labour deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni, Willis said 2300 nurses were being recruited "right now".

"What that means is Health NZ is actively interviewing and placing them in roles around the country," she said.

They would be working in hospitals by Christmas, she said.

Sepuloni said that was a "big call".

The two parties have repeatedly clashed over how many nurses had been hired while the coalition had been in power.

National said the 2100 more nurses hired between September 2023 and March 2024 were its doing.

The government was not sworn into power until the end of November 2023.

But Labour said it was responsible for the recruitment of those nurses when it was in government.

In the two years from March 2024 to March 2026 just 54 extra nurses were hired.

Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall said even if Health NZ could have the nurses working by Christmas, they were unlikely to fill all the gaps.

This afternoon in Parliament, Verrall asked Health Minister Simeon Brown whether 2300 nurses were enough to replace those who have left in the past two years.

She wanted to know whether there would be a net increase in the number of nurses employed.

Brown said he could not give a number, but said retention had improved under the government.

His expectation was Health NZ would fill vacancies and grow the workforce, he said.

Verrall told RNZ she doubted it was enough - but the government was not releasing workforce projections so it was hard for her to suggest how many were needed.

The increase of just 54 nurses in two years was not a good sign, she said.

"It seems highly unlikely they are going to turn that around by Christmas just because the public has noticed," she said.

Health NZ said on 24 August, of the 2378 roles being recruited, 475 nurses had accepted offers and were preparing to join the workforce.

A further 459 New Zealand trained graduates had been "matched to roles" across the country since July, it said.

World.title: 'Simply not good enough' - Barnardos demands more work to protect children
World.content:
Major political parties have agreed more work needs to be done to protect children, as Barnardos warns that inaction will cost Aotearoa $450 billion by 2050.

The children's charity hosted a stand up on Parliament steps this afternoon to endorse its Generational Plan for Children.

Barnardos chief executive Matt Reid called for long-term cross-party commitment to seeing all children thrive by 2050.

"Our children, our tamariki, do not grow up in three-year parliamentary terms," he said.

He urged policymakers to consider children in their decision-making as the challenges faced by children were complex and did not arise in isolation from other issues.

"Far too many children in Aotearoa continue to be challenged by poverty, violence, mental distress, barriers to opportunity, poor housing, poor health outcomes, simply not good enough."

Reid said inaction would cost the country $450 billion by 2050.

He suggested establishing a permanent children's cabinet, responsible for all children.

He also argued for implementing the findings of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse and Care.

On the Phillips case, he said the system should have been "more focused and urgent about dealing with some of those complexities around that family".

But he said it was time to move past inquiries towards action and he suggested increasing investment in children.

"A future made in New Zealand is not just built through roads, mines, infrastructure and investment. It is built through investing in our schools, our early childhood centres and in our communities."

Major political parties appeared to agree with his call for change.

Children from Barnardos early learning centres outside Parliament for the launch of the organisation's Generational Plan for Children. RNZ / Anya Fielding

Labour's spokesperson for children Willow-Jean Prime welcomed the challenge of working across party lines to make a better future for children.

She said much work was needed to make New Zealand the "best place in the world to be a child".

"It's important in this plan that we are providing early intervention, prevention and support at that earliest opportunity," she said.

ACT's Karen Chhour - the current minister for children - said she wanted children not just to survive but thrive.

"Sustained progress requires that our government agencies, iwis, Māori organizations, community organisations, providers, partners, and businesses all work together to understand our responsibilities."

National MP Katie Nimon said there was an ongoing conversation between the party and Barnardos.

"There is work that we do already that absolutely acknowledges so much of what is said in this report, but it is so important for us to continue to work towards it."

Julie Anne Genter spoke for the Greens and endorsed the plan, committing to "an all-of-government approach to ensure that child-centered practices are placed at the heart of decision-making and go beyond electoral cycles".

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong agreed with the plan's long-term approach.

"I believe it is the role of government to look far into the horizon and look at what changes we can make not to improve just our lives tomorrow, but that of the next generation."

World.title: Tszyu changes tune on controversial draw, eyes off fights in US
World.content:
Believing his domestic duties are done, Nikita Tszyu is ready to take on America after changing his tune and claiming victory in his controversial draw with countryman Ben Mahoney.

Tszyu surprisingly but sportingly conceded he thought he had lost the pair's Brisbane bout last month after the judges, with three vastly different scorecards, declared a stalemate.

Mahoney danced around the ring like he had won a world title, prompting derision from Tszyu's brother Tim, before his team cried highway robbery.

But after watching replays of the super-welterweight stoush, Tszyu is now adamant he should have been awarded the contest.

Tszyu's stunning admission, says Mahoney 'edged' thrilling draw Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

"I'm not a very good judge," he said of his initial verdict.

"I scored it 7-3. In a good way, 8-4. I thought I won the majority of the middle rounds. I gave him the first two rounds and the last two rounds, but [I won] everything else in between.

"I don't regret it, because it was what I felt at the time."

The still-undefeated Sydney slayer hopes his best nights lie ahead of him — and ideally in the US.

The 29-year-old and his team have always been happy to take things slowly and not rush into taking big fights in the boxing mecca.

But Tszyu (12-1-0, 10KOs) finally feels ready, despite Tim relinquishing his IBO super-welterweight belt in the US to Sebastian Fundora, as well as losing a rematch and copping a brutal beat down in another world-title loss in America to Bakhram Murtazaliev.

"I think I can figure it out," Tszyu told AAP.

"This fight was a great learning curve for me and it puts things a lot into perspective. I've got to be a lot more professional with the way I do things.

"I can't be landscaping close to the fight. I can't be doing woodworking close to the fight. Just some bad habits I do.

"Yeah, I've got to be a professional athlete."

No Limit Boxing is known to be pushing for Tszyu to feature on the undercard to the David Benavidez-Michal Cieslak unified blockbuster in Phoenix, Arizona, on December 12.

But if a US date does not eventuate, No Limit has confirmed Tszyu will fight at least once more in 2026 in Australia.

AAP

World.title: NRLW greats Elliot, Baxter, announce retirement at end of finals
World.content:
The NRLW will farewell two of its most influential figures with Sydney Roosters pair Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter announcing their retirements.

Elliott and Baxter confirmed on Wednesday that this NRLW season would be their last, leaving the duo on track to go out with another premiership at the Roosters.

Elliott's decision to call it a day is a shock.

She is 28 and hopes to play for Australia at the end-of-year World Cup, but after having a child last year the front-rower wants to prioritise a growing family.

An emotional Baxter said on Thursday she had made the call after returning from last year's ACL rupture.

Corban Baxter was among the Roosters' foundation players. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The 32-year-old has still starred for the Roosters at fullback, but felt her body was finding it hard to keep up with the demands.

Both have been stars of the NRLW since its second season in 2019, with Baxter missing the opening four-week competition through a shoulder injury.

Elliott was the first player to win premierships at three clubs and has also had one of the loudest voices in the growth and direction of the competition.

"In a little while we'll look back and realise how significant this time was and the inception of the NRLW," Elliott said.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

"When the competition came in, let's be honest no-one really cared. I'm not sugarcoating it.

"But the fact we're sitting here in a press conference room, we've got State of Origin where we have millions of people tune in.

"We go to a footy game and people know who we are; that's just crazy."

Elliott won two premierships at Brisbane in 2019 and 2020, before taking a title at Newcastle in 2022 and another at the Roosters in 2024.

The Tri-colours are unbeaten this year, headed into the finals with their only defeat in the past two seasons coming in the 2025 decider against Brisbane.

She was the Roosters' captain for their premiership in 2021 and has set the culture for the club, now a powerhouse of the competition.

In a career halted at times by pregnancy and injury, the mother of three played her first of seven Tests for Australia in 2016 and also played in seven Origins for NSW.

"The Roosters are going to be strong for a very long time because of that foundation that we've built and I'm proud of that," she said.

"What I love is seeing the ones in our systems really thriving from playing football from a young age and coming through and playing with us now."

AAP

World.title: Renshaw reveals secret behind milestone ODI century
World.content:
Matt Renshaw admits he may not have posted his first ODI century had he opened the batting for Australia against Zimbabwe.

Batting at six, Renshaw starred for the tourists in Harare, making 109 off 94 deliveries, as Australia recorded a 59-run win in the first of three ODIs.

The ODI ton was his first for Australia across any format since his only Test century in 2017, when he opened the batting against Pakistan at the SCG.

He recently returned to the Test arena, after a three-year absence, and again opened the batting in Australia's innings victory over Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Aussies defeat Zimbabwe Matt Renshaw plays a starring role with the bat, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

But he played down the batting order in his nine ODI matches prior to Harare.

Renshaw said avoiding the pressure of opening the batting helped him score his century.

"Higher up the order I [get] a bit giddy,'' Renshaw said.

"For me, my tempo when I come in the middle overs is just trying to hit the gaps, hit where the fielders aren't.

"With spin being a very big factor in that middle period … I see it as my strength. I really understood my role. It made it really simple for me."

Renshaw was named in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming series against South Africa.

Australia will face the Proteas in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

The next ODI against Zimbabwe will be played on Friday in Harare.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Messi offered farewell by Argentina after international retirement
World.content:
Lionel Messi has been invited by Argentina to make a farewell appearance in ​a home friendly in October following his international retirement.

Messi, who led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title, announced his retirement from international matches earlier this month.

The 39-year-old has not confirmed whether he will join the team for the friendly in October.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

"We invited the ​best player in ‌the world to play, the icon of our selection, our captain Lionel Andres Messi, to have a deserved farewell … here in Argentina," Argentine Football Association president Claudio ⁠Tapia said on social media.

Argentina will play ‌three home friendlies during FIFA 's international window in September and October, which will be its first matches since the World Cup.

The Argentines will take on Benin in Buenos Aires's Monumental Stadium on October 7, AEST, ​where ‌Messi has been invited to ⁠play his farewell match.

Argentina ‌will also face Bolivia ‌in Córdoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires during the FIFA international window.

Three Argentine players — Leandro Paredes, Nahuel Molina and Thiago Almada — were recently handed bans by FIFA for a scuffle after losing the World Cup final to Spain in New Jersey in July.

Paredes received a 10-match ban.

Reuters

World.title: PGA Tour not considering return program for LIV Golf players
World.content:
The PGA Tour is not considering a returning-member program that would allow players from LIV Golf to return to the US-based circuit the way Brooks Koepka did in January.

Speaking one week after LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection ‌in New Jersey, PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp said accountability and discipline were essential elements for any sports league.

"In terms of where we are ‌today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one ⁠you saw in January," he said.

"Everyone at the PGA Tour, myself included, has been focused on what is best for the organisation."

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Rolapp added: "The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place."

LIV Golf's bankruptcy filing has left the playing futures of some of the breakaway circuit's biggest names in doubt.

Major ‌champions Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, two of the sport's more popular players, were listed as the top unsecured creditors, with each ⁠owed more than $US5 million.

Five-time major champion Koepka ‌took advantage of a limited-time ‌returning member program in January to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV ‌Golf last December.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the former world number one facing a five-year forfeiture of potential ‌equity in the PGA Tour's Player ⁠Equity Program, representing an estimated $US50-85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia owns 100 per cent of LIV Golf's equity, according to its bankruptcy petition.

LIV Golf hopes to exit from bankruptcy by early 2027.

Reuters

World.title: Sturt versus Norwood stirs up 1978 controversy ahead of SANFL final
World.content:
Football Park was barely four years old when Sturt and Norwood last met in a famous grand final that included a brief tussle between players and officials in the Sturt dug-out.

The Redlegs came away with a one-point win in 1978 despite Sturt being favoured, but with both teams meeting again for this weekend's SANFL Grand Final, there are several controversies that remain front of mind for some.

First and foremost, there was the winning goal.

After kicking 5:9 to Norwood's 1:5 in the first quarter, Sturt was in front and living up to expectations, having only lost one game for the entire season.

But, 29 points down in the last quarter, the Redlegs mounted a comeback, briefly taking the lead before Sturt kicked another goal.

"Then there was a rough contest in Norwood's forward pocket, and [Redleg] Phil Gallagher took it out of the ruck, quickly slammed it on his boot, and it went straight to Sturt fullback Colin Casey," said SANFL senior media producer Zac Millbank.

"He kicked it straight back out of the area and then Phil Gallagher went to mark Casey's kick, but he actually dropped it."

Field umpire Des Foster blew his whistle and gave what commentators at the time assumed to be a weak free kick to Gallagher.

Foster later said that he actually called it a mark but admitted it was the wrong call, explaining that his field of vision had been obscured by players at the key moment when the ball came down.

In front of more than 50,000 spectators and a live television audience, Gallagher went back and kicked a goal, putting Norwood in front.

Sturt's Lucas Slade and Norwood's Alex Wright will compete for the SANFL flag on Sunday. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

There were about three minutes left, however, and Sturt made several more 50-metre entries but only managed a point.

Mr Millbank pointed out that Sturt had kicked 14 goals and 25 points that day, so the upset loss could not be blamed on "the Des Foster blunder".

"Fourteen goals and 26 points is just horrendous kicking and some of the shots were very simple ones," he said.

Regardless, the moment went down in history as one of the most contentious free kicks or marks ever played at Football Park, the former stadium that was home to SA football between 1974 and 2013.

Mr Millbank said there had been a lot of commentary on the SANFL's social media pages about the 48-year-old moment since Sunday's match-up was confirmed, proving the incident was very much "still on people's minds".

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and Sturt captain Tom Lewis are playing for the cup on Sunday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt captain Tom Lewis said he was reminded about the 1978 final by a pedestrian walking past his house on Monday morning.

"He reminded me at about 7am how disappointed he was at that grand final and asked us to right a few wrongs," he said.

"Both clubs have such a history; it does bring a lot of excitement, a lot of pressure.

"I'm thoroughly looking forward to it, and the boys are. Everyone's amped up; I know Norwood are as well, so hopefully we get a good turnout."

A dug-out scuffle

Another memorable moment occurred in the third quarter in 1978 when Norwood player John Wynne overran the ball on the boundary and ended up inside the enemy's camp, much to his own apparent amusement.

A skirmish ensued, with more players and officials from the Redlegs getting involved, until umpires quelled the situation and broke the parties apart — even as strong words continued to fly.

"Legend has it that master [Sturt] coach Jack Oatey was a bit ruffled after that incident," Mr Millbank said.

"I don't know how true it is, but there's a bit of thought that Wynne did it deliberately to try and stir him up a bit, put them off their game."

Norwood took the 1978 premiership after a long period of SANFL dominance for Sturt, in which they had won five flags in a row from 1966 to 1970, and then in 1974 and 1976 as well.

The fact they had only dropped one game for the entire season — a feat Sturt repeated in 2025 before winning the premiership — had made them the "raging favourites".

For this year's grand final, however, the shoe is on the other foot, and Norwood are the warm favourites going into the game.

Norwood beat Sturt by 19 points during the second semi-final earlier this month. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

Having won the minor premiership and winning the second semi-final against Sturt two weeks ago, the team has only played one match in three weeks.

Coach Jade Sheedy said that after the team's main training session, they had another strong session on Saturday, "which put the boys through their paces and tried to replicate as much as we can to get them ready for a grand final," he said.

"Our preparation has been good … players are fresh."

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said it was always a big game when Sturt and Norwood met, "so to be able to play in a grand final against them is a bigger deal".

"You can certainly feel the anticipation living in the eastern suburbs and knowing that rivalry, the history, the '78 grand final was obviously huge," he said.

"I've heard a lot about that even though it was 48 years ago now. That famous Gallagher mark, my former number 11, so I know a lot about the history."

Digging deep for a repeat

Sturt, which finished third on the ladder, has played three finals to get to the big dance, and will defend their 2025 premiership with a slightly different list to Sunday's preliminary due to injuries.

This includes midfielder Jared Dakin, who injured his hamstring in the opening quarter against Woodville-West Torrens; key defender Casey Voss, who dislocated his shoulder in the game; and ruckman Amos Doyle, who was a late withdrawal due to a neck injury.

The Superjesus will play a set before the SANFL Grand Final at Adelaide Oval on Sunday. (@they.muse)

Coach Marty Mattner said Doyle had been progressing and may still play on Sunday, depending on Wednesday's training, and there was still a window open for Voss, although his inclusion is considered unlikely.

"The positive is that everyone who hasn't been playing in the league side is fit and ready to go," he said.

"Realistically there’s probably seven or eight in that [reserves] group who have played league footy this year."

The 2026 SANFL Grand Final, which will feature Adelaide rockers The Superjesus in pre-game entertainment, will commence at Adelaide Oval from 2:30pm Sunday.

World.title: Rush to put Zverev in Alcaraz-Sinner tier premature despite twin titles
World.content:
When the latest edition of the ATP singles rankings dropped earlier this week, a 24-year streak came to an end.

After being bounced in the first round of the US Open, Novak Djokovic dropped out of the top-10 for the first time since 2018.

Djokovic's exit marks the first time since October 2002 that neither he nor Rafael Nadal nor Roger Federer is inside the top-10.

For tennis fans who wondered when the 'Big 3' era in the men's game would end, the end is now.

Novak Djokovic's first-round exit at the US Open caused him to drop outside the top-10 for the first time since 2018. (Getty Images: Mike Stobe)

With the Djokovic-Federer-Nadal triumvirate dominating the men's game for so long, the question of who their successors would be has been a popular one around tennis.

Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz have emulated Federer and Nadal's rivalry from the mid-2000s, exchanging grand slam titles while playing some spellbinding epics along the way, but would any other men's players on tour join them as Djokovic joined Federer and Nadal?

Alexander Zverev appears to be the third member of the party, having claimed two of the four available grand slam titles this year.

But questions remain as to whether Zverev's candidacy to join the very top tier of men's tennis is legitimate.

Alexander Zverev wins US Open without realising it Alexander Zverev wins his second grand slam title of the year with a dominant victory over American Ben Shelton in the men's US Open final.

Since first achieving a top-10 ranking in May 2017 as a 20-year-old, Zverev has been one of the most consistent performers on the men's tour.

Zverev has spent 414 weeks as a top-10 ranked player throughout his career, currently 15th all-time. He ranks second among active players in this metric, behind only Djokovic, with 959 weeks, just behind Federer's 968.

At the time of writing, Zverev has spent 102 consecutive weeks ranked inside the top 10 since his most recent streak began in September 2023.

Those numbers are not the problem when it comes to Zverev's bid to be considered the best player in the world.

It is this one.

Career wins against top-10 ranked opponents Wins % Novak Djokovic 69 66 Roger Federer 64 62 Rafael Nadal 55 67 Carlos Alcaraz 16 70 Jannik Sinner 14 50 Alexander Zverev 5 22

Despite being a constant presence in the top-10 rankings over the best part of the last decade, Zverev has consistently struggled to beat the other players ranked in the same vicinity.

The German owns an unenviable 5-18 (21.7 per cent) win-loss record against fellow top-10 opponents in grand slam matches. He has won 59 of his 146 matches against top-10 opponents overall, roughly a 40 per cent conversion rate.

Zverev's record pales in comparison to Alcaraz and Sinner, as well as Djokovic, Federer and Nadal.

Alcaraz has an astounding 16-7 record against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with his 69.6 per cent conversion rate by far the best among the elite cohort, while Sinner has gone 14-14 in such matches.

Zverev has been beaten by Sinner (pictured) in two of his six grand slam final appearances. (Getty Images/Frey)

Nadal, Djokovic and Federer all won over 60 per cent of their matches against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with Djokovic's 69 wins leading the way.

This record against the very best players helped make Zverev a perennial grand slam semifinalist and finalist before he broke through with his first title at Roland-Garros earlier this year.

While Zverev now has two grand slam titles to his name, the calibre of opponents he has overcome suggests he hasn't really gone up a tier.

The German claimed the French Open title without facing a single top-10-ranked opponent, with the runner-up Flavio Cobolli the top-ranked player at No.14.

US Open finalist Ben Shelton is the only top-10 ranked opponent Zverev has beaten en route to his two grand slam titles this year. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

Overall, the average ranking of the players Zverev beat en-route to his first grand slam title is 57.7, with his fourth-round opponent, world No.106, Jesper de Jong the lowest-ranked.

Zverev had a slightly tougher run to the US Open title, but still faced just one top-10-ranked opponent in finalist Ben Shelton (eighth).

On average, Zverev's US Open opponents ranked 45th overall, with his first-round opponent, Lorenzo Sonego, the lowest-ranked at No.89.

Zverev's victories offer hope for the rest of the non-Alcaraz and Sinner division on the men's tour, including players such as Australia's Alex de Minaur.

De Minaur, like Zverev, has struggled against top-10 opponents at grand slams, winning just two of 14 matches.

Zverev's breakthroughs offer hope for the likes of Australia's Alex de Minaur (pictured). (AP: Christinne Muschi)

Despite reaching a career-high ranking of No.5 this year, de Minaur has yet to win a grand slam quarterfinal.

The Australian has a 0-7 record in quarters, with six of those losses coming over the last three seasons.

De Minaur has looked downtrodden after his recent grand slam exits, but will hope that like Zverev, he too can capitalise on the bracket breaking just right for him at some point down the line.

For now, Zverev looks to have graduated above the class featuring the likes of Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Felix Auger-Aliassime, de Minaur and others.

But for him to truly climb into the upper echelon of men's tennis, it is time he starts taking down the big names when it matters most.

World.title: Renshaw scores first ODI century as Aussies defeat Zimbabwe
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has scored his first ODI century, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

Australia chose to bat first, and the surprise decision from captain Mitchell Marsh was vindicated as ​the tourists scored 8-294 from ‌their 50 overs, setting Zimbabwe an imposing target at Harare Sports Club.

In reply, Zimbabwe was dismissed for 235 in 45.1 overs, showing good fight but always behind ‌the required run rate.

Renshaw, who last scored an international ton in ⁠a Test against Pakistan in 2017, made 109.

He featured ‌in some key partnerships, while Cooper ​Connolly made 51.

Renshaw put on 72 runs with Alex Carey for the fifth wicket and 75 with Ollie Peake for the sixth wicket, leaving Zimbabwe with a ​required ‌run rate of 5.90.

The 20-year-old left-arm quick Newman Nyamhuri finished with 5-62, only the second Zimbabwe bowler to take five wickets in ⁠an ODI against Australia.

Zimbabwe lost four ‌wickets quickly before Craig Ervine ‌and Sikandar steadied the innings with a 98-run partnership that offered the hosts hope ‌of victory on a surface that traditionally gets better for batting as the day wears on.

Ellis had taken two ‌wickets ​in his first spell and when he was reintroduced, took three balls to clean bowl Ervine for 59 and put the brakes on Zimbabwe.

Sikandar was dispensed by Spencer Johnson for 57 to leave Zimbabwe ⁠still significantly adrift.

Ellis finished with 5-31 in 9.1 overs, also cleaning up the tail.

The second ODI ‌will be played on ‌Friday in Harare, ​after which Australia moves to South Africa.

Reuters

Tech.title: The Boox Palma 3 gets stylus support and a sleek redesign
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Nearly two years after the last update to Boox’s smartphone-sized black-and-white e-reader, the company announced the Palma 3 with a sleek redesign, new functionality, and a handful of other small updates that may justify its significant price bump depending on how you plan to use it. While the Palma 2 launched in 2024 for $279.99, the Palma 3 will be $339.99 and is expected to be “available soon.”

The most obvious upgrade for the Palma 3 is the hardware itself. It still features the same 6.13-inch, 300ppi E Ink Carta screen as its predecessor (which is now quite a few years old), but it’s wrapped in a new anodized aluminum frame with a paperlike fiberglass backplate. The Palma 3 looks like a significant upgrade to the Palma line, even if under the hood you’ll find more of the same. The pocketable e-reader is powered by a Qualcomm Q-6690 octa-core processor with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage expandable with a microSD card. It also includes a 3950mAh rechargeable battery, a 16-megapixel camera on the back, and a fingerprint reader in the power button.

The original Palma and the Palma 2 came with Android 11 and Android 13, respectively, but the new Palma 3 ships with Android 16, which is just one generation behind the latest version of the OS. That should help it feel like a more modern mobile device. And like the color screen Palma 2 Pro, the Palma 3 supports the Boox InkSense Plus active stylus so you can use the e-reader as a digital notepad with your preferred note-taking app. But it’s not included. The stylus is an optional upgrade that will add another $46 to the cost of the Palma 3, pushing it closer to the price of premium e-notes like the Remarkable Paper Pure.

Tech.title: The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Canon announced the second-generation of its EOS R8 with a new retro-inspired redesign and the addition of in-body stabilization. That feature was one of the most notable omissions from the original R8 that launched in 2023 as a smaller, cheaper, and more accessible alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II for photographers wanting a larger full-frame shooter. While the new EOS R8 Mark II is slightly heavier than its predecessor at 1.2 pounds thanks to the additional stabilization functionality, it’s lighter and cheaper than last year’s EOS R6 Mark III.

The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is expected to be available sometime in late October for $1,899 for the body only, or $2,099 bundled with a Canon 24-50mm stabilized lens. That’s more expensive than the original R8 that launched at $1,499, but more accessible than the $2,799 EOS R6 Mark III thanks to some lower specs and omitted features.

Like its predecessor, the R8 Mark II features the same 24.2-megapixel full-frame CMOS sensor as the R6 Mark II, while the R6 Mark III got a bump to a 32.5-megapixel sensor. The new R8 Mark II still exclusively uses an electronic shutter instead of an additional mechanical one, with high-speed captures maxing out at 40fps again. To ensure you’re not too late to a critical moment, a pre-continuous shooting mode captures up to an additional 20 shots before you press the shutter button.

Image: Canon

The new five-axis in-body stabilization offers up to 7.5 stops of shake correction that can be expanded by pairing the camera with a lens featuring its own stabilization. The R8 Mark II also features Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS AF II system with what the company describes as “more tenacious tracking” than what the R8 offered. The autofocus system can also recognize animals, vehicles, and people, with the option to register up to 10 different people by their faces and rank their priority.

Video capabilities max out at 4K/60fps, but frame rates can be boosted to up to 180fps by dropping the resolution to 1080p. As Canon is targeting the R8 Mark II as a potential full-frame option for amateur photographers, the camera includes 16 different color filters, an easy to way to increase or decrease depth of blur that handles settings like f-stop and shutter speed automatically, and creative bracketing that takes three photos with different brightness and color tones.

Image: Canon

Following other companies drawing inspiration from older film cameras for the design of new digital shooters, the R8 Mark II eschews the curves of the original R8 for a more boxy and angular body. Canon credits the nearly 40-year-old EOS 650 and its pentaprism housing on top as the inspiration for the R8 Mark II. Other hardware upgrades include a new multi-controller joystick above the camera’s screen, which makes it easier to select focal points, and its single SD card slot repositioned on the side of the camera so it’s still accessible when using a tripod. Canon will also sell a matching $99.99 accessory that extends the R8 Mark II’s grip, making it easier to hold when using larger lenses.

In October Canon is also releasing a free new Windows app called Dual Pixel 3D Converter that leverages additional info captured by Canon’s dual-pixel autofocus system to generate 3D imagery from the 2D photos the camera takes. You can use the app to create a 3D photo with a background you can move around, a 3D model with the background completely removed, or short 3D videos demonstrating an animated perspective adjustment of close-up subjects.

Tech.title: AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular in every poll
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Poll data released Tuesday by the New York Times and Siena University confirms what we’ve already been seeing, and what politicians are responding to — AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular. Asked if they support or oppose the construction of data centers to power AI tech, 61 percent of the 1,503 likely voters surveyed in early September (ahead of the recent AI safety slowdown discussion) said they were opposed, with only 14 percent saying they strongly support. The split was about even among 2024 Donald Trump voters, at 49 percent support to 45 percent oppose, while people who had voted for Kamala Harris or who didn’t vote leaned oppose, at 74 percent and 67 percent, respectively.

56 percent of voters surveyed who said they were opposed to data centers said they supported limits, while 38 percent instead preferred a total ban. The list of reasons for opposition is also revealing, with the environment/water usage most common at 32 percent, impact on local communities at 21 percent, general distrust or dislike of AI at 18 percent, followed by regulation concerns and the economy at 10 and 9 percent.

An NBC News poll in March showed AI polling lower than ICE, and a Gallup poll in May revealed seven in ten Americans opposed local construction of AI data centers.

Still, the data released today ranked AI and data centers low on the list of issues that voters saw as most important in deciding their midterm vote. Across the board, AI and data centers registered at less than one percent for most demographics, with exceptions for younger voters like the 18-29 group, where three percent picked that one instead of the most popular responses like the economy, foreign policy, inflation, and opposition to Trump/Republicans. Voters in either party still overwhelmingly picked their own party as the one they trusted to handle the issue, while overall the 554 respondents had 40 percent favoring Democrats, 42 percent favoring Republicans, and 18 percent saying they didn’t know or refused.

Tech.title: Microsoft announces Windows and Surface event for October 7th
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s been more than two years since the last major Windows event, so Microsoft is heading to San Francisco next month to outline the future of Windows and Surface devices. At an event on October 7th, the company says it will host a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.”

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be in attendance, alongside Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri. Even Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will be appearing at the event, which suggests that RTX Spark PCs could be the main focus of this event. If that’s the case, don’t be surprised to hear more about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra pricing and availability.

Microsoft’s event invite. Image: Microsoft

I am also expecting Microsoft to focus on its quality improvements to Windows, and what’s coming next. I am not expecting a surprise announce of Windows 12, though.

Microsoft last held a major Windows event in May 2024, to unveil new Arm-based Copilot Plus PCs and its renewed partnership with Qualcomm. The last major Windows event before that was in June 2021, when Microsoft announced Windows 11 during a live stream.

The Verge will be covering Microsoft’s Windows event next month live from San Francisco on October 7th at 10AM PT / 1PM ET.

Tech.title: What if social media isn’t hurting kids?
Tech.content:
Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis.

Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is.

In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves.

“You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy”

In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says.

Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.”

Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization.

Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.”

Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.”

“We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots”

Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.”

But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution.

With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

Tech.title: Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.

One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.

All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!

Previous Next







1 / 5

The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.

Previous Next









1 / 6

This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.

While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”

PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.

I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.

Tech.title: One of the best 3D printers for beginners is almost $100 off
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If the high price tag of premium 3D printers have kept you from exploring the hobby, this deal is a great entry point. Elegoo has its Centauri Carbon 2 Combo on sale for $369, almost $100 off its usual price of $449. It’s altogether very capable 3D printer for beginners, or just anyone who doesn’t want to spend a lot of time tinkering with settings just to print occasional trinkets and brackets.

The Centauri Carbon 2 is fast and capable right out of the box, though first-time setup is a little involved (I found it tough to get the upper shield and filament hub to fit together, for example).
